AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on utility scale wind towers (wind towers) from Malaysia would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of countervailable subsidies at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Review” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Connor Field, Office V, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-3997.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 4, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the CVD order on wind towers from Malaysia.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce published the notice of initiation of the first sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act) and 19 CFR 351.218(c).[2]
On July 17, 2026, Commerce received a notice of intent to participate in this review from the domestic interested party, within the deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The domestic interested party claimed interested party status under sections 771(9)(C) and (F) of the Act as a U.S. producer and as a coalition consisting of a U.S. producer of the domestic like product.[4]
On August 3, 2026, Commerce received an adequate substantive response from the domestic interested party within the 30-day deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i).[5]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from either the Government of Malaysia or any other respondent interested party to this proceeding. On August 24, 2026, Commerce notified the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that it did not receive an adequate substantive response from respondent interested parties.[6]
As a result, Commerce conducted an expedited (120-day) sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(B)(2) and (C)(2).
Scope of the Order
The products covered by the
Order
are utility scale wind towers. For a full description of the scope,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[7]
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in this sunset review, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of subsidization and the
( printed page 68494)
countervailable subsidy rates likely to prevail if the
Order
were to be revoked, is contained in the accompanying Issues and Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached as an appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Final Results of Sunset Review
Pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(b) of the Act, Commerce determines that revocation of the
Order
would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of countervailable subsidies at the following net countervailable subsidy rates:

articles.title: “China Leans on Exports as the EU Raises Its Defenses”: Trade Tensions Escalate, Fueling Calls for Tougher Measures Including a European Version of Section 301 - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “China Leans on Exports as the EU Raises Its Defenses”: Trade Tensions Escalate, Fueling Calls for Tougher Measures Including a European Version of Section 301  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
EU-China trade tensions deepen, spreading to chemicals
Germany and France urge a European version of Section 301 modeled on the U.S. framework
China’s drive to offload excess output abroad compounds Europe’s economic strain, threatening industrial competitiveness
China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into chemicals imported from the European Union (EU). The move follows a series of recent EU trade remedy actions against Chinese chemicals, prompting Beijing to respond in kind. Market observers expect the trade dispute between the two sides could become structurally entrenched and protracted. China’s growing dependence on exports is colliding directly with mounting European concerns over its trade deficit with China and weakening manufacturing competitiveness.
EU and China Exchange Trade Remedy Actions
According to a report by China’s state-run Xinhua News Agency on October 3, with all dates given in local time, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced that day that it had opened an anti-dumping investigation into para-nitrotoluene imported from the EU. Also known as p-nitrotoluene, the substance is a chemical intermediate used in the production of dyes, pharmaceuticals and pesticides. The ministry said the investigation followed a complaint by Chinese para-nitrotoluene producers and was based on preliminary evidence that EU products were being imported at dumped prices, causing injury to domestic producers. Industry data show that prices of EU-origin para-nitrotoluene fell by approximately 60% cumulatively between 2022 and 2025. The ministry’s investigation covers alleged dumping from July last year through June this year and is scheduled to conclude in October next year.
The investigation is widely interpreted as a response to recent EU trade remedy actions. The European Commission opened three anti-dumping investigations last month into chemical products, including imports from China. The products under investigation are polyvinyl chloride (PVC), acetylsalicylic acid and cellulose ethers. Specifically, on September 23, the Commission launched separate investigations into certain PVC imports from China, South Korea, Mexico and Taiwan, and into acetylsalicylic acid from China. On September 24, it opened another investigation into cellulose ethers from China and South Korea. The EU cited industry complaints alleging that these products were entering the bloc’s market at dumped prices and causing injury to European producers.
The Tariff War Between the Two Sides
This is not the first exchange of trade restrictions between the EU and China. In September 2023, for example, the EU announced plans for an anti-subsidy investigation, arguing that low-priced electric vehicles benefiting from Chinese government subsidies were distorting the European market. In October that year, it formally launched an investigation on its own initiative into battery electric vehicles (BEVs) from China. The EU subsequently introduced provisional countervailing duties in July 2024, completed the investigation in October that year and imposed definitive countervailing duties for five years. The final rates included 17.0% for BYD, 18.8% for Geely and 35.3% for SAIC, while Tesla’s China-made vehicles were subject to a rate of 7.8%. These duties are levied in addition to the EU’s existing 10% tariff on cars.
China responded by expanding trade remedy investigations into EU products. In January 2024, China’s Ministry of Commerce launched an anti-dumping investigation into EU brandy, including French cognac. In June that year, it opened an anti-dumping investigation into EU pork and pig by-products, followed in August by an anti-subsidy investigation into certain EU dairy products, including cheese and cream. China subsequently introduced provisional anti-dumping measures in October 2024 requiring deposits of 30.6–39.0% on EU brandy, before issuing a final determination and confirming anti-dumping measures in July last year. EU pork was also subjected to provisional anti-dumping measures of 15.6–62.4% in September last year, followed by a final decision in December to impose anti-dumping duties of 4.9–19.8%. Certain EU dairy products likewise became subject to countervailing duties of 7.4–11.7% for five years following the conclusion of the anti-subsidy investigation this February.
A Head-On Clash in Public Procurement
EU-China trade tensions have also been pronounced in public procurement. In April 2024, the Commission launched an investigation on its own initiative into China’s public procurement market for medical devices. It cited practices by the Chinese government and public institutions that encouraged purchases of domestically produced equipment or imposed unfavorable conditions on imported products during tendering, restricting European companies’ market access. According to findings released by the Commission in January last year, approximately 87% of the Chinese medical device procurement tenders examined contained conditions excluding or discriminating against imported equipment. The EU said consultations with China had failed to produce an agreement on opening the market and finalized restrictions in June last year. As a result, Chinese companies were generally barred from bidding for EU medical device procurement contracts worth approximately $5.60 million or more. Even where a non-Chinese company won a contract, medical devices originating in China could account for no more than 50% of its total value.
China’s Ministry of Finance retaliated by excluding EU companies from medical device government procurement projects with budgets of approximately $6.71 million or more from July last year. EU companies are excluded from bidding for these projects regardless of their products’ origin, while medical devices imported from the EU must account for less than 50% of the contract value when a non-EU company submits a bid. However, European-owned companies manufacturing products locally in China were exempted from the restrictions, as were cases in which only EU products could meet procurement requirements. China’s Ministry of Commerce publicly described the policy as a “reciprocal restrictive measure” responding to the EU’s medical device procurement restrictions.
Table 1. Key Fronts in the EU-China Trade Dispute
| Sector | EU Measures | China’s Response | 
|---|---|---|
| Chemicals | Launched anti-dumping investigations into Chinese polyvinyl chloride, acetylsalicylic acid, cellulose ethers and other products | Launched an anti-dumping investigation into EU-origin para-nitrotoluene | 
| Automobiles and Agricultural Products | Imposed definitive countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles | Imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties on EU brandy, pork and dairy products | 
| Medical Device Procurement | Restricted Chinese companies’ participation and the share of Chinese-origin products in public procurement contracts above a specified threshold | Restricted EU companies’ participation in major government procurement projects and the share of European-origin products | 
| Trade Policy Framework | France and Germany proposed a European version of Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act to respond swiftly to structurally unfair trade practices | Opposed the proposal as unilateralist and protectionist | 
Calls for a Tougher European Response
As the trade dispute drags on, Europe has recently stepped up efforts to counter China. On October 5, for example, Germany and France released a joint non-paper on responding to the expansion of low-priced Chinese exports and supply chain dependence. They urged the Commission to develop a new instrument capable of restricting third countries’ access to the single market more swiftly and forcefully than existing trade remedy mechanisms. Although the document did not explicitly name any country, it identified an oversupply of Chinese products and heavy dependence on critical raw materials and components as central concerns, leading observers to view the proposal as effectively targeting China.
The framework under discussion resembles Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act. Section 301 authorizes the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate unfair or discriminatory trade practices by foreign governments and, at the president’s direction, take action such as imposing tariffs or restricting market access. The so-called “European Section 301” envisaged by France and Germany similarly focuses on enabling the EU to act swiftly against broader structural issues, including Chinese industrial subsidies and restricted market access, rather than conducting separate anti-dumping or anti-subsidy investigations into individual products. China, however, has warned that the proposal is unilateralist and protectionist and could undermine China-EU trade and the stability of global supply chains.
The Heavy Economic Toll of the China Shock
Behind the escalating trade confrontation lies China’s deepening dependence on exports. As the property downturn erodes household wealth and domestic demand while deflationary pressures persist, the Chinese government is sustaining economic growth by expanding manufacturing output and exports. According to Bloomberg’s calculations published on September 30, based on data from China’s General Administration of Customs, Chinese exports totaled $2.92 trillion in the first eight months of this year. If that growth trajectory continues, annual exports are projected to reach $4.48 trillion, approximately 80% above their 2019 level.
China’s export strategy has dealt a direct blow to Europe. Eurostat data show that last year the EU exported approximately $223.63 billion in goods to China and imported approximately $626.75 billion, leaving a trade deficit of approximately $403.12 billion. Meanwhile, European manufacturing is steadily losing market share and seeing its production base weaken. In an analysis published last month, Bloomberg Economics e

articles.title: Malaysia’s exports to US surge 69.1% to RM282b despite tariff pressures - Newswav
articles.summary: Malaysia’s exports to US surge 69.1% to RM282b despite tariff pressures  Newswav
articles.full_text:
PETALING JAYA: Malaysia’s exports to the United States surged 69.1% to RM282.07 billion in the first nine months of 2026, driven by strong semiconductor demand despite US tariffs putting pressure on several local industries.
The Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry (MITI) said total trade between Malaysia and the US rose 39.6% to RM378.70 billion from January to September, largely driven by the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres.
“The strong export performance was driven mainly by a surge in demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following the rapid development of AI technology and data centres,” it said in a written reply to the Dewan Rakyat.
MITI was responding to Amirudin Shari (Gombak-PH), who asked about the impact of US tariffs on Malaysian industries in 2026 and the alternative markets the government was exploring to help local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) export their products.
The ministry said Malaysia’s strategic advantage in securing exemptions from additional US tariffs on most semiconductor and E&E products had also supported export growth.
“The E&E sector accounted for about 64.2% of Malaysia’s total exports to the US, with semiconductors making up 44% of E&E exports.
“However, exports of rubber gloves to the US fell 1.6% to RM5 billion, furniture exports dropped 19.2% to RM3.77 billion, and medical device exports declined 12% to RM8.74 billion amid tariff pressures,” it said.
MITI said these sectors were among those examined because the US accounted for between 32% and 47% of Malaysia’s total exports of the respective products, which were subject to additional tariffs and were not covered by tariff exemptions.
“This shows that although overall exports to the US continued to record positive growth, several key Malaysian industries faced pressure to absorb US tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to remain competitive, sustain exports and maintain access to the US market,” it said.
To mitigate these risks, the government was diversifying export destinations through free trade agreements (FTAs) and exploring non-traditional markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
MITI added that the strategy had yielded encouraging results, with exports of products affected by US tariffs recording growth in several alternative markets between January and September 2026.
“Rubber glove exports rose 712% to Oman, 84.6% to Brazil, 80.8% to Sweden, 48.1% to Denmark, 43.7% to the Netherlands, 34% to Estonia and 18.4% to Canada.
“Medical device exports increased 206% to South Korea, 74.9% to Singapore, 65% to Sweden, 59.1% to Brazil, 43.9% to Turkiye, 26.6% to Canada and 5% to the United Kingdom.
“Meanwhile, furniture exports surged 586.1% to Guyana, 140% to Taiwan, 135.4% to Switzerland, 99% to Vietnam and 68.3% to New Zealand,” it said.
MITI said the government was also supporting local industries, particularly MSMEs, through grants, targeted incentives, and participation in trade and investment promotion missions to strengthen their export capabilities.
“Diversifying markets and reducing excessive dependence on any single market is the best approach to minimise exposure to external shocks and strengthen the resilience of the country’s trade.”
The ministry added that it would continue monitoring developments in US trade policy and taking proactive measures to safeguard Malaysian exporters, maintain market access, diversify export destinations and strengthen the competitiveness of domestic industries.

articles.title: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari - NST Online
articles.summary: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari  NST Online
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's exports to the United States surged 69.1 per cent to RM282.07 billion in the first nine months of this year, despite additional US tariffs on some Malaysian goods.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said total trade between Malaysia and the US rose 39.6 per cent to RM378.70 billion from January to September.
"This strong export performance was driven mainly by a surge in demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres," Johari said in a written parliamentary reply.
He was responding to Amirudin Shari (PH-Gombak), who asked about the impact of US tariffs on Malaysian industries this year and efforts to identify new markets for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
Johari said Malaysia had also benefited from an exemption from additional US tariffs on most semiconductor and E&E products.
What To Read Next
"This decision by the US underscores the reliance of the US supply chain on the E&E sector."
The E&E sector accounts for about 64.2 per cent of Malaysia's exports to the US, with semiconductors making up 44 per cent of E&E exports.
Johari said the ministry had identified products heavily reliant on the US market that were subject to additional tariffs and did not qualify for exemptions.
The US accounts for about 32 to 47 per cent of Malaysia's exports of rubber gloves, furniture and medical devices.
Exports of rubber gloves to the US fell 1.6 per cent to RM5 billion from RM5.1 billion a year earlier.
Furniture exports declined 19.2 per cent to RM3.77 billion from RM4.67 billion, while medical device exports dropped 12 per cent to RM8.74 billion from RM9.93 billion.
He said some key industries had come under pressure to absorb additional tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to remain competitive and retain access to the US market.
Diversifying export destinations and reducing reliance on any single market remained the best way to limit exposure to external shocks, he said.
The ministry was pursuing free trade agreements and exploring non-traditional markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
It was also supporting SMEs through grants, incentives and trade and investment missions.
Malaysia's rubber glove exports recorded growth in several non-traditional markets, including Oman (712 per cent), Brazil (84.6 per cent), Sweden (80.8 per cent), Denmark (48.1 per cent), the Netherlands (43.7 per cent), Estonia (34 per cent) and Canada (18.4 per cent).
Medical device exports also increased in South Korea (206 per cent), Singapore (74.9 per cent), Sweden (65 per cent), Brazil (59.1 per cent), Türkiye (43.9 per cent), Canada (26.6 per cent) and the United Kingdom (5 per cent).
Furniture exports rose sharply in Guyana (586.1 per cent), Taiwan (140 per cent), Switzerland (135.4 per cent), Vietnam (99 per cent) and New Zealand (68.3 per cent).
Johari said the ministry would keep monitoring US trade policy and act proactively to protect exporters and reduce the tariff impact on SMEs.
The US imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on nearly all Malaysian exports on July 24 after a Section 301 investigation into forced-labour allegations.
Tariff rates from a separate US probe into industrial excess capacity have yet to be determined.

India’s emerging industrial policy for critical minerals value chains entails more than a dozen regulatory, financial, and trade instruments worth nearly $40 billion, as part of a broader industrialization agenda.
The combination of three features distinguishes India’s critical minerals industrial strategy from other lower- and middle-income countries. First, the government is actively supporting multiple stages of the value chain, not only mining. Second, complementary policies, such as manufacturing incentives and consumer subsidies, stimulate domestic demand for critical minerals. Third, India is pursuing measures to secure mineral supplies from abroad, given its heavy import dependence.
But the success of India’s industrial policy will also depend on addressing transnational coordination challenges, both with mineral-rich developing economies seeking to build their own productive capabilities and with advanced economies furthering mineral security and manufacturing goals.
India could address these transnational challenges by positioning itself as a “third way” within the global critical minerals industrial ecosystem, distinct from both China’s state-capital-intensive model and Western security-led strategies. Drawing on its market scale, manufacturing capabilities, and engineering expertise, India could act as an industrial bridge that supports value addition in developing economies and diversification of critical mineral supply for advanced economies.
1. Introduction
India is rapidly developing a more coordinated industrial policy for critical minerals. In 2023, the Ministry of Mines identified 30 minerals as critical to the Indian economy based on their economic importance and supply risk.[i] The following year, the Union Budget proposed a Critical Minerals Mission among its manufacturing and services priorities for “Viksit Bharat”, India’s broader ambition to become a developed economy by 2047.[ii] The National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), followed in January 2025, establishing the government’s principal framework for securing critical mineral supplies and developing domestic capabilities across the value chain,[iii] with the stated objective of establishing a “globally competitive and resilient critical mineral ecosystem.”[iv]
Three features of India’s critical minerals strategy distinguish it from other low- and middle-income countries’ efforts. First, the government is intervening across multiple stages of the value chain rather than concentrating principally on mineral extraction. Second, these interventions are reinforced by policies outside the mining sector that stimulate domestic demand for mineral-intensive technologies, including manufacturing incentives for batteries, rare-earth magnets, solar photovoltaics, and semiconductors, as well as consumer subsidies for electric vehicles and rooftop solar. Third, India is simultaneously pursuing measures to secure mineral inputs from abroad.
Successfully implementing such an ambitious industrial policy is fraught with various fiscal, institutional, and technological challenges. But the need to secure imported inputs to feed a robust critical minerals industry—India depends on mineral resources, technologies, and finance from abroad—places a significant constraint on what domestic policy alone can accomplish.
The effectiveness of India’s critical minerals industrial policy, therefore, is contingent in large part on how it manages two transnational coordination complexities. The first concerns resource-rich producer countries that increasingly seek to expand their own processing, refining, and manufacturing capabilities rather than remain suppliers of raw materials. The second concerns India’s relationships with high-income partners whose interests in diversifying critical mineral supply chains align with India’s, but whose mineral security strategies increasingly favor stricter trade and investment regimes that retain manufacturing within their own economies.
This commentary first examines Indian policies for building out its critical minerals industry before assessing transnational constraints that would need to be addressed to reach its goals. The authors propose that India could articulate a clearer vision of itself as a “third way” within the global critical minerals industrial ecosystem that neither replicates China’s state-capital-intensive model nor simply integrates into Western security-led supply chains. In this role, India could function as an industrial bridge—using joint ventures, long-term offtake arrangements, technology and skills partnerships, and selective co-investment—to build mutually reinforcing value chains across low- and middle-income producer countries and advanced-economy partners.
2. Distinct Features of India’s Critical Minerals Industrial Policy
The NCMM is the organizing framework for India’s critical minerals industrial policy, but the strategy extends beyond the mission itself. In terms of budget, NCMM provides $1.7 billion (₹16,300 crore) in direct support and anticipates a further $1.88 billion (₹18,000 crore) in investments by public-sector undertakings (PSUs) through FY2030–31.[v] When combined with complementary policies by other ministries and departments, the announced financial outlays reach nearly $40 billion (see the appendix for a breakdown of policies). A review of government documents and announcements around these policies reveals three distinctive features of India’s strategy.
A Holistic Approach to Building Mineral Value Chains
First, India is intervening across multiple stages of the critical minerals value chain rather than focusing principally on extraction. The NCMM’s objectives encompass mineral exploration, mining, beneficiation, and recycling alongside technology development, skills, and financing.[vi] There are regulatory reforms to facilitate domestic exploration by opening up a formerly restricted group of commodities to private and foreign investment, the auctioning of exploration licenses, and the approval of 100 percent foreign direct investment (FDI) in exploration and mining activity. These are accompanied by fiscal measures for building various midstream capabilities, including support for domestic and international collaborative R&D, establishment of critical mineral processing parks, and funding a National Critical Minerals Stockpile for at least five commodities by 2031. The Science and Technology Programme for Promoting Research and Innovation in Startups and MSMEs (micro, small, and medium enterprises) (S&T PRISM) initiative pre-dates the NCMM, and funds start-ups working on commercializing technologies in mineral processing, metallurgy, and recycling. Finally, a set of regulations target the recovery of critical minerals from solar PV modules, batteries, and other electronics. Together, these interventions aim to create productive capabilities across upstream, midstream, and downstream segments of the mining value chain.
Complementary Policies to Spur Domestic Demand
India’s critical minerals strategy extends to industrial policy tools that generate domestic demand in industries that use minerals as inputs.
Manufacturing incentives through the Production Linked Incentive Scheme deliver payments tied to quantitative metrics for sales, outputs, and domestic value addition (DVA) requirements for firms. Three of the schemes outlined in the appendix are specific to critical minerals (advanced chemistry cells [ACC], sintered rare earth permanent magnets, and critical mineral recycling), whereas the other schemes target the downstream users of these commodities (solar PV and semiconductors). articles.title: How India's Auto Component Industry Is Capitalizing on Global Supply Chain Shifts - Siliconindia
articles.summary: How India's Auto Component Industry Is Capitalizing on Global Supply Chain Shifts  Siliconindia
articles.full_text:
Global automakers are recalibrating their sourcing strategies to mitigate geopolitical exposure, diversify supplier concentration, and optimize total procurement costs. For India's auto component industry, this realignment creates an opportunity to capture a larger share of global automotive value chains. However, translating sourcing diversification into sustainable export growth requires more than cost competitiveness. Manufacturers must demonstrate production scalability, engineering depth, quality consistency, and the ability to support original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) across the entire product lifecycle.
India's auto component exports nearly doubled from $8.2 billion in 2015 to $16.9 billion in 2024, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 7%, compared with 3% growth in global demand for the component categories examined by NITI Aayog. Yet India's share of this market remained around 2%, highlighting the gap between export expansion and deeper integration into global automotive supply chains.
The commercial imperative is to move beyond opportunistic order acquisition toward recurring contracts, higher-value manufacturing, and long-term integration into international production programs. This requires Indian suppliers to compete not only on manufacturing costs but also on total cost of ownership (TCO), process capability, supply chain resilience, and customer responsiveness.
Global Sourcing Realignment Is Reshaping Procurement Economics
Global automotive manufacturers are increasingly evaluating supplier diversification as a strategic risk-management measure rather than a straightforward cost-arbitrage exercise. Geopolitical uncertainty, trade restrictions, logistics disruptions, and concentrated sourcing of critical inputs have exposed the operational and financial consequences of supply chain vulnerabilities.
For Indian manufacturers, this creates an opportunity to enter approved vendor networks, qualify as alternative suppliers, and secure contracts previously concentrated in established manufacturing hubs. However, supplier diversification does not automatically translate into order allocation. OEMs must assess production readiness, technical compliance, financial stability, and the supplier's ability to meet contractual delivery commitments.
The supplier qualification process can involve factory audits, product validation, production process approvals, and customer-specific quality assessments. These requirements create switching costs for automakers and extend the time between initial sourcing discussions and commercial production.
Consequently, the most attractive opportunities are likely to emerge where Indian suppliers can demonstrate a credible combination of cost competitiveness, manufacturing capability, and supply continuity. A lower quoted price may secure an initial evaluation, but sustained business depends on competitive landed costs, reliable delivery, and consistent performance throughout the contract lifecycle.
For suppliers, the strategic objective is to become a qualified alternative source and subsequently expand their share of customer procurement across additional components and vehicle platforms.
Also Read: How Rising Chip Prices Are Putting India's Electronics Manufacturing Boom to the Test
Segment-Level Opportunities Reveal Where India Has an Advantage
India's strongest export opportunities are not distributed evenly across the component industry. NITI Aayog's analysis of 2024 trade data identifies motorcycle and bicycle parts, pneumatic tires, diesel engines, and engine parts as categories where India has established comparatively stronger positions in global trade.
India accounted for approximately 4.5% of global exports of motorcycle and bicycle parts, 2.9% of new pneumatic tires, 2.7% of diesel engines, and 2.2% of engine parts. Its share of global vehicle-parts exports also increased from 1.1% in 2015 to 1.7% in 2024.
These figures indicate distinct commercial opportunities. Motorcycle components benefit from India's established two-wheeler manufacturing ecosystem, while tires and engine components offer a foundation for expanding existing international customer relationships. Vehicle parts represent a substantially larger addressable market, but competing for a greater share requires stronger capabilities in precision manufacturing, validation, and complex component engineering.
Electrification introduces another growth avenue through motor housings, thermal-management systems, electrical assemblies, and precision-engineered structural components.
However, suppliers must assess the capital expenditure (CAPEX), qualification requirements, and customer demand associated with these segments before committing to new production capabilities.
	The strategic priority is to move up the value chain through targeted product diversification rather than pursuing emerging technologies without a commercially viable route to market.

articles.title: U.S. Bans Imports From China's BGI Over Forced Labor - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: U.S. Bans Imports From China's BGI Over Forced Labor  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
The United States has blocked imports from a Chinese genomics company on forced-labor grounds for the first time.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a Federal Register notice published on the 28th that it had added Chinese genomics firm BGI Group, its listed subsidiary BGI Genomics and spinoff MGI Tech to the entity list under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), Bloomberg reported on the 29th. Products from the three companies are presumed to be made with forced labor and cannot enter the U.S. unless importers prove otherwise.
The department said the companies "conducted genetic testing in cooperation with authorities in China's Xinjiang region and enabled the surveillance, monitoring and repression of ethnic minorities by the government of the People's Republic of China, as well as abhorrent forced labor practices." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement that the action is about enforcing U.S. law and protecting American companies from unfair competition, and about making clear that companies tied to forced labor will not get a pass in the country. The department described the three firms collectively as among the world's largest companies engaged in advanced genetic analysis and the collection of genetic material.
The three companies are already on other blacklists that restrict their access to U.S. technology and government procurement. MGI builds gene sequencers and supplies them to researchers, biotech firms and hospitals, while BGI Genomics sells genetic analysis products and services and runs a medical diagnostics business. The import ban, however, is seen as the most powerful tool for shutting down a business. The UFLPA list, created by law in 2021, now covers 190 companies, and none has yet met the legal standard of proving its goods were not made with forced labor to resume exports to the U.S.
BGI Group and MGI Tech denied the allegations and said they respect internationally recognized human rights and labor standards. BGI said it would communicate actively with the relevant authorities and take appropriate steps as needed, while MGI Tech said it would file an objection and seek removal from the list.
China said the U.S. action had no factual basis and demanded that Washington stop its attacks and smears. It also said it would take necessary steps to defend the interests of its companies. Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the U.S. measure had seriously damaged the legitimate rights and interests of the Chinese companies involved and significantly disrupted the stability of global industrial and supply chains. Last year China placed U.S.-based Illumina, an MGI competitor, on its unreliable entity list and barred it from selling sequencing equipment, and in July it began imposing sanctions on six American companies.
Kit Conklin, chief strategy and global officer at supply-chain artificial intelligence firm Exiger, predicted that more federal restrictions on Chinese biotech companies could follow. Because the forced labor law only blocks imports, he said, the administration is likely to use other tools aimed at activities such as clinical trials, testing and modeling.

articles.title: US Adds Three Chinese Genomics Companies to Forced Labor Import Restrictions - Clinical Lab Products
articles.summary: US Adds Three Chinese Genomics Companies to Forced Labor Import Restrictions  Clinical Lab Products
articles.full_text:
The restrictions took effect Oct 29, limiting US imports of goods produced by BGI Genomics, MGI Tech, and BGI Group over alleged ties to forced labor in China.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has added three Chinese genomics companies—BGI Genomics Co, MGI Tech Co, and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co—to a federal list restricting imports over alleged ties to forced labor in China’s Xinjiang region.
The designation, published in the Federal Register and effective Oct 29, subjects goods produced wholly or in part by the companies to a presumption that they were made with forced labor, barring their import into the US unless that presumption is successfully rebutted. The companies provide genomic sequencing technologies, laboratory instruments, reagents, and genetic testing services.
With the addition of these three companies, the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List now includes 190 organizations.
Findings on Genetic Testing and Sourcing
According to federal officials, the US government determined there was reasonable cause to believe, based on specific and articulable information, that all three entities participated in government initiatives involving genetic testing in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR). Federal authorities stated that these testing activities facilitated the recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring, or receiving of forced labor or persecuted groups out of Xinjiang, placing all three on the UFLPA Section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii) list.
Specifically, the notice details distinct roles for each entity:
- MGI Tech Co: Located in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, MGI focuses on the research, development, manufacturing, and sales of instruments, reagents, and related products in life science and biotechnology. DHS stated that MGI provisioned genetic testing capacity to the Xinjiang government to conduct testing connected to regional labor schemes.
- BGI Genomics Co: Operating in Shenzhen, BGI Genomics provides research services, precision medicine solutions, and health management services through gene testing, mass spectrometry, bioinformatics analysis, and multimodal intelligent analysis models. Alongside the Section 2(d)(2)(B)(ii) designation, the company was added under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(v) for sourcing genetic material of plants, animals, and bacterial diseases from the XUAR.
- Shenzhen BGI Technology Co: Also known as BGI Group and BGI Holdings, the company is the controlling shareholder of BGI Genomics and supplies DNA, RNA, and metabolomics sequencing technologies, equipment, technical support, and precision medicine and health solutions, while managing the China National GeneBank repository. In addition to testing alongside regional authorities, the group was listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(v) for sourcing human genetic material from Xinjiang.
Although separately listed, the three companies have corporate ties. MGI Tech, a former BGI subsidiary that went public in 2022, shares an ultimate controlling shareholder with Shenzhen BGI Technology, according to DHS.
Implications for Clinical Laboratories and Supply Chains
The restrictions could affect US clinical laboratories, sequencing facilities, and diagnostic developers that rely on imported equipment and supplies produced by BGI Group, MGI Tech, or the other listed entity.
Under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, US Customs and Border Protection applies a rebuttable presumption that goods produced wholly or in part by listed entities were made with forced labor and are prohibited from entering the US. Importers may seek an exception by providing clear and convincing evidence that the goods were not produced with forced labor.
Listed companies may request removal from the UFLPA Entity List by submitting supporting documentation to the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force chair demonstrating that they do not or no longer meet the listing criteria. Removal requires a majority vote of Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force member agencies. Although the task force’s decision cannot be appealed, companies may submit new removal requests with additional information.

articles.title: Colombia Targets Shein, Temu, and Amazon in New Tax Plan - ColombiaOne.com
articles.summary: Colombia Targets Shein, Temu, and Amazon in New Tax Plan  ColombiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
Colombia’s government plans to review taxes on international shopping platforms to protect local businesses, but the proposed changes have yet to be detailed.
Colombia is preparing to tighten its tax rules for international e-commerce platforms such as Shein, Temu, and Amazon, in a move aimed at reducing what the government considers an unfair competitive advantage over local merchants.
Mauricio Gomez Amin, Colombia’s Minister of Commerce, Industry and Tourism, announced that the proposed controls would be addressed through the upcoming Fiscal Adjustment Law, which the government plans to submit to Congress in the coming days.
Speaking at the Gondola 2026 retail industry event organized by Fenalco, Colombia’s national federation of merchants, the minister argued that domestic businesses face a heavier financial burden because they must pay taxes, rent and other operating expenses while competing with international platforms.
“It is not possible for you to pay taxes, for you to be paying rent, for you to be paying absolutely everything you have to pay, which is the burden, and for them not to,” Gomez Amin said.
He emphasized the need to “level the playing field,” signaling that the government wants to review the tax treatment of international online retailers operating in Colombia.
However, authorities have not yet disclosed the specific taxes, rates or regulatory changes that the legislation would introduce.
Colombia taxes: The country wants to regulate Shein and Temu
The announcement comes amid growing concerns among Colombian retailers about the rapid expansion of international shopping platforms offering inexpensive clothing, electronics, accessories and household products.
Companies such as Shein and Temu have attracted consumers with aggressive pricing, frequent discounts and extensive product catalogs. Amazon, meanwhile, provides Colombian shoppers with access to a much broader international marketplace.
For local retailers, the concern is not simply the popularity of these platforms but whether all participants in the market face comparable tax obligations.
Traditional businesses must account for expenses such as commercial rent, payroll, inventory, logistics and applicable taxes. Differences in how imported goods and domestic sales are taxed can affect the final price consumers pay.
In June 2026, Colombian media reported that the Colombian Chamber of Electronic Commerce had raised concerns about potential tax advantages associated with low-value international shipments, including the use of arrangements involving goods routed through the United States.
The debate highlights the complexity of applying existing customs and tax rules to an increasingly globalized online retail market.
What could change for Colombian shoppers?
The Fiscal Adjustment Law could lead to changes affecting the cost of purchases made through international platforms. However, it remains too early to determine whether consumers would face higher prices, additional import taxes or changes to existing exemptions.
Colombia already has rules governing value-added tax (VAT), customs duties and low-value shipments. The applicable treatment can depend on factors including the value and origin of a shipment, its transport method and the relevant trade agreements.
Consequently, the government’s announcement should not be interpreted as confirmation that every purchase from Shein, Temu or Amazon will automatically become more expensive.
The final impact will depend on the legislation presented to Congress, its approval and the implementing regulations.
For Colombian consumers, the central question is whether the government will introduce additional costs for international purchases or focus on ensuring that overseas platforms and their supply chains comply with existing obligations.
Retailers call for fair competition
Fenalco president Jaime Alberto Cabal has argued that domestic businesses should not be disadvantaged by differences in the rules governing local commerce and international digital platforms.
The discussion also extends beyond e-commerce. During the same industry gathering, the minister agreed to review a 40% tariff applied to clothing and apparel imports, opening the possibility of reconsidering that measure following discussions with the retail sector.
These issues reflect broader tensions over how Colombia should balance consumer access to affordable imported goods with the need to sustain domestic businesses, employment and tax revenues.
For the government, the challenge will be to design rules that improve competitive conditions without unnecessarily restricting consumer choice or disrupting legitimate cross-border trade.
When will the new rules take effect?
The Fiscal Adjustment Law is expected to be submitted to Congress in the coming days, according to the minister’s announcement.
Until the government publishes the bill and lawmakers debate its provisions, the precise scope and timing of any new requirements remain uncertain.
The proposal could become an important development for Colombia’s retail industry and the country’s growing digital economy. It could also affect millions of consumers who increasingly rely on international platforms for affordable products.
For now, the government’s message is clear: Colombia wants to examine whether international e-commerce companies are competing under conditions comparable to those faced by local merchants. The details of how it intends to achieve that objective will become clearer once the bill is formally presented.

articles.title: Canada, UAE sign trade deal as Ottawa presses Washington to ease tariffs - https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.summary: Canada, UAE sign trade deal as Ottawa presses Washington to ease tariffs  https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.full_text:
Canada and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) aimed at reducing trade barriers, expanding market access and encouraging investment, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to diversify Canada’s economic partnerships amid continuing trade tensions with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing on Tuesday.
As part of the deal, both Ottawa and Abu Dhabi will cut tariffs, reduce administrative barriers and create more opportunities for businesses in both countries.
The deal is an important milestone in Canada’s efforts to expand trade beyond its largest economic partner.
US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have increased pressure on Canadian industries, while the ongoing negotiations between Washington and Ottawa have so far struggled to produce a broader agreement.
Carney has pledged to double Canada’s non-US trade over the next decade, prompting Ottawa to pursue trade agreements across the Asia-Pacific region, Europe and the Middle East.
According to Canada’s Prime Minister’s Office, the agreement will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE once fully implemented.
The government expects the CEPA to enter into force in 2027, subject to the required approval process.
“The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services,” the Prime Minister’s Office said.
ALSO READ | US midterms: ‘Republicans may paint Democrats as a greater risk’
The agreement covers opportunities across industrial machinery, agriculture, forestry, fisheries, environmental services, engineering and other sectors.
The agreement is expected to benefit Canadian exporters seeking new customers in a market that has become an important commercial partner for the country.
Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola could gain from improved market access, alongside manufacturers of industrial machinery and power-generation equipment. Canada’s aerospace industry and other technology-focused businesses are also expected to benefit from lower trade barriers.
The UAE, meanwhile, is seeking to expand commercial links with Canadian companies and attract opportunities in high-growth industries.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing,” UAE Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi said.
Al Zeyoudi signed the agreement with Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu.
The UAE is Canada’s largest export market in the Middle East and an important buyer of Canadian motor vehicles, automotive parts and machinery. Bilateral trade reached CUSD 3.5 billion (USD 2.48 billion) in 2025, with trade between the countries growing by around 10% annually in recent years, according to government data.
Investment is another major part of the relationship.
The UAE committed up to USD 50 billion in investment in Canada in 2025, signalling the potential for closer economic cooperation beyond merchandise trade.
The CEPA is expected to make commercial conditions more predictable by addressing non-tariff barriers and improving access for goods and services.
Such provisions could help businesses navigate regulatory requirements and identify new opportunities in both markets.
ALSO READ | Trump eases Canadian tariffs, repairs ties with Bombardier ahead of US midterms
The signing represents the final step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement.
Although the agreement is not expected to enter into force until 2027, its completion advances Carney’s efforts to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US market and build stronger international trade relationships.
However, the US remains a critical destination for Canadian exports, particularly in industries with integrated supply chains, including automotive manufacturing and steel.
Tariffs on products crossing the border can increase costs for manufacturers, suppliers and consumers on both sides.
Against that backdrop, Carney’s commitment to double non-US trade over the next decade reflects an effort to broaden Canada’s export base and reduce its exposure to changes in US trade policy.
The UAE agreement provides one route toward that objective, although its longer-term economic impact will depend on how quickly businesses use the new market access and investment opportunities.
Ottawa is also seeking to repair relations with Washington and secure relief from tariffs affecting key Canadian industries.
Both sides, as per Reuters, have been currently discussing a possible agreement to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and automobiles.
The talks focus on duties imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on automobiles.
Negotiators are discussing potential relief from the measures as both governments attempt to restore trade relations following the collapse of broader negotiations in August.
The discussions come shortly before the November 3 US midterm elections, when Trump’s trade policies have become a political concern for some Republican candidates in border states.
Trump’s tariff warfare policy, coupled with his alleged poor handling of the American economy, has made him extremely unpopular among voters across party lines. However, candidates in states bordering Canada have called for an end to the trade dispute, highlighting the domestic political pressure surrounding tariffs.
A Canadian source familiar with the negotiations indicated that the parties could reach an agreement on steel and automotive duties before the elections.
US sources, however, said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions.
Section 232 tariffs are administered by the US Commerce Department, placing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at the centre of the negotiations rather than leaving the discussions solely to the office of the US Trade Representative.
“Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently,” one source said.
A spokesperson for LeBlanc said Canada remained engaged with its US counterparts.
“Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” the official noted.
“Ottawa was prepared to work towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respected Canada’s interests,” the person added.
“The Office of the US Trade Representative has also been in contact with Canada in recent days about the overall structure of a potential agreement and other trade issues,” a USTR official said.
Carney, too, confirming the news, said discussions with Washington had experienced “a slight intensification” but stressed that Canada’s position had not changed.
“To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the US is coming closer to our position,” he told reporters, without providing further details.
A Canadian industry source suggested an agreement could be reached quickly but cautioned that it might cover only a limited number of issues.
“If it happens, it’ll happen fast. But my sense is it’ll be a narrowed deal if it even happens,” the source said.
Another Canadian source said they had long expected a possible agreement on Section 232 tariffs before the midterms.
Any deal would ultimately depend on Trump and Carney, the source added, noting that both leaders had indicated that a mutually beneficial outcome was possible.
Carney has said he wants an agreement that delivers meaningful benefits for Canada.
The urgency reflects the economic importance of the automotive sector, where manufacturers rely on cross-border supply chains to move vehicles and components between factories in the two countries.
Trade talks between the two collapsed in August over several issues, including whether duties should be reduced on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are important to Canadian factories.
US automakers had hoped negotiations would produce relief from the original 25% tariffs, which have raised the cost of transporting vehicles and parts across the border.
By September, both sides had imposed tariffs and counter-tariffs on each other, but Trump escalated the situation by announcing a 50% increase in tariffs on Canadian steel and automobile imports, effective January 1, 2027.
During a political rally on Sunday, the Republican predicted a swift resolution to the dispute but offered little detail.
Washington has already taken some steps to adjust its tariff policy.
On Friday, Trump signed an order removing 50% tariffs on certain Canadian agricultural and forestry products, a move that could benefit businesses in Maine.

articles.title: India, ASEAN Can Emerge As Indo-Pacific Manufacturing Hub - Sarkaritel.com
articles.summary: India, ASEAN Can Emerge As Indo-Pacific Manufacturing Hub  Sarkaritel.com
articles.full_text:
India and ASEAN can turn the global China+1 strategy into a shared production network and emerge as a major manufacturing hub in the Indo-Pacific. By combining India’s large market and industrial capabilities with ASEAN’s supplier networks, ports and export strengths, both sides can strengthen regional supply chains across key sectors.
Key Highlights
- India and ASEAN can convert the China+1 strategy into a shared regional production strategy.
- India offers a large domestic market, technology capabilities and an extensive industrial and labour base.
- ASEAN brings established supplier networks, ports, industrial zones and export experience.
- Electronics, semiconductors, EV batteries, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery are potential areas for cooperation.
New Delhi, Oct 30: The global shift in manufacturing under the China+1 strategy presents a major opportunity for India and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to strengthen their economic partnership and build a shared production network. By combining their respective industrial strengths, the two sides can emerge as a major manufacturing hub in the Indo-Pacific, offering multinational companies an alternative to concentrated production in China, according to an article published by India Narrative.
The article argues that the China+1 strategy should evolve into a shared India-ASEAN production strategy, rather than becoming a competition between individual countries to attract investment. A study by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) indicates that ASEAN has relatively strong connections with global production networks, while India’s integration into global value chains has further scope for improvement. The study highlights the importance of cross-regional investment and identifying manufacturing complementarities between the two economies.
India and ASEAN bring different but complementary strengths to the partnership. India has a large domestic market, technological capabilities and a broad industrial and labour base. ASEAN offers established supplier networks, ports, industrial zones, export experience and access to markets across East Asia and the Pacific. By connecting these capabilities, companies could manufacture components in one country, process them in another and assemble finished products at the most competitive location. Such integration could reduce duplication of investment and improve the region’s collective manufacturing competitiveness.
The article identifies electronics, semiconductors, electric vehicle batteries, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery as potential priority sectors for cooperation. It calls for a cross-regional supply chain map to identify priority industries, missing suppliers, technology requirements and the most competitive production stages in each country. Trade arrangements between India and ASEAN could also be oriented towards facilitating the movement of intermediate goods and components, while investment cooperation should extend beyond individual countries’ efforts to attract foreign investors.
India, according to the article, needs to improve manufacturing competitiveness, provide regulatory certainty and create more opportunities for technology partnerships. Its domestic market can help manufacturers achieve production scale, while the country can strengthen its role in design, engineering, industrial software and selected component manufacturing. ASEAN, meanwhile, can improve connectivity among member states, harmonise standards and link industrial zones and ports more closely with Indian supplier networks.
Individual ASEAN economies can contribute specialised capabilities. Indonesia can support the partnership through critical minerals, battery materials and downstream industrial development. Malaysia has strengths in semiconductors and electronics, Thailand in automotive manufacturing, and Vietnam in electronics production and export networks. Coordinating these capabilities with India’s industrial base could help create more integrated and resilient regional supply chains.
A coordinated India-ASEAN production strategy could transform the China+1 opportunity into a long-term regional manufacturing advantage. Stronger supply chain integration, investment cooperation, trade facilitation and technology partnerships would be essential for both sides to establish a competitive manufacturing hub in the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia reports interception of Houthi drone targeting Mecca - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia reports interception of Houthi drone targeting Mecca  Al JazeeraSaudi-led coalition says it downs drone over oil-rich Eastern Region  ReutersIran war updates: Houthis target Riyadh as coalition intercepts missiles  Al JazeeraHouthis Claim Fresh Strikes on Saudi Oil Refineries and Aramco Facilities  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comDrone launched by Houthis intercepted, destroyed over Mecca, Saudi-led coalition says  The Jerusalem...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.
The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.
A Houthi spokesperson denied targeting the Muslim holy city or surrounding region, reiterating that the group’s cross-border attacks remain strictly focused on Saudi energy and military infrastructure.
The Saudi-led coalition has previously accused the Houthis of launching drones towards Islam’s two holiest cities: Mecca and Medina.
“Our operations target [Saudi] oil facilities and military bases, and there is no longer anyone in this world who believes these fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Al Saud regime,” the Houthi spokesman wrote.
Escalating hostilities
The opposing claims come as hostilities continue with no sign of slowing, and humanitarian agencies warn of worsening conditions for civilians.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted western Saudi Arabia.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported later that coalition air attacks were targeting the Mahliyah district in Marib, Haifan in Taiz, and Huwaishan in al-Jawf in the country.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Hadeel al-Yamani reported from Taiz that fighting along the front lines was persisting.
The governor of Taiz said the city was suffering heavy shelling, with residential neighbourhoods taking hits.
“Aircraft can be heard frequently over the city, which remains under a suffocating siege, with no medical supplies, water or fuel getting in,” al-Yamani reported.
“On the western front, there were intermittent clashes around dawn. The northern fronts were relatively calm, but still saw sporadic fighting. There has been a notable escalation in hostilities around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi,” he said.

articles.title: U.S.-China Relations Enter a More Managed Trade Phase as New Tariff Deal Reshapes Business Risk - Startup Info
articles.summary: U.S.-China Relations Enter a More Managed Trade Phase as New Tariff Deal Reshapes Business Risk  Startup Info
articles.full_text:
The United States and China are moving toward a more structured way of managing parts of their economic relationship after a September state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington. The two governments announced an arrangement covering roughly $30 billion in non-sensitive goods in each direction that could receive more favorable tariff treatment, while also advancing new bilateral mechanisms for trade, investment and artificial intelligence discussions.
For American companies, the significance is not that U.S.-China economic tensions have disappeared. Instead, the latest agreements point to a more selective system in which consumer goods, agriculture and other non-sensitive products may receive easier treatment even as semiconductors, critical minerals and other strategically important technologies remain subject to tighter scrutiny. That creates a business environment in which commercial opportunity and policy risk increasingly exist at the same time.
A Narrow Opening Inside a Much Larger Economic Relationship
The latest development follows several years in which tariffs, export controls and supply-chain security became central features of U.S.-China economic policy.
Trade between the two countries remains substantial, but the pattern has changed. U.S. government data show that the U.S. goods deficit with China fell to about $202.1 billion in 2025, down $93.4 billion from the previous year. U.S. goods exports to China declined to about $106.3 billion, while imports fell more sharply to roughly $308.4 billion.
The shift has continued in 2026. Through July, the United States exported approximately $65.2 billion in goods to China and imported about $156.4 billion, according to Census Bureau data. During the same January-to-July period in 2025, imports were roughly $194 billion, meaning direct U.S. imports from China were about 19% lower year over year while exports were broadly unchanged.
That does not necessarily mean economic links are simply disappearing. China has also diversified its international trade. An International Monetary Fund analysis published in September found that the U.S. share of China’s trade declined from 12.6% in 2020 to 8.8% in 2025, while trade shares involving Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America increased.
The result is a more complicated form of economic adjustment: less dependence on some direct trade channels, greater geographic diversification and continued bilateral commerce in areas where both governments consider cooperation manageable.
The New Trade Framework Focuses on Non-Sensitive Products
The most immediate development is the U.S.-China Board of Trade, created during President Donald Trump’s May 2026 visit to Beijing and advanced during Xi’s September visit to Washington. USTR said the mechanism has recommended approximately $30 billion in non-sensitive trade on each side for more favorable tariff treatment.
The products involved illustrate the deliberately limited scope of the arrangement. Chinese authorities said U.S. tariff reductions would cover categories such as toys, household appliances, baby products and kitchen and bathroom goods. China’s reductions would cover U.S. exports including agricultural products, personal-care products, medical devices and coal.
Associated Press reported that strategic categories such as semiconductors and electric vehicles were excluded from the arrangement. That distinction matters because it shows that tariff relief on everyday goods does not automatically translate into broader liberalization across the entire economic relationship.
| Area | Recent development | Why it matters to U.S. businesses | 
| Non-sensitive goods | Around $30 billion of trade in each direction has been identified for more favorable tariff treatment. | Importers and exporters may need to reassess landed costs and market-access opportunities by product category. | 
| Advanced semiconductors | The Commerce Department moved to case-by-case licensing for exports of Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X and comparable chips to approved Chinese customers under specified conditions. | Technology companies still face licensing and compliance requirements even as some commercial channels remain open. | 
| Direct goods trade | U.S. imports from China totaled about $156.4 billion through July 2026, while exports were about $65.2 billion. | China remains a significant trading partner despite supply-chain diversification. | 
| Tariff policy | USTR began a second four-year review of China-related Section 301 tariff actions in May 2026, while certain exclusions currently run through Nov. 10, 2026. | Companies still need to monitor regulatory deadlines rather than assume today’s tariff treatment is permanent. | 
Technology Shows Why “Decoupling” Is Too Simple a Description
Advanced technology offers one of the clearest examples of the selective nature of the relationship.
In January, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security revised its licensing policy for certain semiconductor exports to China. Applications involving Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X and comparable chips can now be reviewed case by case when exporters and buyers meet specified security and compliance requirements.
That is different from unrestricted trade, but it is also different from a complete technology cutoff. Companies operating in semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing increasingly have to distinguish between products that are prohibited, products that require licenses and products that remain commercially available.
The September talks added another layer. China and the United States announced plans for a bilateral AI dialogue focused on the risks and benefits of artificial intelligence, with another exchange scheduled for November 2026. They also agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents.
For technology companies, this means geopolitical risk is becoming more granular. Compliance decisions may depend not simply on where a customer is located but on chip performance, end use, customer screening, licensing requirements and future changes to export-control rules.
American Companies Face Product-Level Decisions Rather Than One China Strategy
The practical impact will vary widely by industry.
A U.S. medical-device company seeking greater access to Chinese buyers may see the latest tariff framework differently from an advanced-chip supplier operating under export controls. A retailer importing toys or household products could face different tariff conditions from an electric-vehicle or semiconductor company whose products fall outside the non-sensitive trade arrangement.
Manufacturers also have to consider where components come from rather than looking only at the country in which final assembly occurs. As production networks expand across Southeast Asia and other regions, supply-chain decisions increasingly involve tariffs, rules of origin, logistics costs, geopolitical exposure and supplier concentration simultaneously.
For companies planning procurement or investment, several questions are therefore becoming more useful than simply asking whether U.S.-China relations are improving or deteriorating: Which products receive preferential treatment? Which technologies require licenses? When do tariff exclusions expire? And how concentrated is the company’s exposure to a single supplier, country or transportation route?
This matters beyond the two countries themselves. The IMF has warned that worsening geopolitical fragmentation and renewed trade tensions remain downside risks for global growth and financial stability. Its April outlook projected global growth of 3.1% for 2026 under its baseline assumptions. Following the Relationship Requires More Than One Headline
The latest developments also show why U.S.-China relations are difficult to summarize as either confrontation or cooperation. Tariffs may fall on one category while export controls remain in place on another. Diplomatic talks can expand while existing trade investigations continue.
Readers following the relationship through a USA vs China perspective can also compare how developments are presented in broader reporting from Chinese state broadcaster CGTN. As with coverage from any national or international outlet, tariff rates, trade figures and regulatory changes are best cross-checked against primary documents from agencies such as USTR, the Commerce Department and the U.S. Census Bureau.
That distinction is especially important for businesses. A diplomatic announcement can signal policy direction, but companies generally need the implementing tariff schedules, licensing rules and customs guidance before changing prices, orders or long-term sourcing decisions.
The Next Tests Are Already on the Calendar
Several near-term developments could determine how much practical impact the new framework has.
First is implementation of the tariff arrangement. The size of the announced trade package is significant, but the effect on individual companies will depend on which products qualify, the tariff reduction applied and when the changes become operational. USTR said the Board of Trade’s recommendations concern products that could receive more favorable treatment, making implementation details important for importers and exporters.
Second is technology policy. The semiconductor licensing system remains active, while the newly announced U.S.-China AI dialogue is expected to continue in November. These parallel tracks mean commercial access and national-security controls are likely to remain separate policy questions rather than moving together.
Third is the existing tariff review process. USTR initiated its second four-year review of China-related Section 301 measures in May, while 178 product exclusions previously extended by the agency are scheduled to run through Nov. 10, 2026. Companies relying on those exclusions have a concrete policy date to monitor.
