articles.title: Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records - CNBC
articles.summary: Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records  CNBC
articles.full_text:
A top House Democrat on Wednesday accused President Donald Trump of using tariffs as a “tool for grift and self-enrichment,” pointing to what he says are suspicious import-tax exemptions for industries whose leaders have curried Trump’s favor with gifts and donations.
“You took care to cut lots of sweetheart deals with corporations and industries that won carve-outs from your tariffs when you saw you could get something good in return,” Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told Trump in a fiery letter obtained first by CNBC.
Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the former top Democrat on the House oversight committee, highlighted three such tariff carve-outs — for Brazilian meat, diamonds and smartphones — that he says “make little to no sense” under the criteria set by the Trump administration.
“They do, however, make sense when factoring in the now world famous Trump Tariff Discount,” Raskin wrote, coining a term to describe the president’s alleged willingness to cut breaks for his allies and benefactors “when the price is right.”
The letter asks Trump to hand over multiple categories of records spanning his second term, including communications between the White House and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, or USTR, related to any form of tariff relief for more than a dozen industries.
It makes a similar request for communications involving private-sector representatives, including Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Rolex CEO Jean-Frederic Dufour. Raskin asked for those records by Nov. 11.
Raskin’s pugnacious letter directly accuses Trump of “profound corruption,” asserting that his heavy-handed use of tariffs is really about clinching “levers of power that you could maliciously pull to extract exciting concessions for yourself.”
The missive — which cites the Judiciary Committee’s “jurisdiction over corruption, conflicts of interest, and effective enforcement of criminal and civil laws” — could offer a preview of how Democrats will flex their oversight powers against Trump should they win majority control of the House or Senate in the midterm election.
Raskin also drew a link between Trump’s alleged misuse of tariffs and Americans’ affordability concerns, connecting two of voters’ top concerns in the final stretch of the election cycle.
“While you have protected your personal investments and crocodile skin connoisseurs from the giant bite of your tariffs, the American people are suffering. Independent analysts expect that your latest round of tariffs will cost an average of $820 per U.S. household this year,” he wrote, citing data from the nonpartisan Tax Foundation.
The most recent CNBC All-America Economic Survey found voters are most concerned about government corruption, followed by high grocery and gas prices. Democratic candidates have deliberately tailored their campaign messaging to make connections between corruption and high costs.
“The only special interest guiding the Trump administration’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people,” a White House official told CNBC on condition of anonymity to respond to Raskin’s letter.
The USTR did not respond to CNBC’s request for comment.
Raskin homed in on the far-reaching tariffs the U.S. imposed in July using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
The Trump administration says those duties, which apply to more than 80 countries and cover nearly all U.S. imports, are meant to crack down on foreign forced-labor practices. But Raskin and other critics, including plaintiffs in a major lawsuit challenging the tariffs, argue they are actually intended to replace the sweeping “liberation day” duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
“One could be forgiven for doubting the sincerity of your Administration’s sudden concern for the victims of forced labor,” Raskin wrote.
He pointed to Trump’s decision last year to lift forced-labor-related restrictions on Dominican sugar producer Central Romana, despite allegations that the company’s abusive practices persisted.
Central Romana’s owner, José Francisco “Pepe” Fanjul, reportedly hosted a $50 million fundraiser for Trump in 2024, and his family corporation that year donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC. He has also been listed as a donor to Trump’s White House ballroom project.
The USTR only offers exemptions to the Section 301 tariffs in certain cases, including where additional duties would not help reduce forced-labor practices. But the trade office’s exemption list “contains conspicuous —and suspicious — carve-outs for a few industries,” Raskin wrote.
Raskin referenced tariff exemptions for beef and bovine products, which took effect despite opposition from U.S. cattle producers who strongly opposed the move, citing “the well-documented use of forced labor in the Brazilian cattle sector and the documented surge of Brazilian beef.”
In late August, Trump reportedly met in the Oval Office with Brazilian billionaire Joesley Batista, co-owner of JBS, the world’s largest meat processor. The next day, Trump announced the U.S. would allow the import of up to 300,000 metric tons of “product for ground beef” below market prices.
“Coincidentally, JBS’s U.S. subsidiary, Pilgrim’s Pride, made a $5 million donation to your 2024 inaugural fund, the largest donation of any single company!” Raskin wrote.
Diamond jewelry is also exempt from the Section 301 tariffs, which Raskin called “laughably indefensible” because the precious stones are identified by the U.S. Labor Department as a good produced using forced or child labor.
Raskin suggested the exemption was the result of Belgium’s Antwerp World Diamond Centre gifting Trump an opulent gold ring — studded with 321 natural diamonds and 75 other gemstones — in June. The company’s press release about the ring said it was given to Trump as a symbol of “the historic trade relationship between Antwerp and the United States” and in honor of the 250th birthday of the U.S.
“A diamond is truly the President’s best friend!” Raskin quipped in his letter.
He also wrote that USTR exempted Chinese smartphones from the Section 301 tariffs, even though “abusive working conditions are a hallmark of smartphone manufacturing, including the Apple iPhone.”
He listed multiple examples of Cook’s flattery toward Trump, including reportedly donating $1 million to Trump’s inaugural committee in 2025 and gifting Trump a gold plaque in the Oval Office. Raskin also noted Apple’s donation of $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom project, a tie for the largest contribution.
“The exemptions above only scratch the surface of your profound corruption,” Raskin wrote.

articles.title: Comments to USTR on Foreign Trade Barriers for the 2027 National Trade Estimate Report. - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.summary: Comments to USTR on Foreign Trade Barriers for the 2027 National Trade Estimate Report.  Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.full_text:
Contents
The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) is pleased to submit the following comments for the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) consideration as it prepares the 2027 National Trade Estimate (NTE) Report. ITIF is an independent, nonprofit, nonpartisan research and educational institute focusing on the intersection of technological innovation and public policy.
This filing is structured in four sections that outline recent ITIF developments to help strengthen the NTE report. First, it describes non-tariff attacks (NTAs), a useful framework for distinguishing foreign unfair trade practices that particularly harm U.S. competitiveness, advanced-technology leadership, and intensive research and development (R&D). ITIF suggests the NTE report have a separate section outlining NTAs. This section describes Canada’s Online Streaming Act and South Korea’s Food Delivery Act as examples of NTAs.
Second, this filing presents ITIF’s Foreign Fines Tracker, a database documenting regulatory fines that foreign governments have levied on U.S. technology companies. The tracker details $21.7 billion in regulatory penalties against U.S. technology companies from 2018 through July 2026. These fines, often tied to global turnover, disproportionately burden American firms.
Third, ITIF builds on the 2026 and previous NTE reports’ concerns about the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) by documenting its discriminatory design and substantial economic costs. ITIF recommends incorporating this evidence into the 2027 report and, if negotiations fail to secure nondiscriminatory treatment, pursuing a focused Section 301 investigation with targeted remedies that preserve the broader transatlantic economic relationship.
Finally, ITIF presents new evidence suggesting that the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) imposes disproportionately high penalties on American technology companies. Between 2016 and 2025, the average corrective order surcharge penalty imposed on leading U.S. technology companies was nearly seven times the criminal referral average for Korean chaebols, despite the latter’s greater severity. These findings warrant closer scrutiny of Korea’s compliance with its 2025 bilateral nondiscrimination commitments.
Non-tariff attacks are foreign government measures presented as neutral domestic regulations designed to protect local industries and consumers but enforced in ways that target U.S. firms.[1] Unlike conventional non-tariff barriers (NTBs), which encompass any non-tariff measure affecting trade, NTAs constitute a narrower category whose calibrated thresholds, scope, and enforcement priorities fall almost exclusively on American firms while leaving domestic competitors largely untouched. They impose costly obligations and penalties designed to extract revenue from leading U.S. technology companies, eroding the capital available for frontier innovation and undermining these firms’ competitive position.
ITIF urges USTR to allocate a dedicated section to distinguish NTAs. This enhanced section would map measures country by country, identify affected sectors and firms, and provide clear cost bands for (a) fines and fees, (b) compliance and localization spending, and (c) mandated product or design changes, drawing on established international restrictiveness indicators and nontariff-measure datasets. ITIF’s Non-Tariff Attack Tracker, a knowledge base that systematically catalogs such laws and regulations worldwide, can be used as a source.[2] Many of these policies can weaken technology firms that serve as America’s strategic assets in the techno-economic competition with China, ultimately allowing Chinese competitors to benefit from their diminished competitiveness.[3]
The examples below highlight some of the legislation ITIF tracks. The tracker is a living document, updated regularly as new developments emerge.
The Online Streaming Act, enacted in 2023, gives the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) the power to require streaming services to fund Canadian and Indigenous content.[4] The CRTC applied this to services that earn CAD $25 million or more in Canadian revenue and are unaffiliated with a Canadian broadcaster, predominantly U.S. firms.[5] In May 2026, it raised that requirement to 15 percent of revenues in Canada—previously 5 percent—while cutting Canadian broadcasters’ requirement from 30–45 percent to 25 percent, which they can largely meet through existing programming.[6]
That change faced backlash, largely due to pressures from U.S. stakeholders.[7] In June 2026, the government ordered the CRTC to review the decision and later pledged to replace the 5 percent with CAD $600 million in annual federal funding.[8]
A parallel discoverability framework requires platforms to prominently feature Canadian content on landing pages and in recommendations.[9] Violations of any of these rules carry penalties of up to CAD $10 million, rising to CAD $15 million for repeat violations.[10]
The following foreign policy developments are under discussion and, if enacted, would merit inclusion in the NTE report and exploration of appropriate trade measures in response. USTR should monitor them closely and raise concerns with the relevant trading partners before they take effect.
Brazil’s Digital Markets Bill, first submitted to Congress in September 2025, would amend the country’s competition law to create an ex ante regulatory regime for large digital platforms.[11] It would establish a Digital Markets Superintendency within Brazil’s competition authority, the Administrative Council for Economic Defense (CADE), empowered to designate firms as having “systemic relevance in digital markets.” Only firms with revenue above BRL 5 billion ( $900 million) in Brazil or BRL 50 billion ($9 billion) globally would be eligible for designation. According to Brazilian government estimates, the bill would capture only 5 to 10 companies, primarily American firms, while sparing domestic ones.[12] This imposes a discriminatory burden that effectively penalizes U.S. firms for their scale.
Non-compliance carries fines of up to 20 percent of a firm’s Brazilian revenue from the business area where the violation occurred.[13] The bill’s revenue thresholds would capture mostly American firms while sparing domestic ones, imposing a discriminatory burden that penalizes firms seeking to achieve global scale in their operations.
In May 2026, Indonesia’s Ministry of Law released a draft revision of its Copyright Law (Law No. 28 of 2014) that primarily aims to bring artificial intelligence (AI) under copyright regulation.[14] If enacted, it would impose significant obligations on digital platforms, predominantly U.S. tech firms, requiring them to license and pay for copyrighted works used to train AI models and to disclose AI use in content. As of October 2026, Indonesia’s parliament is still deliberating the bill.
The Food Delivery Platform Service Fees Act—currently under discussion in South Korea’s National Assembly—would require covered platforms to offer preferential service fees to small merchants and prohibit practices such as forcing restaurants to use a particular delivery method or shifting the costs of preferential rates onto delivery workers.[15] This proposal would let the KFTC set detailed fee requirements, investigate suspected violations, and issue corrective orders, including adjustments to service fees and delivery charges. The KFTC could fine platforms that break the rules up to 10 percent of their related Korean sales, and platforms that ignore corrective orders could face criminal penalties.[16] Lawmakers are now pushing for a combined review, along with two other similar proposals, following an October 2026 parliamentary audit.[17] These bills would fall hardest on U.S. firms, which lead Korea’s food delivery market.[18]
ITIF’s Foreign Fines Tracker is a database documenting regulatory fines that foreign governments have levied on U.S. technology companies.[19] It quantifies the financial burden on some of America’s most innovative firms, diverting capital that could otherwise strengthen research and development to meet complex, cumbersome compliance requirements. The European Union and its member states issue these fines most frequently, though the practice is now spreading globally as more countries adopt similarly excessive penalties.[20] Because these fines are typically calculated on a firm’s global turnover rather than the revenue earned in the imposing jurisdiction, they disproportionately penalize U.S. companies with a large international presence.[21]
The scale of these fines has grown rapidly. The cumulative total has risen from $4.7 billion in 2018 to $21.7 billion as of July 2026, with nearly 60 percent imposed since 2024, as shown in figure 1. Had this capital remained in the innovation economy, it could have covered the training costs of 274 frontier AI models, the flight costs of five Artemis IV missions, or three years of the National Science Foundation’s budget. Redirected to domestic priorities, it could have paid the salaries of 290,732 teachers, provided a year of nutrition assistance to 9.6 million SNAP recipients, or funded 137 new hospitals. The EU and its member states handed down the five largest fines by value, led by a staggering $4.7 billion penalty against Google in 2018.[22]
Figure 1: Cumulative foreign government fines imposed on U.S. technology firms from January 2018 to July 2026 (in current US$ billion)
The tracker covers all fines greater than $1 million issued since 2018, spanning a range of policy areas including competition policy, data transfer and protection, platform regulation, interoperability, and market access. The database draws on primary sources, including official government announcements and enforcement records, as well as secondary sources such as news reports. articles.title: India's trade deficit to persist amid oil import dependence, petroleum exports offer relief: IIFT VC - Big News Network.com
articles.summary: India's trade deficit to persist amid oil import dependence, petroleum exports offer relief: IIFT VC  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
New Delhi [India], October 30 (ANI): India's trade deficit is likely to persist as long as the country remains dependent on oil imports, although rising exports of value-added petroleum products are helping narrow the gap, K. Rangarajan, Vice-Chancellor of the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), said on Friday.
"Trade deficit will continue to be there till the time we have more and more dependence on oil. It cannot be reduced, but it is getting somewhat reduced because of those value addition," Rangarajan told ANI in an exclusive interview.
Explaining the factors behind India's trade deficit, he said the country's dependence on imported oil remained a structural challenge.
However, India has emerged as an important destination for refining and exporting value-added petroleum products, particularly following disruptions caused by the war and the Middle East crisis. Refining activities and subsequent exports were helping partly offset the impact of oil imports, he added.
On India's foreign trade outlook for FY27, Rangarajan expressed optimism about the country's ability to surpass the USD 1 trillion export milestone, citing a more conducive environment for external engagements.
"I am also very optimistic about it. We will be able to surpass that $1 trillion as well. So, it should not be a surprise," he said, adding that his optimism was based on the emerging global trade landscape.
On the broader economic outlook, he estimated that India's growth rate could reach around 6-7 per cent, supported by expanding external engagements and changing geopolitical dynamics.
Highlighting the challenges facing the manufacturing sector, Rangarajan said government policy announcements and industry-friendly interventions alone would not be sufficient to improve competitiveness.
Their effective implementation at the ground level, including by state governments, and the industry's ability to adapt to changing trade conditions would be equally important, he said.
He said businesses needed to understand the implications of free trade agreements (FTAs), including product-specific tariff concessions, tariff lines and rules of origin, rather than leaving such assessments entirely to policymakers.
Describing India's new-generation FTAs as more comprehensive, he said they were no longer limited to tariff reductions but also covered supply chains and services. The industry needed to adapt to these integrated arrangements to translate market access into higher exports.
Citing the India-UAE trade agreement, he said exports had started increasing following its implementation. He expressed optimism about the benefits of other agreements, including the India-New Zealand FTA, while indicating that the European Union agreement could also be implemented and an arrangement with the United States was on the horizon.
On concerns over US President Donald Trump's tariff policies, Rangarajan said frequent changes, additional conditions and uncertainty surrounding tariffs could eventually put pressure on the US market itself.
"The market and its tolerance make a difference," he said, pointing out that China continued to emerge as a major exporter to the US despite the imposition of tariffs as high as 100 per cent.
On foreign investment, he said India needed greater inflows into technology and digital sectors to strengthen its ambition of becoming a global manufacturing hub.
At the same time, overseas investments by Indian companies were increasingly becoming strategic, allowing businesses to explore alternative production and export destinations amid tariff-related uncertainties.
Addressing geopolitical disruptions in West Asia, including concerns surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, he said India was relatively better positioned because of its diplomatic relationships with various countries.
He noted that global trade was estimated to grow by around 1 per cent, while growth in the ASEAN region and India was projected to exceed 2 per cent.
Rangarajan said India's diplomatic engagement had helped it navigate disruptions during the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other international crises. He also expressed confidence that India could contribute to rebuilding countries affected by wars and infrastructure destruction.
"Whenever there are problems in other countries, India is the first country to help, be it in our neighbour Nepal or somewhere in Africa," he said, adding that India could play a significant role in supporting reconstruction efforts while strengthening its own trade prospects. (ANI)

articles.title: 【SMM Analysis】Vietnam Proposes Aluminium Export Duty Cuts, Implications for Southeast Asian Billet and Extrusion Trade - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: 【SMM Analysis】Vietnam Proposes Aluminium Export Duty Cuts, Implications for Southeast Asian Billet and Extrusion Trade  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
Vietnam is proposing to cut export duties on selected aluminium products, potentially giving domestic suppliers more room to adjust export offers. According to the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI)'s account of the accompanying government draft, duties on relevant unwrought aluminium (HS7601), aluminium bars, rods and profiles (HS7604), and aluminium wire (HS7605) would fall from 5% to 1%. VCCI has called for a further reduction to 0%. If implemented, the changes could improve export netbacks and commercial terms for Vietnamese billet and extrusion suppliers, affecting competition with Chinese, Malaysian and other regional suppliers.
The measures remained proposals at this article's research cut-off on October 30, 2026. No published instrument bringing the proposed 1% or 0% rates into force had been identified. A separate draft resolution published by the Vietnamese authorities would lower the statutory export duty range for products including HS7601 and HS7604 from 5–40% to 0–30%, providing legal scope for the government to reduce specific rates. A 0% floor would not automatically make these products duty-free. Applicable rates, tariff coverage and implementation dates remain subject to the final instruments.
For Southeast Asian billet trade, the immediate commercial effect of a duty cut would be on Vietnamese suppliers' export netbacks and pricing options. With the taxable value and other conditions unchanged, lower export duties could increase sellers' net proceeds or support lower offers to secure orders. How suppliers allocate the savings would depend on inventories, available material, order books and bargaining power. The reduction in duty cannot be treated as an equivalent percentage decline in billet prices or processing fees.
If Vietnamese suppliers pass part of the savings through to export offers, regional extruders could gain more attractive sourcing options, putting competing offers for comparable billet from China, Malaysia and other origins under pressure. Sustained trade growth would still depend on the specifications, delivery schedules and customer acceptance of Vietnamese export material. HS7601 covers a broad range of unwrought aluminium and cannot be treated entirely as 6063 billet. Billet made from primary aluminium and remelt billet also need to be assessed separately for alloy composition, impurity control, homogenisation and processing performance. A tax change alone does not demonstrate an increase in substitutable supply.
For Vietnamese extruders, lower duties on covered HS7604 products would directly increase flexibility in export offers. Suppliers could retain more earnings at existing prices or offer concessions to compete for regional orders. Export duty, however, is only one element of a buyer's procurement cost. Comparisons with Chinese, Malaysian and other supplies must also account for specifications, surface treatment, certification, freight, delivery times, destination import duties and rules of origin. HS7604 coverage should not be extended to all finished aluminium products. Any benefit for doors, windows or structural components classified under other headings would depend on the final scope.
Simultaneous duty cuts for billet and profiles could also change sales decisions within Vietnam's aluminium supply chain. Better export netbacks for unwrought aluminium alloy could prompt billet casters to reassess the returns from exports against domestic sales. Where available material is limited, more attractive export opportunities could intensify competition for feedstock among domestic extruders. If suppliers can expand output of billet that meets customer requirements, they may instead be able to serve both domestic processors and export markets. Lower duties on extrusion exports therefore would not necessarily reduce domestic billet procurement costs. The eventual benefit would depend on supply and demand along the chain and on contract pricing.
Another trade channel to watch is the sale of aluminium products by Vietnamese domestic suppliers to export-processing enterprises and non-tariff zones. Supplies from the domestic market into non-tariff zones can fall within the scope of export duty, while goods brought from overseas into qualifying non-tariff zones and used exclusively within them can fall outside the scope of import duty. VCCI argues that this difference weakens the appeal of domestic aluminium supplies and has requested an explicit 0% export duty rate for domestically produced aluminium sold to export-processing enterprises and non-tariff zones for production use.
If adopted, that recommendation could narrow the tax disadvantage faced by Vietnamese suppliers serving these customers, giving domestic billet and profiles more scope to compete for procurement contracts. For orders previously supplied from overseas, competition would increasingly depend on delivery reliability, quality and total delivered cost. The treatment would remain conditional: it should not be extended to all aluminium imports or interpreted as a blanket tax cut on ordinary domestic sales. Enterprise and zone eligibility, use within the zone and customs supervision requirements would still need to be met.
At this stage, the proposals create potential for Vietnamese suppliers to adjust offers and sales channels. They do not establish that Southeast Asian billet prices have already fallen as a result, or that extrusion orders have shifted. The market impact will depend primarily on the final rates and implementation arrangements, changes in Vietnamese suppliers' actual offers and delivery schedules, and any shifts in regional buyers' sourcing. If duty cuts are implemented and translate into reliable supplies that meet customer requirements, Vietnam could strengthen its competitive position in Southeast Asian billet and extrusion trade.

articles.title: Vietnam's cashew industry maintains its position as the world's number one. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam's cashew industry maintains its position as the world's number one.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Foreign businesses are exploring opportunities for cooperation with Vietnamese cashew processing and exporting companies at the 15th Vietnam International Cashew Conference in 2026. | 
 Chairman of the Vietnam Cashew Association (VINACAS), Pham Van Cong, affirmed: As one of the world 's major cashew processing and export centers, the Vietnamese cashew industry is ready to continue to cooperate with countries, organizations, associations, and the international business community to build a stable, transparent, and value-generating cashew supply chain.
 Maintaining export records
 According to VINACAS, in 2026, the cashew industry will face many challenges such as: changing international environment - tariff policies; increasing trade barriers; rising production, transportation, logistics costs and financial pressure; and a volatile global economy ... However, in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's cashew industry still exported more than 594,000 tons of cashew kernels, earning nearly 4.2 billion USD; an increase of over 3.5% in volume and nearly 7.4% in value. This is a positive sign because Vietnam's cashew exports are shifting from exporting quantity to increasing value. It is expected that in 2026, the Vietnamese cashew industry will continue to maintain its record export turnover with over 5 billion USD.
 However, behind these record figures, Vietnam's cashew industry faces a major challenge: its processing relies heavily on imported raw cashews, accounting for 85% of its raw material supply. Specifically, in the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam spent over $4.4 billion importing nearly 2.8 million tons of raw cashews. This dependence on imported raw materials creates significant difficulties for domestic cashew processing businesses, especially as many raw cashew exporting countries are focusing on developing their own cashew processing industries and thus limiting the export of raw materials.
 VINACAS Chairman Pham Van Cong stated: To achieve sustainable development, the cashew industry needs to invest more heavily in advanced processing technology and the development of new products. The industry must increase its competitive advantage through product quality, branding, technology, and added value. Furthermore, major markets are increasingly demanding higher standards regarding environmental protection, product origin, quality, and corporate responsibility. Therefore, the cashew industry must proactively adapt, paying more attention to traceability, emission reduction, efficient use of raw materials and energy, and developing green and sustainable production. Businesses that prepare early will have more opportunities when new standards are implemented.
 Sharing the success story of exporting processed cashew products to demanding markets, Mr. Ta Quang Huyen, Chairman of the Board and General Director of Hoang Son 1 Joint Stock Company (Nghia Trung commune), emphasized: “Our company is a pioneer in investing in high technology for deep processing. Currently, our processed products are available on the shelves of European supermarkets and some other demanding markets. The most crucial factor for processed products to enter demanding markets is ensuring food safety and hygiene while maintaining a good price.”
 Creating a sustainable value chain
 The 15th Vietnam International Cashew Conference in 2026 is organized to strengthen international cooperation based on information sharing and the search for new solutions, especially in building a more stable, transparent, and value-generating cashew supply chain for all parties.
 Mr. Ashok Krishen, Chairman of the International Nut and Dried Fruit Council, stated that: Increased cooperation among countries is needed to develop common standards for quality and technical requirements for nuts and dried fruits, including cashews. Harmonizing standards will facilitate trade and enhance the competitiveness of the industry. With its significant position in global cashew processing and export, Vietnam has the foundation to continue playing a role in the international value chain.
 Technology, mechanization, and automation have played a crucial role in the development and success of Vietnam's cashew processing industry. Currently, many major cashew-producing countries in Africa are seeking cooperation with Vietnam in processing development, especially in processing technology.
 Mr. Ojo Joseph Ajanaku, Head of the Nigerian Cashew Business Delegation (Federal Republic of Nigeria, West Africa), shared: “I have collaborated closely with Vietnam for the past two decades, and the cooperative relationship is very good. We hope this cooperative relationship will continue to develop. Nigeria produces high-quality cashews and is a major exporter of raw cashews to Vietnam. We look forward to continuing our partnership with Vietnam in the new journey of developing cashew processing, especially in processing technology.”
 The new context demands that the cashew industry innovate its thinking, make breakthroughs in action, and shift strongly from exporting quantity to exporting quality; moving from selling ready-made products to providing value-added solutions for the global market. The cashew industry also needs to innovate its approach to the market through cross-border e-commerce and sustainable supply chains; promote a linked chain mindset from raw cashew production to processing and proactively invest abroad.
 Mr. Tran Ngoc Hai, representative of the Trade Promotion Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade )

articles.title: IEA Nations Boost Critical Minerals Security in Crisis Drill - Mirage News
articles.summary: IEA Nations Boost Critical Minerals Security in Crisis Drill  Mirage News
articles.full_text:
The IEA recently brought together more than 100 participants from Member countries, along with market and industry experts, for a two-day Table-Top Exercise and Diversification Workshop at its headquarters in Paris.
Organised under the IEA's Critical Minerals Security Programme, the event on 22-23 October aimed to strengthen governments' preparedness for potential supply disruptions and advance international cooperation on developing more resilient and diversified critical mineral supply chains.
Building on the success of previous editions of the exercise, participation doubled this year, reflecting growing international attention to the security of critical minerals supply chains. This year's event also extended to two days, allowing participants to examine both immediate supply security challenges and longer-term diversification strategies in greater depth.
The first day featured a table-top exercise focused on rare earth elements, which are essential for a wide range of strategic industries, including the automotive, energy and high-tech sectors.
Through realistic simulations of potential supply disruptions and market developments, participating governments tested their ability to assess supply risks, identify appropriate policy responses and coordinate actions with international partners.
The exercise examined two distinct challenges: a sudden disruption to rare earth supplies and prolonged market pressures threatening the economic viability of diversified supply projects. The scenarios highlighted the importance of both emergency preparedness and maintaining resilient supply chains over the longer term.
Participants engaged in intensive discussions and simulated negotiations, exploring potential bilateral and multilateral responses and identifying areas in which stronger international coordination could improve preparedness.
The second day focused on practical approaches to diversifying critical minerals supply chains, with a focus on rare earths and tungsten, a strategic mineral needed for a variety of applications across energy, defence and industrial components. Participants worked in groups to examine strategic project opportunities, assess policy and market instruments to support diversification, and identify critical dependencies related to technologies, equipment, chemicals and technical know-how.
The workshop featured new analytical tools developed by the IEA, including a Critical Minerals Information Dashboard and a Policy Tool Simulator. These tools enabled participants to assess strategic project opportunities, explore international partnerships, and evaluate how different policy measures could influence project economics and fiscal costs. The exercises also highlighted the importance of addressing bottlenecks in the specialised technologies and expertise needed to bring new projects into operation.
Participants welcomed the practical and interactive format, which provided opportunities to test policy approaches, exchange experiences and identify potential areas for cooperation.
Building on the IEA Ministerial Declaration in February 2026 and the G7 Leaders' Declaration in June 2026, which called for stronger international cooperation on critical minerals security, the IEA is further strengthening its Critical Minerals Security Programme as a key international platform to enhance emergency preparedness and accelerate supply chain diversification. Drawing on its longstanding experience in oil security, the IEA is also working with Member countries to explore the development of a structured emergency response procedure for critical minerals.

articles.title: Why asset-light execution and supply chain orchestration are emerging as the new engines of growth - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Why asset-light execution and supply chain orchestration are emerging as the new engines of growth  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The textile sector is experiencing a profound transformation driven by global supply chain issues and geopolitical challenges. To navigate this landscape, companies must focus on building resilience rather than merely prioritising cost efficiency. By adopting an asset-light model, businesses can swiftly adjust their production in response to actual customer needs. Strategic collaborations within supply chains are crucial for timely deliveries.
However, the age of interconnected supply chains and evolving customer expectations means that companies are judged on their abilities to control their suppliers, business partners, distributors and customers. In today's age of growth, those companies that do not just possess value and assets but are instead capable of managing a network around customer demand will prosper.
The textile and apparel industry is currently going through a structural change all across the globe. The occurrence of geopolitical uncertainty, supply chain disruption, and increased usage of sourcing strategies like 'China+1' has motivated many brands to diversify their manufacturing capability and give priority to resilience more than cost efficiency.
This indicates a larger transformation in how companies are run. Legacy firms are combining the tried and tested methods used by traditional companies, i.e, their ability to create reliable reputations and good relations with clients, and also with new practices that allow them to work faster and more efficiently than before.
From manufacturing strength to network-led execution
In a competitive and commoditised marketplace, consumers focus on quality, reliability, pricing and timely delivery instead of the country where the product is manufactured. While production assets are still important, significant fixed capacities may hinder flexibility as fixed costs and the need to keep utilization high remain even with changing demand.
The strongest competitive advantages in the textiles business usually do not come from our physical assets. Trust in the brand, relationships with clients that span decades and successful execution capabilities are usually much harder to duplicate than pieces of equipment. These strengths enable companies to adopt the asset-light strategy.
The success of this model relies on appropriate collaboration across the supply chain. Companies may leverage partnerships with manufacturers, providers of products, and logistics companies in order to enhance their capabilities, enter new markets, and react to tan increase in demand.
Cutting edge technology that brings visibility in terms of inventory and order management and demand allows improving the process of planning and execution. The importance of those technologies increases in the procurement of institutions, when they need reliable products and services of high quality.
From a financial perspective, reducing dependence on fixed assets allows companies to deploy capital more effectively towards product development, technology, quality systems, partnerships and customer engagement. It also enables businesses to scale in line with demand rather than installed capacity.
Building more resilient growth
The true test of business discipline is often during periods of strong growth rather than downturns. Rising demand can encourage companies to expand capacity, increase procurement and build inventory on the assumption that market conditions will continue. When demand normalises, these decisions can put pressure on margins and working capital.
Instead of maximising, calibrating seems to result in better sustainability. This means that production, purchasing and inventory need to be driven not by the optimism of the market in the short term but by the actual demand and customer needs. By using an asset-light model businesses can make their production more flexible in accordance with real demand and regulate costs better as well.
Since international brands pursue diversification in their sourcing strategies, supplier partnership expectations are changing as well. Corporations are looking forward to others, which can supply not only with stable schedules and turnaround times, but also with compliance issues, transparency, and effective deliveries in the value chain. Competitive advantage is now not just operational capabilities but also networking capabilities.
India's presence in the textile industry grows, as multi-national companies consider new sourcing strategies and trade deals continue to provide new opportunities for success in different markets. To achieve this, companies need to come together to implement plans within sourcing, production, distribution, technological innovation and customer relations.
For the future development of the textile industry in India, the drivers of growth are not going to be companies with the highest asset base, but rather those that have a combination of expertise in manufacturing along with their existing customer relations and the ability to execute in a flexible manner, develop strategic alliances and manage their supply chains effectively. Asset-light execution and supply chain orchestration are the key factors involved in this process.
(The author is Managing Director & CEO, Mafatlal Industries Limited. Views are personal.)

articles.title: Vietnam cashew sector looks to reshape global supply chains - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam cashew sector looks to reshape global supply chains  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) - More than 500 delegates from 40 countries and territories have gathered in Ho Chi Minh City for the 15th Vietnam International Cashew Conference, which opened on October 27 to discuss ways to strengthen global supply chain links and increase value across the industry.
The event, themed “From raw materials to added value - Connecting value chains and shaping the future of global cashew supply chains,” was organised by the Vietnam Cashew Association (VINACAS) in coordination with the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
According to VINACAS Chairman Pham Van Cong, Vietnam exported nearly 800,000 tonnes of cashew nuts in 2025, earning a record 5.4 billion USD. For nearly two decades, the country has led the world in cashew processing and exports, accounting for more than 80% of global exports.
However, shifting tariff policies, trade barriers, and rising production, transport, logistics, and financial costs are putting pressure on the entire value chain. The industry must address immediate challenges while pursuing a long-term strategy for the next 10–20 years, with a focus on deeper processing, product diversification and higher-value products rather than semi-processed exports.
Cong stressed that cashew production is part of a global supply and value chain in which stakeholders’ interests are closely linked. Sustainable development therefore depends on cooperation among countries, suppliers, processors and distributors, rather than individual efforts. Stakeholders should improve market transparency, share data on supply, demand and price fluctuations, and jointly manage opportunities and risks.|
Tran Ngoc Hai, a representative from the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency, said the cashew industry faces long-term structural challenges. He noted that shifting global supply chains, sustainability-related technical barriers, rising demand for green consumption and competition from raw-material-producing countries are forcing businesses to rethink their export strategies.
Vietnam imports around 80% of the raw cashew nuts used for processing, while land available for domestic cultivation is increasingly limited. This dependence underscores the need to secure supplies, improve processing efficiency and increase the value of finished products.
Hai urged businesses to shift from selling existing products to offering higher-value goods, while building brands and establishing a direct presence in overseas markets. He said the ministry plans to modernise trade promotion, using artificial intelligence (AI) and big data for market forecasting, promoting green and digital trade, and helping businesses meet international standards.
These efforts are linked to the 2026–2030 programme for expanding into international markets, approved by the Prime Minister, which aims to help businesses improve management, build brands, identify target markets, develop distribution channels and integrate more deeply into global value chains.
Cashew companies should fully tap available support mechanisms to develop and protect their brands, expand deep processing and introduce Vietnamese-branded products into international distribution networks, reducing reliance on foreign partners’ labels, Hai said.
Ashok Krishen, Chairman of the International Nut and Dried Fruit Council (INC), said the global nut market had grown by an average of around 8% annually over the past decade. Annual demand for nuts and dried fruit stands at about 1.4 million tonnes, with cashews accounting for the largest share.
According to Krishen, consumers, particularly young people, are becoming increasingly health-conscious and paying greater attention to their diets. Vietnam’s cashew sector could benefit by developing products that meet modern consumer preferences, provided businesses understand market demand, maintain quality and meet import-market requirements.
He also underlined the need to boost international cooperation to establish common quality and technical standards for nuts and dried fruit, saying harmonisation would facilitate trade and strengthen competitiveness.
Vietnam’s leading position in cashew kernel processing and exports provides a strong foundation for further integration into global value chains, he added./.

articles.title: Bangladesh-Malaysia FTA: New route to export diversification ahead of LDC graduation - Daily Sun
articles.summary: Bangladesh-Malaysia FTA: New route to export diversification ahead of LDC graduation  Daily Sun
articles.full_text:
Print: 31 Oct 2026
Bangladesh-Malaysia FTA: New route to export diversification ahead of LDC graduation
Both sides aim to finalise deal in 2027 as first-round talks end on positive note; next round set for January
As Bangladesh prepares to graduate from the least developed country (LDC) category, a proposed free trade agreement (FTA) with Malaysia is expected to help diversify its export markets, attract investment and sustain competitiveness in international trade.
The two countries concluded their first round of formal negotiations in Dhaka on Thursday following three days of talks that began on 27 October at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel.
Both sides tentatively agreed to hold the second round in January 2027 and expressed their commitment to finalising a mutually beneficial agreement within the agreed timeframe.
During the negotiations, 13 working groups reviewed draft chapters and structural issues covering trade in goods and services, rules of origin, customs facilitation, digital trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and the interests of small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
The proposed agreement comes amid a substantial trade imbalance between the two countries, with Bangladesh importing far more from Malaysia than it exports.
According to data from the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) and Bangladesh Bank, bilateral trade stood at around US$2.84 billion in the 2024-25 fiscal year (FY25), compared with $2.89 billion in FY24, $3.86 billion in FY23 and $3.80 billion in FY22.
Bangladesh’s exports to Malaysia amounted to just $282 million in FY25, down from $293.51 million in FY24, $371.86 million in FY23 and $337.81 million in FY22.
The figures indicate a trade deficit of more than $2 billion in FY25, highlighting the need to expand Bangladesh’s export basket and improve access to the Malaysian market.
Bangladesh also received only $773.36 million in investment from Malaysia between 2001 and March 2025, according to the data.
Export diversification key to tapping Malaysian market
Speaking to the Daily Sun, Bangladesh-Malaysia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BMCCI) President Md Anwar Shahid expressed hope that the FTA would be signed next year, as both governments seek to strengthen bilateral trade ties.
“The main reason for our trade deficit with Malaysia is our limited range of export products. We import much more than we export, so we need to focus on increasing exports rather than simply balancing trade,” he said.
He stressed the need to identify products with export potential and develop strategies to make them more competitive in the Malaysian market.
“It is important to keep these issues in mind during the negotiations,” he added.
Anwar said an FTA could create opportunities to expand trade, business and investment, contributing to economic growth and strengthening foreign investors’ confidence in Bangladesh’s economy.
Highlighting processed food as a promising sector, he said the chamber had long advocated greater attention to halal products.
“We need to improve our halal certification system and ensure Malaysia recognises our certificates. This would help more Bangladeshi products enter the Malaysian market,” he said.
Besides processed food, he identified ready-made garments, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, home textiles, frozen food and furniture as sectors with potential for export growth.
He also highlighted opportunities in services exports, particularly in technology and skilled employment.
“When we talk about manpower exports, we usually think of construction workers or plantation workers. But the services sector is much broader. We have opportunities in technology- and skills-based work as well, including semiconductor design,” he said.
With appropriate training and skills development, Bangladesh could create more employment opportunities for its workforce in Malaysia and other international markets, he added.
New export destinations crucial ahead of LDC graduation
M Masrur Reaz, chairman and chief executive officer of Policy Exchange of Bangladesh, said securing market access and diversifying export destinations would be critical as Bangladesh approaches LDC graduation.
He noted that more than 80% of Bangladesh’s exports were concentrated in the garment sector, while a similarly large share was destined for three major markets: the European Union, the United States and the United Kingdom.
Reaz said Asian markets could play a greater role in Bangladesh’s export expansion after graduation, making trade agreements with Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and other countries increasingly important.
Bangladesh’s export growth has benefited from preferential market access associated with its LDC status, he said, stressing the need to secure alternative trade arrangements as those preferences change.
He also identified Malaysia as a potential gateway to the wider Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) market, offering opportunities for Bangladesh to diversify trade and participate in regional supply chains.
FTA could take bilateral ties to new economic level
Speaking at the closing ceremony of the first round of negotiations, Bangladesh’s chief negotiator Khadija Nazneen, an additional secretary at the Ministry of Commerce, said the proposed agreement could elevate the two countries’ longstanding friendly relations to a new level of economic cooperation.
She highlighted Malaysia’s strengths in electronics, semiconductors and digital technology, saying the agreement could facilitate technology transfer, investment and industrial collaboration.
Malaysia’s chief negotiator, Dr Rashidi Said, noted that Bangladesh’s graduation from LDC status could result in the loss of some preferential market access, making new trade partnerships increasingly important.
Both delegations reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a balanced and mutually beneficial agreement within the agreed timeframe. The next round of negotiations is expected to focus on resolving differences over various chapters and reaching mutually acceptable positions.
Experts said an FTA with Malaysia, a major ASEAN economy, could expand market access for Bangladeshi goods and services, strengthen industrial and technological capabilities and facilitate integration into regional supply chains.
However, they cautioned that the actual benefits would depend on the final terms of the agreement, particularly tariff concessions, safeguards for domestic industries and effective implementation.

articles.title: Transshipment Crackdowns Won’t Fix the U.S.-China Trade Imbalance - CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies
articles.summary: Transshipment Crackdowns Won’t Fix the U.S.-China Trade Imbalance  CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies

source_detail.name: CSIS | Center for Strategic and International Studies

articles.full_text:
U.S.-China trade relations continue to enjoy a fragile détente, but recent dialogues between Washington and Beijing have not resolved underlying tensions. One point of friction is the White House’s condemnation of Chinese “transshipment” of trade goods, articulated most clearly in its August 2026 report The Great Transshipment Scam. The report critiques a wide range of trade practices that it argues constitute a coordinated strategy to illegally avoid U.S. tariffs imposed on Chinese goods. In doing so, it sets the stage for future actions toward China and other commercial partners.
The “transshipment scam” report reflects the Trump administration’s continued dissatisfaction with the United States’ and China’s respective roles in the global trade landscape. Despite the flurry of U.S. actions against China since early 2025, Beijing’s export-oriented economic growth model continues to perpetuate global trade imbalances, stoking political backlash in Washington, Brussels, and other capitals around the world. Moreover, the overarching U.S. trade balance has not durably shrunk, and concerns of threatened U.S. industrial competitiveness vis-à-vis China remain as strong as ever. U.S.-China relations are likely to remain strained as long as these factors persist.
The White House muddies the policy debates surrounding these issues, however, by blaming them all on transshipment. The most novel contribution made by the report is an attempt to stretch the definition of transshipment beyond its traditional definition—i.e., the rerouting of unmodified goods through intermediate countries—to include substantive overseas manufacturing using Chinese-origin inputs. The analysis below examines the extent to which transshipment is taking place, both in the traditional sense and under the White House’s expanded definition, and unpacks potential policy options for addressing these respective phenomena.
Empirical Evidence on Rerouting Chinese-Origin Products
A core aspect of the White House report’s argument is that Chinese-origin products are continuing to flow into the United States even though direct bilateral trade has shrunk. This allegedly takes place through more than 40 economies that reroute intermediate or final Chinese goods from China to the United States to benefit from lower tariff rates. CSIS’s own analysis shows that some of these economies have indeed experienced disproportionate growth in imports from China and in exports to the United States since 2024, a signal that these countries may be serving as “connectors” of U.S. and Chinese economic activity (see Figure 1). These countries, which fall into the top-right quadrant of Figure 1 below, are thus sometimes referred to as connector economies.
The first part of the White House’s claim has strong empirical support. A 2026 Peterson Institute for International Economics policy brief examines the share of U.S. import value that originated in China, either through direct imports from China or from Chinese upstream inputs embedded in products imported from elsewhere—a measure known as “value added.” It finds that Chinese value added flowing into the United States has grown since 2018 even as U.S. direct imports from China have fallen (see Figure 2), meaning that Chinese value added increasingly enters the United States via third countries. The Peterson paper and other analyses identify Mexico and Vietnam as two prominent conduits linking U.S. and Chinese supply chains, providing a pathway for 23 percent and 15 percent of indirect Chinese value added entering the United States in 2024, respectively.
The key question is how this value added reaches the United States. A factory in Mexico exporting specialized products using Chinese inputs may simply reflect an efficient supply chain responding to comparative advantages. This is a wholly different phenomenon than a logistics company importing products from China and directly re-exporting them without modification (i.e., the traditional definition of transshipment). Legal and policy implications are determined by how Chinese goods pass through connector economies, and specifically whether or not they have been substantially transformed along the way.
One way to assess the predominance of rerouting versus substantial transformation is investigating whether the six-digit Harmonized System (HS-6) code—the international standard taxonomy for classifying traded goods—changes for a certain good between its import from China and its export to the United States. If a country’s imports from China and exports to the United States are both growing, and a growing share of its U.S.-bound exports match its Chinese imports, transshipment may be occurring. On the other hand, a flat or declining share of overlapping trade suggests transshipment is not growing as a share of that country’s total trade activity.
Building on prior research, CSIS analysis shows that for many economies singled out in the White House report, the overlap in imports from China and exports to the United States has not meaningfully grown. Figure 3 shows the percentage-point difference in overlapping Chinese imports and U.S.-bound exports by identical HS-6 product code from 2024 to 2026, measured with the Finger-Kreinin Export Similarity Index. This analysis challenges the view that transshipment is the dominant way that Chinese-origin products end up in the United States. Some economies, such as Laos and Cambodia, do show a growing trade overlap, but several other economies show the opposite trend.
Mexico, Canada, and several Southeast Asian economies have particular scrutiny for their potential role in transshipment networks, and it is worth examining them more closely to assess these critiques. Of this group, U.S.-bound exports from Cambodia and Laos, and to a lesser extent from Singapore and Indonesia, increasingly overlap with the product categories these countries import from China (see Figure 4). Particular areas of overlapping growth in these countries include photovoltaic cells and steel products—both of which have been identified by Commerce Department duty circumvention investigations.
More surprising, Malaysia, Mexico, Thailand, and Vietnam show no overall rise in their share of overlapping U.S. and Chinese trade; Malaysia and Thailand even show a decline. The divergence appears to be driven largely by specialization within electronics supply chains, in which these countries import simple electronics components from China and export advanced electronics to the United States (see Table 1). Some transshipment is still occurring in these economies—as illustrated by the investigations cited above—but it does not appear to be growing as a share of these countries’ trade.
Overlapping HS-6 baskets provide clues to where transshipment might be occurring, but identifying illegal or problematic activity requires more granular analysis. Many HS-6 codes cover broad baskets of goods, and products can often be substantially transformed without changing HS-6 codes. Conversely, different HS-6 codes might be used for the same product in different contexts or by different countries. Also, analysis of government-reported trade statistics cannot account for instances of misreported value, classification, or origin—which recent research suggests have spiked since new tariffs were levied on China in early 2025. Products as diverse as tungsten carbide, quartz, plastic bags, and batteries have all been found by investigations to have been involved in illicit rerouting schemes.
These examples are plainly fraudulent, but transshipment itself is not inherently illegal or undesirable from a policy perspective. Companies route goods through third countries for several legitimate reasons, including port access, logistics synergies, and inventory storage. Problematic behavior, by contrast, involves concealing or misrepresenting a product’s true origin to evade regulation or obtain a lower tariff rate. Even then, trade practices may be undesirable from a policy perspective without necessarily being prohibited under current trade law. By branding all such undesirable activity as illegal, the White House report conflates entirely legitimate business actions with criminal behavior.
The evidence above suggests that transshipment activity as conventionally defined explains only a subset of Chinese-origin value added flowing into the United States. The remainder is likely explained by routing through more substantial transformation steps in a multistage supply chain. International Monetary Fund research illustrates how such trade reallocation can be driven by Chinese businesses investing abroad, foreign firms relocating from China overseas, and local firms in connector economies turning Chinese inputs into products for the U.S. market. Other research reinforces this finding. A 2026 Federal Reserve study, for instance, found that Chinese production in Mexico accounted for about 14 points of Mexico’s export gains after the 2018–19 tariffs, while direct transshipment accounted for less than 1 point.
Why Have Tariffs Failed to Reduce U.S. Imports of Chinese Value Added?
U.S. tariffs and trade actions from 2025 onward have shifted supply chain contours but have not reduced underlying U.S.-Chinese trade imbalances. Transshipment fraud explains part of this phenomenon but overlooks more fundamental macroeconomic determinants of the lopsided trade relationship.
China’s economic model accounts for much of the macroeconomic situation. As China’s domestic economic performance continues to underwhelm, its leaders have remained committed to an export-oriented growth strategy that props up supply-side economic activity. An undervalued real exchange rate, tepid consumer spending, and entrenched state support for key technology sectors all contribute to China’s widening trade surplus. articles.title: Vietnam's import and export turnover of goods surpassed the 1 trillion USD mark after 10 months of 2026. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam's import and export turnover of goods surpassed the 1 trillion USD mark after 10 months of 2026.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to estimates, Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025, officially surpassing the US$1 trillion mark. In October alone, import and export turnover is estimated at US$122.2 billion, an increase of 47.6% compared to the same period last year.
 Notably, exports continued to grow strongly, with estimated turnover reaching $499 billion in the first 10 months, an increase of 27.4%, creating positive momentum to achieve and surpass the export growth target of 15-16% for the whole year of 2026.
 Export growth occurred in both the domestic and foreign direct investment (FDI) sectors, with processed industrial goods continuing to play a leading role, accounting for 87.4% of total export turnover. Exports also recorded positive growth in many major markets such as China, the United States , the EU, South Korea, and ASEAN.
 Regarding the trade balance, October is estimated to have a trade surplus of $6.8 billion, marking the second consecutive month of surplus and bringing the cumulative trade deficit for the first 10 months down to approximately $12.7 billion. This result shows that import and export activities continue to maintain positive growth momentum, affirming the important role of goods trade in economic growth. 
 Imports and exports achieved high performance in the first 10 months of 2026.
 Currently, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing a draft strategy for goods import and export until 2030, with a vision to 2045. According to the draft, the goal is to achieve an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in goods export turnover during the 2026-2030 period; and an average annual growth rate of 12-13% in imports. The trade balance aims for a sustainable surplus, with the proportion of export surplus to total export turnover averaging 3-6% during this period. By 2045, Vietnam strives to be among the top 10 countries with the largest export and import turnover in the world; with a trade surplus ratio of 7-10%.
 One of the key objectives is to enhance the role of domestic enterprises and increase the processing and technological content in exports. Accordingly, the proportion of export turnover from the domestic enterprise sector in the total national export turnover is targeted to reach approximately 28-30% by 2030, increasing to 38-40% by 2045. The proportion of processed or refined goods in the total export turnover is expected to reach 89-90% by 2030 and over 92% by 2045. The proportion of high-tech product exports in the total value of processed and manufactured goods exports is targeted to reach approximately 50% by 2030 and over 55% by 2045.
 Regarding trade scale, the draft presents growth scenarios up to 2030. In the medium scenario, export turnover is expected to reach US$953.7 billion by 2030; the high scenario targets US$1,041.1 billion, while the low scenario is US$765 billion. These scenarios indicate the need to expand export scale in conjunction with improving domestic production capacity, developing processing and manufacturing industries, and increasing the competitiveness of goods.
 In the fourth quarter, the Ministry of Industry and Trade identified key areas for boosting exports, diversifying markets, and improving compliance capacity. This includes focusing on effectively utilizing signed Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), expanding into new markets; and enhancing early warning capabilities regarding trade defense cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability, and rules of origin.
 Simultaneously, support businesses in improving product quality, building brands, and ensuring transparency in the supply chain. Promote official exports, expand agreements/protocols on agricultural product quarantine; strengthen investment in cold chain logistics infrastructure and standardize growing areas and packaging facilities to meet the regulations of each partner market.

articles.title: TES Inaugurates $24 Million Rayong Smart Manufacturing Base to Strengthen Global Supply Chain Resilience - citybuzz -
articles.summary: TES Inaugurates $24 Million Rayong Smart Manufacturing Base to Strengthen Global Supply Chain Resilience  citybuzz -
articles.full_text:
TES (SZSE: 003019.SZ), a leading provider of touch display solutions, has officially inaugurated Phase I of its manufacturing base in Rayong Province, Thailand. The ceremony, held on October 29, 2026, was attended by TES Chairman Kevin Lee, local government officials, and supply chain partners. With an initial investment of US$24 million, the new plant marks a significant expansion of TES’s manufacturing footprint in Southeast Asia and signals a new stage in its global strategic layout.
The Rayong facility is a cornerstone of TES’s ‘Dual-Core Smart Manufacturing’ strategy, which balances production across China and Thailand. In his opening speech, Chairman Kevin Lee emphasized that the plant’s output—including interactive smart displays, interactive all-in-one PCs, and smart automotive displays—is expected to generate tens of millions of US dollars in production value for the local economy. He noted that the dual-base setup will provide higher supply chain resilience and more flexible delivery capabilities, helping global customers mitigate trade risks and capture market opportunities.
Located within the WHA Industrial Estate in Rayong, the plant covers a total land area of 42,399 m² with a building area of 26,630 m², making it TES’s largest single manufacturing base in Southeast Asia to date. The company plans to systematically migrate and integrate its Chonburi and Rayong operations in phases. Phase I includes production facilities, administrative offices, and employee living support facilities, with a current workforce of approximately 300 employees. Monthly planned capacity includes 65,000 units of 7–55″ touch monitors and all-in-one PCs, 300,000 SMT-related products, 120,000 sets of automotive touch display modules, 120,000 units of automotive optical bonding products, and 30,000 units from automotive assembly lines. Future plans include adding one assembly line and two bonding lines to meet medium-to-large batch OEM and ODM orders.
The strategic location of the Rayong plant offers significant logistical advantages. Situated in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC), it is about 1.5 hours (113 km) from Bangkok Suvarnabhumi International Airport and 1 hour (70 km) from Laem Chabang Deep Sea Port. The plant has received Investment Promotion Privileges (BOI) certification from the Thai government, ensuring a high-quality production environment and on-time delivery. For global OEM/ODM partners, the new base provides efficient and fast delivery, operational stability, diversified trade risks through flexible country-of-origin options, and enhanced supply chain resilience via cross-regional multi-base synergy.
Upholding its mission of ‘Combining Humanity and Technology to Serve the World,’ TES has implemented its globally unified quality management system at the Rayong plant, enforcing standardized control from supplier management to final outgoing inspection. The official operation of the Rayong plant represents a key milestone in TES’s globalization journey, and the company plans to continue cultivating the Southeast Asian industrial ecosystem. For more information, visit https://www.tes-tec.com/.

Explore South Korea trade data for 2025-26, including its top 10 imports and exports, major trade partners, trade surplus, & semiconductor growth.
South Korea is one of the world's leading trading economies, with a strong presence in semiconductor manufacturing, automobiles, electronics, shipbuilding, petrochemicals, and industrial machinery. Its advanced manufacturing sector and extensive global supply chains make the country a major exporter of high-value products & a significant importer of energy, raw materials, and technology components. According to South Korea import data and South Korea export data, the country recorded around $709.3 billion in exports & $631.9 billion in imports in 2025, generating a substantial trade surplus. In 2025, South Korea imports increased by 1%, while South Korea exports increased by 4% from the previous year. South Korea's total trade turnover reached $1.34 trillion in 2025.
Semiconductor demand played a major role in export growth, while crude oil, natural gas, and advanced manufacturing equipment remained important import categories. South Korea's trade momentum accelerated further in 2026. From January–September 2026, exports reached around $814.5 billion & imports reached $562.1 billion, resulting in a total trade turnover of $1.37 trillion, exceeding the full-year 2025 total. This growth was driven largely by semiconductors & rising global investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to global trade data. This blog explores South Korea trade data for 2025–26, including the country's top 10 imports and exports, major trading partners, trade performance, and emerging opportunities for global businesses.
South Korea Trade Data 2025–26: Key Statistics
South Korea's international trade performance reflects the country's technological capabilities, industrial production, and integration into global manufacturing networks, according to South Korea's Ministry of Trade.
Key South Korea trade statistics:
- Total exports in 2025: around $709.3 billion.
- Total imports in 2025: around $631.9 billion.
- Trade surplus in 2025: around $77.4 billion.
- Export growth in 2025: around 3.8%.
- Exports from January to September 2026: around $814.5 billion.
- Imports from January to September 2026: around $562.1 billion.
- Trade surplus in January–September 2026: around $252.5 billion.
South Korea's exports crossed the $700 billion threshold in 2025, reflecting the strength of its manufacturing & technology industries. The country benefited from semiconductor demand, while shipbuilding, automobiles, and other industrial products contributed to overseas sales. In 2026, exports increased sharply, particularly in technology-related categories. The substantial year-on-year increase should be interpreted in the context of semiconductor prices, global AI investment, and comparisons with the corresponding period in 2025.
Top 10 Imports of South Korea: What Does South Korea Import?
South Korea imports many goods to meet its needs. Top imports include machinery and equipment used to make products, and crude oil for energy. South Korea also imports cars and chemicals for various industries. Electronics, such as smartphone parts, are also important imports. Other key imports are food items, steel, plastics, & natural gas. These imports support South Korea's strong economy, helping the country produce high-quality goods for local & global markets. The top 10 main imports of South Korea, as per South Korea's import statistics for 2025, include:

8. Precious stones & metals (HS code 71): $13.32 billion (2.11%)
9. Plastics & articles thereof (HS code 39): $13.31 billion (2.11%)
10. Iron & steel (HS code 72): $11.83 billion (1.87%)
South Korea's Top Imported Product Categories
1. Semiconductors
Semiconductors were among South Korea's largest import categories in 2025, with reported imports of around $75.8 billion. Imports include components and chip types used in electronics manufacturing, industrial equipment, communications products, and other applications. The country can simultaneously record substantial semiconductor imports and exports because different chips and components move between countries during production.
2. Crude Oil
Crude oil imports reached around $75.3 billion in 2025. South Korea relies heavily on overseas crude oil supplies to operate its refineries and meet energy demand. Import expenditure depends on international oil prices, the quantity purchased, exchange rates, and the sourcing strategies of energy companies.
3. Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment
Imports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment reached around $26.4 billion in 2025. Specialised equipment is essential for wafer processing, lithography, testing, and other stages of semiconductor production. These imports support South Korea's advanced chip manufacturing facilities and reflect investment in technology and production capacity.
4. Natural Gas
Natural gas imports were valued at around $26 billion in 2025. South Korea imports natural gas, including liquefied natural gas, for electricity generation, industrial consumption, and heating. International gas prices, seasonal demand, and long-term supply contracts all influence import expenditure.
5. Petroleum Products
South Korea imported around $21.2 billion in petroleum products in 2025. Imported refined fuels complement domestic production and supply energy users across the economy. Import values can change according to fuel prices, refinery operations, and demand from transportation and industrial sectors.
6. Computers
Computers and related hardware are imported for commercial, industrial, and consumer applications. Imports also reflect the international movement of computer components and finished products through electronics supply chains.
7. Automobiles
South Korea imports foreign-made automobiles to serve consumers seeking different brands, models, and vehicle technologies. Import demand depends on household purchasing power, exchange rates, vehicle prices, and the availability of conventional, hybrid, and electric models.
8. Precision Chemical Materials
Precision chemicals and specialised materials are important inputs for electronics, batteries, pharmaceuticals, and advanced manufacturing. South Korean manufacturers rely on consistent access to high-quality materials to maintain production standards and meet the technical requirements of sophisticated products.
9. Clothing and Apparel
Imported clothing supplies South Korea's retail & consumer markets. Apparel sourcing is influenced by manufacturing costs, fashion trends, product variety, & trade relations with overseas production centres.
10. Coal
Coal remains an import category associated with electricity generation and industrial applications. Import demand depends on power consumption, industrial activity, energy policy, international prices, and the availability of alternative fuels.
Key takeaway: South Korea's major imports demonstrate the importance of overseas energy supplies and advanced manufacturing inputs. Crude oil and natural gas support energy security, while semiconductors & specialised production equipment help sustain the country's high-tech industries.
