South Korea is known for its strong economy and exports a variety of products around the world. The top ten exports include electronics like smartphones & televisions, which are very popular. Other important exports are cars, ships, and machinery. South Korea also sells a lot of chemicals and steel. South Korea's export economy is dominated by advanced manufactured goods & industrial products. Semiconductors are a particularly important export category, supplying electronics manufacturers, data centres, automotive companies, and technology businesses worldwide.

articles.title: Exporting to ASEAN: How to avoid the risk of losing money? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Exporting to ASEAN: How to avoid the risk of losing money?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Orders are increasing, but cash flow may still be tight.
 At the workshop "Providing Risk Management Advice in Trade Promotion and Export Business with ASEAN Markets," organized by the Trade Promotion Department of the Ministry of Industry and Trade on October 27th in Hanoi, experts emphasized the need for risk prevention throughout international business operations.
 According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Thu Thuy, Deputy Director of the Center for Trade and Investment Promotion Support, Trade Promotion Department, ASEAN has advantages in geography, transportation, distribution, and similar consumer demand. Agricultural products, processed foods, seafood, consumer goods, textiles, and construction materials have opportunities to access the market. This is also a place where small and medium-sized enterprises can learn.
 However, ASEAN is not a homogeneous market. Singapore excels in finance and logistics; Malaysia has its own specific requirements regarding standards and certifications; Indonesia demands thorough understanding of licensing, import, and distribution procedures… The approach needed varies from country to country.
 Ms. Thuy noted six risk groups: partners and trade fraud; payments, credit, and exchange rates; contracts; import and customs standards; logistics and delivery; along with business culture, market information, and competitiveness. One mistake can lead to significant costs.
 Specifically, according to Ms. Thuy, there have been cases where businesses successfully exported goods but encountered difficulties in collecting payment, and had to seek advice from the Trade Promotion Department to resolve the issue. The contract value differed from the actual amount received.
 An order may be recorded as revenue but not yet received as cash. While awaiting payment, the business still has to purchase raw materials, pay salaries, cover shipping costs, and pay suppliers. If using borrowed capital, the longer debt collection period increases interest expenses and narrows profit margins.
 Therefore, when evaluating an ASEAN order, businesses need to consider the number of days capital is tied up, the payment terms, and their ability to withstand delays from their partners. A lack of working capital can cause businesses to lose new orders.
 Assess potential partners before providing funding.
 Drawing from practical experience in supporting businesses, Mr. Phung Van Thanh, Commercial Counselor in Malaysia, cited the case of a Vietnamese company in 2024 that deposited approximately $150,000 USD to import copper ore from the Philippines but did not receive the goods. According to information shared by Mr. Thanh, at the time of the transaction, the Philippines was no longer able to export this type of ore. Consulting with the trade office from the beginning can help identify the risks.
 This is an import transaction, not an export. However, the general lesson is that it's necessary to check the partner's capabilities, legal status, and market information before transferring money or delivering goods. Mr. Thanh also mentioned a case where a partner registered an address on a remote island in the Philippines, making it difficult to verify signs of fraud.
 In Indonesia , Mr. Pham The Cuong, Commercial Counselor and Head of the Vietnamese Trade Office, warned of mistakes in building market strategies, defining partner roles, and protecting brands and licenses. If rights are not clearly defined from the outset, businesses may lose control or have to spend more money to rectify the situation.
 For exporters, partner vetting shouldn't stop at business registration. It's necessary to verify the contract signatory, transaction history, payment capacity, and the actual recipient of the goods. For new customers, consider trial orders, low trade credit limits, and strict payment terms before expanding.
 That's how capital is protected. When delivering goods on deferred payment terms, businesses are essentially granting a form of trade credit to the buyer. Without factoring the risk of debt into the selling price and transaction limits, projected profits may not offset losses from delayed payments.
 Control documentation, maintain financial efficiency.
 Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Ngoc Ha from the Foreign Trade University recommends that businesses familiarize themselves with specific regulations in import markets, from product standards, labeling, and registration to distribution conditions. He also advises businesses to seek support from regulatory agencies, trade offices, and legal consulting organizations when drafting and implementing contracts and handling disputes.
 According to Mr. Hoang Duc Minh, from the Goods Origin Department of the Import-Export Bureau (Ministry of Industry and Trade), when goods may fall under the scope of multiple trade agreements, businesses need to correctly identify the rules of origin and the corresponding document mẫu, ensuring that the information on the Certificate of Origin (C/O) is consistent with the invoice, shipment, and related documents. Errors in declaring or proving origin can cause difficulties during customs clearance and verification, and affect the ability to enjoy preferential tariffs.
 Preferential tariffs under the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) provide a competitive advantage for businesses, but enjoying these benefits depends on the ability to meet the conditions regarding the origin of goods and related documentation. Errors in documentation can require businesses to provide explanations, supplementary documents, or wait for origin verification, affecting processing times and the application of preferential tariff rates. In some cases, additional costs or tax obligations may reduce profit margins, altering the financial efficiency projected when quoting prices and signing export contracts.
 Businesses need to connect sales, import/export, accounting, and legal departments in the control process. Before signing a contract, delivery terms, insurance, applicable law, dispute resolution mechanisms, and the point of risk transfer must be determined. Before shipping, documents, payments, and accounts payable must be reviewed.
 More importantly, it's crucial to monitor both profit margins and cash conversion cycles simultaneously. A contract with a high selling price but extended payment terms and significant financing costs may be less efficient than a contract with a lower price but faster collection and less risk. The ability to collect payments on time and control costs determines the sustainability of a business's exports.
 According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Thu Thuy's recommendations, businesses need to manage risks from market research, partner selection, negotiation to production, transportation, payment, and contingency planning. Expanding market share in ASEAN is only sustainable when orders do not weaken cash flow and growth resources.

articles.title: Vietnam must strengthen domestic capacity to move up global supply chains: Deputy PM - Báo Cần Thơ
articles.summary: Vietnam must strengthen domestic capacity to move up global supply chains: Deputy PM  Báo Cần Thơ
articles.full_text:
Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang speaks at the Autumn Economic Forum 2026 on October 28. (Photo: VNA)
  
Vietnam must proactively position itself in global production networks and strengthen its domestic capacity to capture greater value from the restructuring of global supply chains, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang said at the Autumn Economic Forum 2026 on October 28.
The global economy is undergoing profound restructuring amid geopolitical conflicts, technological breakthroughs and the twin transitions of digitalisation and green development. Growth centres are shifting increasingly towards Asia, Africa and Latin America, while value and supply chains are being reorganised to diversify risks, strengthen regional links and improve resilience, he noted.
Investors are no longer choosing destinations based solely on costs. They are increasingly considering safety, flexibility and long-term strategic connections, while artificial intelligence (AI), automation and environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards are becoming important conditions for participation in global value chains, Thang said.
These changes offer Vietnam opportunities to attract capital, access new technologies and expand markets, but also put pressure on the country's ability to absorb technologies, develop skilled workers and meet international standards.
Thang stressed that Vietnam could not remain a passive recipient or an outside observer. Instead, it must build its own capacity and actively define its role in global production networks. The goal is not simply to join existing or emerging value chains, but to create the conditions, mechanisms and capabilities for Vietnam and its international partners to participate more directly in value creation.
He outlined four priorities: developing domestic capabilities in human resources, technology and governance; establishing a stable, transparent and predictable institutional framework that allows room for experimentation; strengthening connectivity and multilateral and South-South cooperation; and mobilising green capital and technology while linking them with domestic businesses to upgrade value chains.
As Vietnam's leading economic city and an innovation hub, Ho Chi Minh City is well positioned to turn capital, knowledge and technology into new forms of cooperation and value, he said, adding that the city should strive to become a credible, responsible growth centre that is ready to integrate with international partners.
Dialogue must be translated into commitments, policy frameworks and concrete cooperation projects, Thang emphasised, calling for coordinated action on the role of megacities, breakthrough technologies, innovation ecosystems, new cooperation models and private-sector participation.
 
Devendra Jain, Head of AI and Frontier Technologies at the World Economic Forum (WEF), said Vietnam has established an impressive growth model, emerging as a major manufacturing centre, an investment destination and an increasingly connected economy. Its next stage of development should focus on becoming a smart, connected economy rather than simply expanding physical and digital links.
Competitiveness depends not only on building factories, seaports, roads and industrial parks, but also on how effectively these assets work together. Smart infrastructure combines physical facilities with connectivity, data and AI to improve operational decisions and coordination.
For Ho Chi Minh City, Jain identified two opportunities: creating a reliable coordination system linking factories, logistics providers, warehouses and seaports along production and export corridors; and developing shared smart infrastructure to help businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), adopt advanced technologies.
The city aims to connect innovation, manufacturing, logistics and seaports within a broader economic area and increase exports by 10–11% annually over the next five years. Achieving this target will require faster, more reliable and better-integrated operations, he said.
Shared infrastructure could allow SMEs to access 5G networks, AI tools and digital twins without bearing the full investment costs themselves. Jain added that better coordination and AI adoption could also help reduce logistics costs, which currently account for around 16–17% of Vietnam's gross domestic product (GDP).
Denis Depoux, Global Managing Director of Roland Berger, said international capital is flowing strongly into digital technologies and AI, while the real economy still needs long-term financing for roads, seaports, power, telecommunications, manufacturing and logistics. He described the two areas as “Token”, referring to the digital and AI economy, and “Concrete”, representing the real economy and physical infrastructure, and called for stronger links between them.
He noted that Asian supply chains had been reshaped by geopolitical and economic changes, with ASEAN attracting a larger share of foreign direct investment than China since 2018. Vietnam is part of this shift, but must raise productivity and move into higher-value activities to sustain growth.
Depoux said a financial centre could provide services to domestic and foreign companies and support supply-chain financing. He recommended developing the corporate bond market, improving credit ratings for projects, unlocking capital from completed infrastructure assets and modernising manufacturing, while positioning Ho Chi Minh City and surrounding areas as a financial hub serving more flexible supply chains.
VNA

U.S. oil giants raked in billions of dollars in profits in the third quarter as oil prices surged amid supply constraints caused by conflicts around the world, contributing to higher prices at the pump for consumers.
ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil producer by market capitalization, reported having more revenue from refining operations than from its exploration and drilling operations for the first time in at least six years.
Chevron's third-quarter downstream earnings also reached their highest point over the same timeframe.
The surge in revenue for the oil giants comes as Americans are facing higher prices at the gasoline pump, as the war in Iran's disruption of oil flows from the Middle East and the war between Russia and Ukraine has led to the targeting of energy infrastructure.

American consumers have faced a significant uptick in gas prices this year, with prices surging above $4 a gallon nationally at times, according to AAA data.
AAA data showed that the national average price of a gallon of regular gas was $4.20 a gallon on Friday, down slightly from $4.43 a month ago but well above the average of $3.03 a gallon a year ago.
Diesel prices also reached their highest recorded average price last month, when they reached $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22, AAA found.
Diesel costs are particularly significant for the trucking industry, and those costs can affect the price paid by consumers for groceries and other goods that are transported to stores around the country.
Recent data from the Labor Department also reflects the surge in gas prices that Americans have faced over the past year.
The September consumer price index (CPI) released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that gas prices surged 9.1% on a monthly basis and were up 34.2% from a year ago.
Gas prices have undergone significant shifts since the Iran war began in late February, with the BLS data showing monthly swings to the upside of 21.2% in March, 5.4% in April and 7% in May.
A cooldown in the conflict over the summer allowed gas prices to decline on a monthly basis by 9.7% in June and 2.9% in July.
However, concerns over the prospect of a resumption of hostilities and the impact on energy supplies caused prices to rise again in the last two months, with prices up 3.9% in August and 9.1% in September, per the BLS data.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran for more than 12 hours on Friday in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran and avoid an outbreak of war after the midterms, according to diplomatic sources.
The discussions will continue in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday.
Why it matters: The U.S. is now just days away from a possible military operation that would inflict enormous damage on Iran and likely lead to retaliatory strikes against Israel and a host of Gulf countries.
Driving the news: A diplomatic source said Qatari mediators were in regular contact with the White House during Friday's daylong session.
"There was positive progress. Talks are still ongoing in an effort to unlock a deal between the U.S. and Iran," the source said.
The Qataris are prodding the U.S. and Iran to agree on a set of reciprocal steps that would be implemented over a few days and get the parties back to direct talks on the Iranian nuclear program and other issues.
A U.S. official said two competing demands have stymied the talks so far: the Trump administration's insistence that Iran make nuclear concessions as part of resuming talks, and Iran's stipulation that the U.S. first lift its naval blockade, release frozen funds and allow it to sell oil.
The Qataris are trying to convince Iran to allow U.N. inspectors to visit its bombed nuclear sites as a confidence-building measure that the U.S. would respond to with some sanctions relief.
The intrigue: Inside Trump's inner circle, there are different opinions on what he should do.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are highly skeptical that any nuclear agreement can be reached with the current Iranian regime. They think Trump's legacy should be to weaken the regime even more, including with further strikes, a U.S. official said.
The person said that while Vice President Vance and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner want to resume negotiations, Trump is skeptical Iran will ever agree to a deal he finds acceptable.
"There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking. ... We have time, frankly. It's a war, but it is not a typical war," Trump told reporters on Friday.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is leading an economic pressure campaign dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast," is one of Trump's closest aides urging him to let the initiative play out rather than rush back into combat.
Zoom out: Countries in the region like Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have been urging Iran to agree to resume negotiations before the midterms, a regional source said.
One U.S. official said Trump might be more inclined to order a major military operation if Republicans lose badly in the midterms.
"If he feels embarrassed or disenfranchised he will do something bold. That's what everyone are telling the Iranians. Their best shot to get a deal is right now," the official said.
A White House official said the election results won't be a factor in Trump's decision-making about Iran.
The leaders of Saudi Arabia and Turkey urged Trump in recent days to allow more time for diplomacy.
At the same time, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is lobbying Trump to launch a joint operation against Iran immediately after the election.
The big picture: Renewed war could lead to massive destruction not only in Iran but in Gulf countries, exacerbating the global energy crisis.
Iran has vowed to respond to any U.S. strikes on its energy infrastructure by attacking oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain.
Any U.S. attack on Iran would be conducted jointly with Israel. Iran would likely retaliate with missile strikes, while Hezbollah could also wage attacks on Israel.

Published Document: 2026-22007 (91 FR 67782)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the State of New York is transferring a portion of their 2026 commercial bluefish quota to the State of North Carolina. This quota adjustment is necessary to comply with the Atlantic Bluefish Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial bluefish quotas for New York and North Carolina.
DATES:
Effective October 27, 2026 through December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Rigdon, Fishery Management Specialist, (978) 281-9336.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the Atlantic bluefish fishery are found in 50 CFR 648.160 through 648.167. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through Florida. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.162, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (91 FR 7896).
The final rule implementing amendment 1 to the FMP, as published in the
Federal Register
on July 26, 2000 (65 FR 45844), provided a mechanism for transferring bluefish commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can request approval to transfer or combine bluefish commercial quota under § 648.162(e). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined these criteria have been met for the transfers approved in this notification.
New York is transferring 200,000 pounds (lb) (90,718 kilograms (kg)) of Atlantic bluefish to North Carolina through mutual agreement of the states. This transfer was requested to ensure North Carolina would not exceed its 2026 state quota. The revised bluefish quotas for 2026 are: New York, 596,248 lb (270,454 kg); and North Carolina, 1,943,521 lb (881,566 kg).
( printed page 67783)
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR 648.162(e)(1)(i) through (iii), which was issued pursuant to section 304(b), and is exempted from review under Executive Order 12866.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the Commonwealth of Virginia is transferring a portion of its 2026 commercial summer flounder quota to the State of New Jersey. This adjustment to the 2026 fishing year quota is necessary to comply with the Summer Flounder, Scup, and Black Sea Bass Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial quotas for Virginia and New Jersey.
DATES:
Effective October 27, 2026, through December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Rigdon, Fishery Management Specialist, (978) 281-9336.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the summer flounder fishery are found in 50 CFR 648.100 through 648.111. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through North Carolina. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.102, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (91 FR 7896).
The final rule implementing amendment 5 to the FMP, as published in the
Federal Register
on December 17, 1993 (58 FR 65936), provided a mechanism for transferring summer flounder commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can transfer or combine summer flounder commercial quota under § 648.102(c)(2). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers or combinations would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined that these three criteria have been met for the transfer approved in this notification.
Virginia is transferring 9,745 pounds (lb; 4,420 kilograms (kg)) of summer flounder to New Jersey through a mutual agreement between the states. This transfer was requested to repay landings made by an out-of-state permitted vessel under a safe harbor agreement. The revised summer flounder quotas for 2026 are: Virginia, 2,423,982 lb (1,099,500 kg); and New Jersey, 2,119,613 lb (961,440 kg).
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR 648.102(c)(2)(i) through (iv), which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempted from review under Executive Order 12866.

Published Document: 2026-22269 (91 FR 68478)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for navigable waters of the Gulf of America. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the M/T KALAHARI that will be conducting repairs at anchorage due to both auxiliary boilers being out of service rendering the inert gas system inoperable. Entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector Mobile, or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective without actual notice from October 30, 2026 through December 27, 2026. For the purposes of enforcement, actual notice
( printed page 68479)
will be used from October 28, 2026, through October 30, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact LT Zachary West, Sector Mobile Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (251) 382-8653, or email
sectormobilewaterways@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
IGS Inert Gas System
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received notification from the M/T KALAHARI that both the vessel's auxiliary boilers are out of service rendering the Inert Gas System (IGS) inoperable. To fix both the boilers and IGS system, the vessel must conduct repairs at anchorage, in the Gulf of America south of Pascagoula, MS. The IGS is a critical safety system on tank vessels, and the Captain of the Port (COTP) Mobile has determined that the inoperable IGS on the M/T KALAHARA presents an increased risk of fire or explosion. Therefore, the COTP is issuing this rule under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone, until repairs can be completed on the vessel.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard was notified of this issue on October 12, 2026, and we must establish this safety zone immediately to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary safety zone from October 28, 2026, through December 27, 2026. The safety zone will cover all navigable waters in the Pascagoula Anchorage, within 1,000 meters of the M/T KALAHARI, at approximate position 30°05.533′ N, 088°24.958′ W. Vessels and persons will not be allowed to enter the zone during this time, unless authorized by the Captain of the Port. The safety zone will be enforced upon the arrival of the MT Kalahari in the anchorage described above. Enforcement will be terminated when repair work on the M/T KALAHARI is completed. The COTP will announce the specific enforcement dates and times via Broadcast Notice to Mariners, or other public advisories.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, 5 U.S.C. 601-612, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under Executive Order 13132, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary moving safety zone around the S.S. UNITED STATES and all vessels involved in its towage through the Mobile River Channel, Mobile Bay, and the Gulf of America. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards created by the dead ship tow. Entry of persons and vessels into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port (COTP), Sector Mobile.
DATES:
This rule is effective from November 6, 2026 through November 16, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact Lieutenant Zachary West, Waterways Management—Division, U.S. Coast Guard Sector Mobile; telephone (251) 382-8653, email
SectorMobileWaterways@uscg.mil.

II. Background and Authority
The Coast Guard received notification that S.S. UNITED STATES, a former commercial ocean liner, will be moved, via dead ship tow, from its current location in Mobile, AL to a point in the Gulf of America where it will be sunk as an artificial reef. The entities involved in this operations have requested that the Coast Guard establish a safety zone around the S.S. UNITED STATES, and all vessels involved in its towage, as it is towed from its pier in Mobile, Alabama, through the Mobile River Channel, Mobile Bay, and into the Gulf of America. Hazards from the departure of the S.S. UNITED STATES include restricted maneuverability of tow, wake from passing traffic, and potential for significant vessel congestion. The Captain of the Port Sector Mobile (COTP) has determined that these potential hazards associated with towing the S.S. UNITED STATES are a safety concern for anyone within 100 yards of the towing evolution. Therefore, the COTP is issuing this rule under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, which is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the vicinity of this dead-ship towing operation.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. The schedule for this towing operation was not finalized until October 20, 2026, and therefore the Coast Guard was unable to publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking for this safety zone prior to the dead-ship tow operation beginning as early as October 12, 2026. This safety zone must be established by November 6, 2026 to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from the hazards associated with the operation. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reasons, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary moving safety zone that will be in effect from November 6, 2026, through November 16, 2026. The safety zone will cover all navigable waters within 100 yards of the S.S. UNITED STATES and all vessels involved in the dead ship tow operation. While the rule will be effective 10 days, the zone will only be enforced during active dead ship tow operations for the transit of the S.S. UNITED STATES from the pier in Mobile, AL until it reaches the limit of the United States Territorial Sea, approximately 12 Nautical Miles (NM) offshore of Destin, FL. The date and time of the vessel's departure will depend on weather and sea conditions in the area. In advance of the vessel's departure, the COTP will issue a Broadcast Notice to Mariners via marine channel 16 (VHF-FM), as well as other public advisories, to inform the local maritime community of the exact dates(s) and times that the safety zone will be enforced. No vessel or person would be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.

articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
                    SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the State of Rhode Island is transferring a portion of their 2026 commercial bluefish quota to the State of North Carolina. This quota adjustment is necessary to comply with the Atlantic Bluefish Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial bluefish quotas for Rhode Island and North Carolina.
                    DATES:
Effective October 29, 2026, through December 31, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the Atlantic bluefish fishery are found in 50 CFR 648.160 through 648.167. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through Florida. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.162, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (91 FR 7896).
                    The final rule implementing amendment 1 to the FMP, as published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     on July 26, 2000 (65 FR 45844), provided a mechanism for transferring bluefish commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can request approval to transfer or combine bluefish commercial quota under § 648.162(e). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined these criteria have been met for the transfers approved in this notification.
                
Rhode Island is transferring 100,000 pounds (lb) (45,359 kilograms (kg)) of Atlantic bluefish to North Carolina through mutual agreement of the states. This transfer was requested to ensure North Carolina would not exceed its 2026 state quota. The revised bluefish quotas for 2026 are: Rhode Island, 310,612 lb (140,891 kg); and North Carolina, 2,043,521 lb (926,926 kg).
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR 648.162(e)(1)(i) through (iii), which was issued pursuant to section 304(b), and is exempted from review under Executive Order 12866.

articles.title: Hong Kong records highest export growth in 40 years. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Hong Kong records highest export growth in 40 years.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
|  Hong Kong's export volume has just set a record for growth after more than 40 years. Photo: SCMP/Nora Tam . | 
 According to SCMP , Hong Kong's (China) exports hit a record high in September, the first in over 40 years. The main driver of this growth came from products related to artificial intelligence ( AI ).
 According to preliminary figures just released by the Census and Statistics Bureau, the special administrative region's total exports in September reached HK$762.6 billion (equivalent to US$97.8 billion ), continuing the 53% growth trend of August.
 According to the special administrative region's leadership, September's exports marked a 20-month streak of double-digit growth, setting a year-on-year growth record for over 40 years.
 Regionally, Hong Kong's total exports to Asia in September increased by nearly 68% year-on-year, driven by strong performance in key markets. Notably, significant growth was seen in Malaysia (+132%) and Thailand (+118%).
 In terms of import value, South Korea continues to top the list of partners with the strongest growth, with Hong Kong experiencing a surge of 231% in September compared to the same period last year. This is followed by Vietnam with a 119% increase and Malaysia with a 74% increase.
 In September, the special administrative region's imports also increased by 58%, reaching HK$808.9 billion ( US$103.1 billion ), resulting in a trade deficit of HK$46.3 billion ( US$5.9 billion ), equivalent to nearly 6% of the value of imported goods.
 In the first nine months of 2026, Hong Kong's trade maintained strong growth momentum, with total import and export values increasing by 45% year-on-year, resulting in a trade deficit of HK$417.7 billion ( US$53.2 billion ).
 In terms of product structure, global competition for artificial intelligence (AI) products was the driving force behind growth. Specifically, exports of machinery and electrical parts increased by 66%, reaching HK$390.8 billion ( US$49.8 billion ).
 In addition, the office equipment and automated data processing equipment category recorded growth of up to 184%, reaching HK$135.4 billion ( US$17.3 billion ).
 Explaining these figures, Lee Shu-kam, Director of the Centre for Business, Economics and Public Policy Research at Shue Yan University of Hong Kong, suggested that this growth stems from an early strategy focused on developing AI products, amidst market impacts from US tariff policies.
 "Before policies become clear, the market tends to rush to buy and hoard AI products," he observed , adding that with the current hoarding wave, Hong Kong is playing the role of a major trade intermediary, importing large quantities of goods and then exporting them.
 Mr. Lee predicted that this export growth momentum would continue until the tariff policy is announced at the end of 2027, and that the growth rate in the following months might slow down compared to September.
 The surge in exports has boosted Hong Kong's economic growth this year, with second-quarter growth at 4.3% year-on-year. Thanks to these positive signs, in August the special administrative region's government raised its full-year economic growth forecast to 3.5-4.5%, higher than its previous forecast of 2.5-3.5%.

articles.title: Thailand Targets Global Pet Hub Status as Pet Food Exports Reach $3.28 Billion - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand Targets Global Pet Hub Status as Pet Food Exports Reach $3.28 Billion  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Rising global demand and supply chain strengths bolster Thailand’s push to become the world’s leading exporter of premium pet nutrition.
Thailand is accelerating its ambition to become the world’s leading exporter of dog and cat food, backed by robust international trade figures and solidifying its position as the global pet industry’s second-largest supplier.
According to the Department of International Trade Promotion (DITP) under the Ministry of Commerce, Thai pet food exports exceeded USD 3.28 billion (THB 111 billion) in 2025, representing an 8.15 per cent year-on-year increase.
The figures highlight Thailand’s expanding footprint in the global pet care ecosystem, driven by surging international demand for specialised nutrition, high-protein formulations, and premium private-label manufacturing.
Dog and cat food continue to anchor the sector, accounting for nearly 88 per cent of total shipments. The expansion has been propelled by double-digit export growth in key developed and emerging markets, including Western Europe, Australasia, and Asia-Pacific trade corridors.
Analysts attribute this momentum to the global "pet humanisation" trend—where owners increasingly treat companion animals as family members—creating sustained demand for functional, health-focused, and sustainable pet care products.
Delivering the opening address at the fifth edition of Pet Fair South East Asia 2026 at the Bangkok International Trade & Exhibition Centre (BITEC) on Wednesday (October 28), Surinthorn Sunthornsanan, Deputy Director-General of the DITP, highlighted how shifting consumer habits are reshaping the industrial landscape.
"In recent years, the global pet industry has experienced tremendous growth, driven by increasing demand for premium pet food, wellness products, and specialised services—a trend widely known as pet humanisation," Surinthorn stated. "In 2025, our pet food exports exceeded USD 3.28 billion, an impressive 8.15 per cent growth on the previous year. This remarkable achievement speaks to the strength, excellence, and adaptability of our industry."
Surinthorn reaffirmed the Thai government's commitment to supporting domestic enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), by deploying free trade agreements (FTAs), offering on-site advisory services, and leading trade delegations abroad to connect local manufacturers with global markets.
Thailand’s robust agricultural supply chain, advanced processing technology, and strict international quality standards have enabled domestic manufacturers to capture roughly 10 per cent of total global pet food exports.
To capitalise on this competitive advantage, industry stakeholders are increasingly focusing on higher-value contract manufacturing, brand development, and sustainable packaging solutions.
Organised jointly by VNU Asia Pacific and Globus Events Limited, the three-day B2B trade exhibition serves as a critical business gateway, connecting manufacturers, exporters, brand owners, distributors, and buyers across the complete supply chain.
The 2026 event brings together 450 exhibiting companies from 35 countries, with international participants comprising 70 per cent of the exhibition floor.
Organisers expect to welcome more than 12,500 trade professionals from over 80 nations across three days, building upon the previous edition’s attendance of 11,169 visitors.
Beyond driving international trade, the event serves as a substantial economic catalyst for Thailand's domestic hospitality and business travel sectors.
Duangdej Yuaikwarmdee, Chief Executive Officer of VNU Asia Pacific, revealed that the exhibition is projected to generate roughly THB 580 million (USD 17.1 million) in direct economic impact, including THB 300 million (USD 8.87 million) in visitor travel expenditure while supporting around 300 local jobs.
Duangdej also emphasised a strong commitment to environmental and social responsibility, detailing eco-conscious event measures such as recycled carpeting, reduced single-use plastics, digital ticketing, and converting suitable event waste into alternative fuel rather than sending it to landfill.
"For us, a successful show creates business opportunities while leaving a positive impact on both the community and the environment," he noted.
The exposition encompasses the full spectrum of the pet industry, ranging from ingredients, nutrition, and hygiene products to automated processing machinery, packaging systems, and OEM services.
Technical knowledge exchange remains central to the summit, featuring a comprehensive conference programme that includes the Petfood Extrusion & Nutrition Conference and the Pet Innovators Pitch platform, designed to explore technological advancements and investment trends shaping global pet care.
The expanding network of regional trade events also highlights deepening economic links within Asia.
David Zhong, founder and president of Globus Events Limited and Pet Fair Asia Limited, pointed to the growing integration between regional markets since the network launched in 1997.
He noted that the recent Pet Fair Asia in Shanghai, which drew over 2,600 exhibitors and 130,000 trade visitors from more than 100 countries, featured a dedicated Thailand Pavilion and recorded its highest number of international attendees from Thailand.
"Asia, with its dynamic market, manufacturing strength, and energy, will play an increasingly important role in the industry's next chapter," Zhong remarked.
He added that regional research initiatives led by the Asian Pet Alliance (APA) Research Institute would soon release English-language market reports to assist international executives in navigating emerging regional opportunities.
Supporting Thailand’s broader MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conventions, and Exhibitions) sector, Kanokporn Damrongkul, director of the Exhibitions Department at the Thailand Convention and Exhibition Bureau (TCEB), highlighted the structural importance of trade platforms to the national economy.
"Within our national agriculture, pet food manufacturing has become a standout performer," Kanokporn noted. "International trade exhibitions are far more than product displays; they are catalysts for knowledge exchange, cross-border partnerships, and economic value creation. The continued participation of international exhibitors and buyers reflects deep confidence in Thailand as a premier destination for business collaboration."
As global pet ownership continues to expand and premiumisation drives consumer spending, Thailand’s integration of high-value manufacturing, raw material resilience, and international trade infrastructure positions the Southeast Asian nation to capture a larger share of the multi-billion-dollar global pet care market.

BEIJING, Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A conference on enterprises going global in the Yellow River basin was held in Jinan City, capital of east China's Shandong Province, on Tuesday.
The conference aimed to implement the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) through high-quality cooperation and promote resource matching for enterprises in the Yellow River basin.
During the conference, the Department of Commerce of Shandong Province released three major outcomes, including a list of cooperation demand of enterprises in such fields as foreign labor service, outward investment, and construction machinery, a catalogue of services for enterprises going global, and investment cooperation reports on Indonesia, Thailand, Uzbekistan and Hungary.
The conference also saw the launch ceremony for the official operation of the Shandong Global Business Service Hub and the unveiling ceremony for the Yellow River Basin Enterprise Maritime Service Window.
It is reported that during its trial operation, the Shandong Global Business Service Hub has already served more than 700 enterprises from Shandong and other regions. The Yellow River Basin Enterprise Maritime Service Window has been set up in Jinan, Qingdao and Yantai, providing targeted shipping services for customers in the green petrochemical industry and others.
In the experience-sharing session, Pan Haiping, chairman of China Economic Information Service (CEIS), and Shu Hai, vice president of Haier Group, delivered keynote speeches. They shared their practices in supporting high-quality overseas business expansion and promoting global brand building.
During the signing ceremony, enterprises from the Yellow River basin inked 17 cooperation agreements with professional overseas service providers, covering foreign-related legal services, financial leasing, overseas engineering projects, industrial investment and global business collaboration.
Participants noted that Chinese enterprises' outbound investment has kept expanding, driving robust market demand for high-quality, professional global business services. Shandong boasts strong opening-up momentum and has consistently pioneered integrated development of trade and investment. The Shandong Global Business Service Hub has laid a solid service foundation for enterprises to pursue high-quality global expansion.
The conference was hosted by the Department of Commerce of Shandong Province and co-organized by CEIS and the China Council for International Investment Promotion (CCIIP).

articles.title: Chinese New Energy Enterprises Expand Overseas Amid Intense Domestic Homogeneous Competition: Latest Industry Dynamics Unveiled Ahead of All Energy Australia - eu.36kr.com
articles.summary: Chinese New Energy Enterprises Expand Overseas Amid Intense Domestic Homogeneous Competition: Latest Industry Dynamics Unveiled Ahead of All Energy Australia  eu.36kr.com
articles.full_text:
Cutthroat homogeneous competition in China's domestic new energy industry has become unsustainable, pushing local enterprises to expand overseas. On the eve of the All Energy Australia event, Chinese enterprises have brought the latest industry dynamics to Australia.
The domestic energy storage market is contracting, while Australia sees strong demand for energy storage, shifting the core competition focus of Chinese enterprises going global to channels and local services.
On October 28, All-Energy Australia kicked off at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre. Among more than 490 exhibitors, the Chinese exhibition group is the largest overseas cluster, with over 150 Chinese enterprises already present at the previous edition.
The day before the exhibition opened, Sungrow held a channel event with more than 600 attendees in Melbourne, rolling out new product launches and customer banquets simultaneously. Behind the event pace is a set of figures: In the first half of 2026, the newly installed capacity of new-type energy storage in China reached 17GW/45GWh, with a year-on-year power decline of 19.6%, marking the first semi-annual negative growth in three years of explosive growth; in the same period, Chinese enterprises signed 298GWh of overseas energy storage orders, up 83% year on year, with Australia ranking first among all single markets at 32.91GWh.
With one market contracting and the other expanding, enterprises naturally shift their pace to the latter.
0.4999 yuan is not a price, but a threshold
To understand why Chinese enterprises book larger exhibition booths year by year, we need to first go back to the domestic bidding records.
Huadian's 12GWh energy storage system framework procurement attracted bids from 59 enterprises, with the overall quotation range from 0.4923 to 0.6207 yuan/Wh, and the lowest winning bid price was 0.4999 yuan/Wh.
While the market pie is shrinking, the number of bidding enterprises has not decreased, making the expression of the supply-demand relationship on the quotation form extremely straightforward.
Further pressure comes from revenue.
The actual implementation rate of a large number of filed independent energy storage projects is only 30% to 40%, the actual rate of return of most power stations falls in the range of 3% to 4%, and more than half of the projects are in a loss-making state.
Investors cannot make the accounts add up, so the construction pace naturally slows down, and orders at the equipment end change from "increment allocation" to "stock competition".
Sungrow Power's overseas gross profit margin of energy storage systems in 2025 was 40.36%, compared with 18.49% in the domestic market, a gap of more than 20 percentage points that needs no rhetorical embellishment.
Sunwoda New Energy wrote "deep cultivation of overseas markets to hedge against internal competition" into its business statement during investor communications, which is not the preference of a single enterprise, but a unified action taken by a group of enterprises facing the same profit statement.
As a result, going global has changed from an "option" to an "outlet". But the problems faced after going global are far more complex than just "where to go".
Australia's door is wide open, and what you compete on after entering is not product brochures
Australia is indeed the most attractive single market for residential energy storage across the globe at the moment.
The penetration rate of rooftop photovoltaics is close to 40%, with a stock of over 4.3 million sets, while the energy storage matching rate has long stayed at around 10%. The federal government's "Cheaper Home Battery Program" has shortened the payback period of residential energy storage from 7-8 years to 4-5 years, driving a surge in corresponding demand.
Chinese brands occupy more than 70% of the market share in the residential energy storage battery and inverter market. The high density of supply side determines that competition will not stay at the level of "whether there are goods available".
The sales chain of residential energy storage in Australia runs from brands to distributors, from distributors to installers, and from installers to end households.
OSW has been the platform with the largest market share in Australia's residential solar and energy storage distribution market for seven consecutive years, and its distribution network covers more than 80% of installers. This means that even if a Chinese enterprise adds 500 extra cycles to the cycle life description and extends the warranty period by one more year on its Melbourne exhibition booth, such advantages weigh far less in the installer's procurement decision than another question: Can the goods arrive at the warehouse within two weeks, can a technical support call be answered within ten minutes, and can spare parts be delivered together with the installer's truck?
Maitian Energy's success in Australia in the first half of 2026 did not come from translating its domestic price list into Australian dollars, but from first signing distribution agreements with OSW and Solar Juice.
Sungrow took another path, building awareness among installers and end users with the brand logic of consumer electronics, making installers pay more attention to its products on the shelf and save more time during installation.
The two paths point to the same conclusion: The competitive medium in Australia is no longer product parameters, but the depth of channel embedding and the certainty of local service response.
While domestic competition focuses on the decimal points on the quotation form, in the southern hemisphere, the competition targets the warehouse turnover rate of distributors, the operation efficiency of installers and the coverage radius of the spare parts network. The same kind of "involution" has a higher threshold after changing the competitive medium.
The landscape of large-scale energy storage is quieter and more realistic. CATL's layout in Australia is not on rooftops, but on the grid side. The first and second phases of the Supernode project, with a capacity of 520MW/1858MWh, have been fully put into commercial operation. After the third phase is completed, the total scale will exceed 3GWh, making it the largest operating battery energy storage project in Australia's National Electricity Market.
This is not a channel business, but a business that tests the closing of project financing, the pace of large-scale delivery and the availability rate throughout the full life cycle. Competition in large-scale energy storage does not take place in the aisles of exhibition halls, but at the windows of financing delivery documents and grid connection approval. The people who can sit at that negotiation table and those who can only distribute brochures on the exhibition booth breathe the same air in the same exhibition hall, but are not at the same competition table.
Exhibition booths will be dismantled, but channels will not
More than 150 Chinese enterprises flew to Melbourne, competing on energy density, cycle times and the industrial design of all-in-one machines on their booths. These parameters have already been competed over in a full round in the domestic market, and doing the same in Australia is essentially not breaking out of the old script.
The real variables are outside the exhibition hall: whose distribution agreement covers more active installers, whose spare parts warehouse is closer to the installers' operation radius, and whose local technical team can give a transfer-free answer when the installer makes a call.
The penetration rate of residential photovoltaics in Australia is already close to 40%, and the stock of rooftops available for residential energy storage is real. But the path to turn the stock into orders is not under the spotlights of exhibition booths, but on the roads that installers drive every day.
The domestic market shrinkage forces enterprises to go global, but after going global, they find that competition has not become lighter, but deeper. In China, the depth of competition is measured in "minutes"; in Australia, the depth of competition is measured by the payment collection cycle counted in "weeks", the response speed counted in "hours" and the service radius counted in "kilometers".
The scoreboard for the next round of competition is not on the exhibition booths, but in those places outside the booths.

articles.title: Thailand Watches US Midterms for Signals on Trade, Investment and Regional Stability - Thailand Business News
articles.summary: Thailand Watches US Midterms for Signals on Trade, Investment and Regional Stability  Thailand Business News
articles.full_text:
The outcome of the US midterm elections is being closely monitored across Asia, with potentially significant consequences for Thailand’s export-driven . The United States remains one of Thailand’s most important trading partners, with Thai exports to the US valued at approximately US$72.6 billion in 2025, led by electrical and electronic products, machinery, rubber products and vehicles.
For Thailand’s electronics sector, the stakes are particularly high. Electronics and electrical appliances have been the primary drivers of Thai export growth, supported by rising global demand for AI infrastructure, semiconductors and data-centre technologies. Thai exports reached a record US$339.6 billion in 2025, with electronics playing a leading role. Any shift in US policy toward China, technology exports or semiconductor supply chains could directly affect and manufacturing activity in Thailand.
Thailand’s automotive and EV industries are also paying close attention. Motor vehicles and parts remain one of the country’s top export categories, accounting for more than 662 billion baht in exports during the first eight months of 2026. Future US trade measures and industrial policies could influence global production networks, investment decisions and demand for Thai-made vehicles and components.
Meanwhile, Thailand’s agricultural exporters, including rice, rubber and processed food producers, remain vulnerable to shifts in global trade patterns and tariff policies. Recent trade data show agricultural exports facing increasing competitive pressure despite strong performance in some processed food categories.
While the elections are a domestic US event, their impact could extend across global supply chains, trade flows and financial markets. For Thai , the key question is whether post-election policies support stable economic engagement with Asia or deepen strategic and economic divisions between the United States and China.

EFTA expects trade and investment with Vietnam to grow

The EFTA–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement is expected to open up significant business opportunities for Vietnamese enterprises. (Photo: baochinhphu.vn)
Hanoi (VNA) – According to UK-based Trade Finance Global, the four member states of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), namely Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, believe that a free trade agreement (FTA) with Vietnam will expand market access opportunities, reduce trade costs and provide a more stable and transparent framework for business and investment.
Regarding market access and trade benefits, the EFTA countries expect the agreement to gradually eliminate tariffs on almost all goods exported by the four countries to Vietnam, either upon its entry into force or within a maximum period of 16 years.
Asdis Olafsdottir, Head of Communications at the EFTA Secretariat, said the agreement will open up new opportunities across a range of sectors, from seafood and machinery to watches and chocolate.
According to the Norwegian Government, around 50% of Norwegian goods exports will be exempt from tariffs upon entering Vietnam, with the proportion expected to exceed 98% within seven years. In return, Vietnamese exports to EFTA countries will also benefit from tariff exemptions or reductions.
On facilitating business operations, EFTA representatives said lower trade costs, simplified customs procedures and greater transparency will particularly benefit small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which are considered the backbone of the member states’ economies.
The agreement covers goods, services, investment, intellectual property, sustainable development and other areas, thereby providing a predictable framework for trade and investment activities.

Meanwhile, the European Union (EU) upgraded its relations with Vietnam to a comprehensive strategic partnership in January 2026 and is seeking to strengthen access to Vietnam’s critical mineral resources./.
