articles.title: Australian recession now a coin toss, says major bank - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: Australian recession now a coin toss, says major bank  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Australia has a dirty little secret.
Despite four Reserve Bank interest rate hikes, supposed fiscal restraint, and a recent small improvement in productivity, inflation is rising.
At face value, it makes no sense. Millions of households continue to struggle to make ends meet.
Dig a little deeper, though, and the logic of why the country continues to struggle with inflation is painfully simple.
There's simply too much money chasing too few goods and services.
There appears to be only one solution: Lower demand until the economy breaks.
While there were some whisperings that Australia could move into recession, now the case is growing with a second leading economist today adding his voice to concerns the worst could still be ahead. More about that later.
Moving pieces of economic puzzle
To understand Australia's inflation problem, look no further than the Reserve Bank's commentary.
Following its most recent decision to raise the cash rate, the RBA's statement began by saying inflation was already too high.
It went on to say "… and some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising".
"The conflict in the Middle East has broadened, and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts," it wrote.
"AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods.
"And there remains pressure on domestic capacity."
Put simply, the economy is struggling to supply the goods and services to meet current demand, and higher energy prices are adding to the cost-of-living pain.
The solution then is to boost the nation's ability to meet demand.
Failing that, demand needs to come down.
Inflation slipping away from us
Better news on the supply front came in the most recent national accounts, where GDP per hour worked (one measure of productivity) moved out of negative territory, albeit to zero.
But over the year, it sits at -0.2 per cent.
Lacklustre productivity means the only near-term option is for demand to fall.
Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Wednesday the government was doing its bit.
"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … we accept our part in the fight against inflation," he said.
And while private (or business) investment did not contribute to GDP in the June quarter, it was driven by household consumption (+0.2 percentage points).
It has put a target on the back of households as the ones to blame for the "excess" demand.
Iran war making inflation sticky
And this is the critical point. The Iran war is squeezing oil supplies and forcing fuel prices higher.
The Reserve Bank says its liaison program shows businesses are passing higher production costs on to customers.
Worse still, as RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said this week, is that businesses don't really see an end in sight to elevated costs.
"There's just some sign that some companies might be thinking, 'You know what? Maybe prices aren't going all the way back. And if they're not, we're going to have to take that into account with the pricing decisions.'"
This paves the way for his "nightmare" central banker scenario of unanchored inflation expectations.
Sledgehammer to demand
One way to reverse this vicious cycle is to ensure consumers don't have money in their pockets to spend, or at least not as much.
Hence, interest rate rises take money out of consumers' pockets.
So, rather than supply not meeting demand, demand can't meet supply.
Economic theory tells you prices then stop rising and actually fall.
Why? Because business owners are forced to lower prices to bring customers back into their stores.
To be fair, the Reserve Bank has tried to set this path in motion but its "cautious" approach has proved too cautious.
But if households spend so little that the corner store doesn't replace a leaving staff member, the person who would otherwise have landed that job buys fewer items and saves more … and so on.
This environment could push the unemployment rate beyond 5 per cent, former NAB chief economist Alan Oster says.
But interest rates need to rise higher for this to occur.
"My worst-case scenario would be two or three further rate rises, which I think would clearly cause you recession,"
Mr Oster said.
"And I think you're probably going to struggle anyway.
"Certainly, I'd expect, I'll wait until they've actually done it before I review my forecast, but I would expect to see lower growth and higher levels of unemployment and probably unemployment with the five in front of it," he said.
HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham forecasts the damage to demand this year and next will see the unemployment rate hit 5.1 per cent.
He also has updated his economic growth forecasts and now sees the chances of an Australian recession in 2027 as a coin toss.
"We see a recession as a 50:50 chance," he said.
So will rates keep rising?
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese does not think the RBA will need to hike interest rates beyond November, but concedes Australia would likely enter a recession if it did.
"All up, my base case is that RBA will raise rates next week but then leave rates on hold at the last meeting of the year in December, providing households at least a small pre-Xmas reprieve," he said.
Loading
"Given gathering signs of weakness in the economy, particularly the very weak outlook for house prices, my expectation is the RBA won't need to raise rates further in 2027, though the risk still lay firmly to the upside.
"Should rates need to rise even further next year, the risk of recession would no doubt intensify."
The number of interest rate hikes from here, says State Street Investment Management economist Ma Krishna Bhimavarapu, will depend on how much weaker the economy gets in coming months.
"We still expect the cash rate to ultimately have a five handle, but the path from here will depend on how quickly the economy slows," he said.
The nation faced two options 12 months ago: improve productivity or else.
The exogenous shock of an oil-sensitive war made improving productivity urgent, but we've missed the boat.
The Reserve Bank is now left with the unenviable task of taking a sledgehammer to demand for the greater good.
Let's be honest, it's positively sinister, as are most dirty little secrets.

articles.title: US Bans Imports From Chinese Genomics Firms BGI and MGI - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: US Bans Imports From Chinese Genomics Firms BGI and MGI  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
The US has barred imports from Chinese genomics companies BGI Genomics, MGI Tech, and BGI Group under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, one week after Treasury proposed restrictions on US investment in Chinese biotechnology. The measures widen US trade controls into life sciences as the USMCA review increases scrutiny of Chinese inputs in North American supply chains. Pharmaceutical, diagnostics, and laboratory supply chains linked to US exports, including those operating in Mexico, face more pressure on compliance and sourcing.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) added BGI Genomics, MGI Tech, and Shenzhen BGI Technology, also known as BGI Group, to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List on Oct. 28, 2026, barring their goods from the US market over alleged links to the tracking of persecuted minorities in Xinjiang.
According to DHS, the three companies “helped collect genetic material used to track persecuted ethnic minorities, including people subjected to forced labor.” The UFLPA Entity List identifies entities that work with the Xinjiang government to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, or members of other persecuted groups. Goods produced by listed companies are presumed to involve forced labor and are blocked at the US border unless importers can rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. DHS also framed the action as “enforcing our laws, protecting American businesses from unfair competition.”
China’s Ministry of Commerce says it “strongly condemns” the measure, which it describes as lacking “factual basis.” “The US side continues to exploit the issue of ‘human rights,’ using it as a pretext to carry out unilateral protectionism and bullying,” says a ministry spokesperson. Beijing urged Washington to “immediately cease its political manipulation and smear campaigns” and says it will take the necessary measures to safeguard its interests. BGI and MGI reject the allegations and say they oppose all forms of forced labor. MGI says it will challenge the designation, while BGI says it will communicate with the relevant authorities.
The designation builds on a broader US enforcement push around Xinjiang. In 2022, the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights warned that abuses in the region may constitute crimes against humanity, including the detention of more than 1 million Uyghurs and members of other Muslim minority communities in camps. Beijing has repeatedly denied the allegations.
The UFLPA list has grown throughout 2026. On July 31, 2026, DHS announced 43 new entities, the largest single expansion in the list’s history, bringing the total to 187 and including nine pharmaceutical companies. With the genomics firms, the list reaches 190 names. The BGI companies were already subject to other US restrictions: in March 2023, the Department of Commerce added two BGI subsidiaries to its Entity List over risks that their genetic data collection could contribute to surveillance.
The companies’ direct exposure to the region is small. BGI Genomics reported that the Americas accounted for less than 2% of its 2025 revenue, while about 8% of MGI’s revenue comes from the region. In February 2026, MGI agreed to divest its US unit, Complete Genomics.
The import ban arrives one week after the US Department of the Treasury proposed adding biotechnology to its Outbound Investment Security Program under the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act. Published on Oct. 22, 2026, the proposal would restrict certain US investments in China and other countries of concern in areas such as biological design and sequencing tools, bioinformatics, and biomanufacturing equipment, extending a regime that already covers semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technologies. Public comments are open until Dec. 7, 2026.
For Mexico, the measures add to a trade environment in which Washington is scrutinizing Chinese participation in North American supply chains. Mexico imported about US$133 billion in Chinese goods in 2025, and US proposals in the ongoing USMCA review reportedly include tighter rules of origin and possible screening of Chinese capital, as Samuel Campos, Executive Managing Director, Newmark, explains in an MBN expert contribution. Mexico has also imposed tariffs of 5% to 50% on more than 1,400 product lines from countries without a trade agreement, Campos adds.
The life sciences sector is particularly exposed to this scrutiny. A US Senate Special Committee on Aging analysis estimates that China supplies about 70% of acetaminophen precursors and up to 90% of the active ingredients for widely used antibiotics, MBN reports. Industry leaders interviewed by MBN describe heavy dependence on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) as a vulnerability for Mexico’s supply chain, as companies such as Bayer expand local production with an eye on US exports starting in 2027.
Genomics is also an emerging priority for Mexico’s health system. Jorge Meléndez, General Director, National Institute of Genomic Medicine (INMEGEN), writes that about 80% of rare diseases have a genetic basis and that the limited availability of high-complexity testing, such as genomic panels, delays diagnosis. He proposes public-private pilot programs for genomic diagnostics to demonstrate cost-effectiveness before scaling them nationwide. Under the UFLPA, the presumption covers goods produced wholly or in part by listed entities, a standard that applies to any exporter shipping to the US, including companies operating in Mexico.
Risk analysts expect further US action. Kit Conklin of risk management firm Exiger says additional US measures against Chinese biotechnology firms are likely. Other technologies already under US scrutiny include artificial intelligence and semiconductors, central fronts in the ongoing economic competition between Beijing and Washington.

articles.title: The end of de minimis doesn’t mean the end of China-based fulfillment - Supply Chain Management Review
articles.summary: The end of de minimis doesn’t mean the end of China-based fulfillment  Supply Chain Management Review
articles.full_text:
Many direct-to-consumer brands, especially smaller Shopify, Amazon and TikTok Shop sellers, built their entire fulfillment model around shipping individual orders straight from Chinese factories or fulfillment centers to U.S. doorsteps.
However, a major policy shift in the United States has upended global trade for these companies, forcing them to rethink their supply chains and even their overall business models because of the potential impact on their bottom lines. The conventional advice for importers is to find a U.S. fulfillment option to ship and store products domestically.
But there is another way. Brands don’t need to choose between China and U.S. fulfillment. These models are not mutually exclusive. They can be integrated into a fulfillment strategy that evolves with the brand. Before providing operational insights into this hybrid approach, let’s dig into how we got here.
De minimis changed the e-commerce supply chain
For decades, the U.S. has allowed certain low-value imports to enter the country duty-free and with simplified customs procedures. This “de minimis” treatment, mirrored in some form by many other economies, was intended to streamline and facilitate global trade.
In 2016, the U.S. raised its de minimis threshold from $200 to $800. The higher exemption helped enable retailers to redesign their supply chains around direct-to-consumer cross-border fulfillment. It also contributed to the growth of low-cost Chinese online retailers such as Temu and Shein.
The use of the de minimis exemption has exploded, growing from 224 million shipments in 2016 to more than 1 billion in 2023. A 2023 Congressional report found that Temu and Shein alone were likely responsible for nearly half of all de minimis shipments to the U.S. from China.
The Trump administration said the exemption was overused and abused, and suspended duty-free de minimis treatment for products from China and Hong Kong in May 2025, then extended the suspension to shipments from all countries effective Aug. 29, 2025. The suspension continued into 2026. The European Union followed with a similar change in July 2026, abolishing its €150 customs-duty exemption and introducing a temporary €3 customs duty per item on qualifying low-value imports.
The new math of cross-border fulfillment
The abrupt end of de minimis created chaos in cross-border e-commerce. Many industry observers initially predicted that the end of the exemption would signal the death knell for fulfillment from China. In reality, it simply transformed the math. The loss of duty-free status significantly reduced the tariff advantage of direct-to-consumer cross-border fulfillment, but it did not eliminate the structural advantages of manufacturing and staging in China and the deeply entrenched supply chains that fuel global trade.
The policy shift has forced DTC brands to tailor their supply chains to their growth stage:
- Early stage: Stay close to the factory. For brands just starting, the priority is minimizing inventory risk and preserving cash. By fulfilling orders directly from China, near the point of manufacture, businesses can avoid the heavy capital outlay required to pre-ship large quantities of bulk inventory to U.S. warehouses before demand is proven.
- Growth stage: Get closer to the customer. As a brand gains traction, the focus shifts to speed and consistency. At this stage, high-growth sellers should migrate to a distributed warehousing model in the U.S. Staging inventory domestically allows brands to offer the fast delivery speeds American consumers expect while generally calculating customs duties based on the value of the goods at import rather than the product’s eventual U.S. retail selling price. Under the standard transaction-value method, CBP generally bases the customs value on the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods, subject to applicable adjustments.
- Mature stage: Go global. Truly mature brands require global expansion capabilities. This stage calls for a network of fulfillment centers across key international markets to provide a seamless, localized experience wherever customers live.
Think about inventory velocity, not just geography
Brands can also segment their inventory based on turnover rates. Proven, high-velocity core products, the best-sellers that drive consistent sales, are routed in bulk to U.S. fulfillment centers. For these high-volume items, bulk ocean freight spreads out customs clearance fees, port fees, and tariffs across thousands of units. This brings the per-unit shipping cost down while enabling the fast domestic delivery speeds that U.S. consumers increasingly expect.
Staging in China near the production line still makes sense for long-tail items, new product launches and seasonal variations. For unproven inventory, storing products in U.S. warehouses can add significant storage, handling and labor costs before demand is established. If a new product launch underperforms, the brand can limit its exposure to the additional overseas shipping, domestic handling and long-term storage costs that would come with pre-positioning large quantities of inventory in the U.S. If the product is a breakout success, the brand can seamlessly transition the next manufacturing batch into a bulk ocean shipment to replenish U.S. fulfillment centers.
About the author
William Yu is the founder and CEO of NextSmartShip, serving over 2,000 DTC brands globally. Coming from a marketing background, he founded NSS after identifying a critical gap between China’s manufacturing ecosystem and the global fulfillment infrastructure for modern ecommerce brands. He brings a customer-first perspective to logistics—treating fulfillment as a growth engine, not just a cost center. Today, NextSmartShip operates 20+ fulfillment centers across 13 countries, helping brands optimize inventory, reduce risk and scale internationally.
.

AGENCY:
Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In compliance with the requirement for opportunity for public comment on proposed data collection projects of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, HRSA announces plans to submit an Information Collection Request (ICR), described below, to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). Prior to submitting the ICR to OMB, HRSA seeks comments from the public regarding the burden estimate, below, or any other aspect of the ICR.
DATES:
Comments on this ICR should be received no later than December 29, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments to
paperwork@hrsa.gov
or mail the HRSA Information Collection Clearance Officer, Room 13N82, 5600 Fishers Lane, Rockville, MD 20857.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
To request more information on the proposed project or to obtain a copy of the data collection plans and draft instruments, email
paperwork@hrsa.gov
or call Samantha Miller, the HRSA Information Collection Clearance Officer at (301) 443-9094.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
When submitting comments or requesting information, please include the information request collection title for reference.
Information Collection Request Title:
AIDS Drug Assistance Program—Transformation: Optimization and Best Practices in the Evolving Health Care Landscape, OMB No. 0906-XXXX—New.
Abstract:
HRSA's HIV/AIDS Bureau administers the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program, including the AIDS Drug Assistance Program (ADAP). ADAPs help low-income people with HIV access therapeutics to treat HIV/AIDS or prevent the serious deterioration of health arising from HIV/AIDS, including measures for the prevention and
( printed page 68526)
treatment of opportunistic infections and health care coverage assistance. As health care coverage environments, treatment options, and program financing mechanisms continue to evolve, ADAPs face increasing operational complexity related to eligibility determination; client enrollment and retention; health care coverage navigation; pharmacy management; rebate administration; and data infrastructure. HRSA currently lacks comprehensive, national-level information about how ADAPs manage these operational functions and address emerging challenges.
To address these information gaps, HRSA developed the ADAP Transformation: Optimization and Best Practices in the Evolving Health Care Landscape study. Through this effort, HRSA will collect program-level information from ADAPs nationwide through a web-based survey, qualitative interviews with a purposeful sample of ADAP staff, and virtual listening sessions with the broader ADAP community. The study will identify operational best practices, barriers, and opportunities for technical assistance to strengthen ADAP capacity and support access to HIV care and treatment services. No client-level information, personally identifiable information, or protected health information will be collected.
Need and Proposed Use of the Information:
The proposed information collection will provide HRSA with systematic information on operational and administrative practices across ADAPs nationwide. Survey, interview, and listening session data will help HRSA identify effective strategies for managing eligibility processes; client enrollment and recertification; health care coverage continuity; pharmacy operations; rebate management; cost-containment efforts; and data systems modernization.
Findings will support the development of tailored technical assistance, tools, guidance, and dissemination activities designed to strengthen ADAP operations. Results will also inform HRSA program planning and future data collection efforts. Study findings will be reported only in aggregate or de-identified form and will not be used for compliance monitoring or funding decisions.
Likely Respondents:
Respondents will consist of staff from state and territorial ADAPs, including program administrators, eligibility and enrollment staff, pharmacy and benefits coordinators, financial and rebate management staff, data systems personnel, and other staff responsible for ADAP operations. HRSA will also invite ADAP staff to participate in virtual listening sessions focused on validating and contextualizing study findings.
Burden Statement:
Burden in this context means the time expended by persons to generate, maintain, retain, disclose, or provide the information requested. This includes the time needed to review instructions; to develop, acquire, install, and utilize technology and systems for the purpose of collecting, validating, and verifying information, processing and maintaining information, and disclosing and providing information; to train personnel and to be able to respond to a collection of information; to search data sources; to complete and review the collection of information; and to transmit or otherwise disclose the information. AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This action amends the Class D airspace and establishes Class E airspace at Chandler and Phoenix, AZ. This action is the result of biennial airspace reviews pursuant to FAA Order JO 7400.2R, Procedures for Handling Airspace Matters. The name and geographic coordinates of the Mesa Gateway Airport, Phoenix, AZ, are also being updated to coincide with the FAA's aeronautical database. This action brings the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and supports instrument flight rule (IFR) procedures and operations.
DATES:
Effective 0901 UTC, February 18, 2027. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
ADDRESSES:
A copy of the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), all comments received, this final rule, and all background material may be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from
www.federalregister.gov.
FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at
www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/. You may also contact the Rules and Regulations Group, Office of Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jeffrey Claypool, Federal Aviation Administration, Operations Support Group, Central Service Center, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177; telephone (817) 222-5711.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it amends the Class D airspace and establishes Class E airspace at the affected airports to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2025-5571 in the
Federal Register
(90 FR 59081; December 18, 2025) proposing to amend the Class D airspace and establish Class E airspace at Chandler and Phoenix, AZ. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. The FAA appreciates the public's participation in the rulemaking process. Ninety-six comments were received and all comments have been reviewed and considered. The following responses are provided.
The airspace requirements for airports with public instrument procedures and air traffic control towers (ATCT) are outlined in FAA Order JO 7400.2R and 14 CFR part 71, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; and Reporting Points. The FAA only designates controlled airspace required under FAA orders and 14 CFR part 71 and makes every effort to respect and protect the public's right of transit.
A majority of the airports within the Phoenix area have not received a complete airspace review in 25 years or longer. During that timeframe, instrument procedures and FAA orders and regulations governing airspace requirements have changed, thus requiring the airspace modification to bring the airspace into compliance with FAA orders and regulations and to support IFR operations. The changes to FAA orders and regulations require the modification and expansion of the controlled airspace at Chandler Municipal Airport and Mesa Gateway Airport.
Two comments expressed general dissatisfaction with the proposal without identifying any specific aspects to which they object or making any recommendations on how to revise the proposal. Due to the lack of specificity, the FAA is unable to provide a detailed response but acknowledges the general objections.
Fifty-nine comments raised concerns regarding the impact the proposed airspace modifications would have on VFR operations within the Phoenix area. The majority of these comments did not provide recommendations for how to revise the proposal or recommended either leaving the current airspace in place or reducing the current controlled airspace. All of these 59 comments expressed dissatisfaction with raising the vertical limits of the Chandler, AZ Class D airspace from 3,000 feet MSL to 3,700 feet MSL and the possible safety implications of leaving only 300 feet between the top of the Chandler, AZ, Class D airspace and the bottom of the Phoenix, AZ, Class B airspace. A comment from the Arizona Pilots Association objects to the lateral increase in the Chandler Municipal Airport Class D airspace, which “would close the distance” between that Class D airspace and the Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport Class B airspace, further constraining and concentrating VFR traffic.
The proposed modification to the vertical limit was derived from FAA Order JO 7400.2R, paragraph 17-2-8 which states that “Class D areas should normally extend upward from the surface up to and including 2,500 feet AGL.” As such, reducing the vertical limit from what was proposed is not consistent with the referenced FAA order. In response to the safety concern expressed in the comments, the vertical limit of the Class D airspace at Chandler, AZ, is being raised from 3,000 feet MSL to up to but excluding 4,000 feet MSL rather than 3,700 feet MSL as initially proposed. SUMMARY:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it modifies Class E airspace to support IFR operations at Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-5064 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 47156; July 28, 2026), modifying the Class E airspace area at Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. The FAA received three comments and provides the following responses.
One comment opposed the modification on the basis that it converts uncontrolled airspace to controlled airspace to support private instrument procedures, benefiting commercial enterprises over general aviation. The commenter requested that the FAA “reconsider or narrow this amendment”. Although FAA attempts to preserve navigable airspace to the maximum extent possible, its internal policies require it to designate Class E airspace to accommodate arriving IFR operations.
Another comment suggested an administrative correction to the city name to read, “Lincoln City, OR.” The FAA has made that correction.
The final comment was in support of the modification, but requested additional information regarding the FAA's compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act, which is also discussed in the “Environmental Review” section of this document. However, in response to this commenter's questions, the FAA determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. 4321,
et seq.) and in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5.a, which applies to “[r]ulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points”. In compliance with FAA Order 1050.1G, the FAA reviewed this action for factors and circumstances in which a normally categorically-excluded action may have a significant environmental impact requiring further analysis. It determined that no such extraordinary circumstances exist. The FAA also assessed the potential for impacts to coastal areas or protected-species habitat and determined the impacts would be negligible or non-existent. The FAA also assessed the need for coordination under the Coastal Zone Management Act and found that no such coordination is required. This is an air traffic action, which does not involve land acquisition, physical
( printed page 67769)
ground disturbance, construction, excavation, development activities, or discharges to water bodies.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action amends 14 CFR part 71 by modifying a Class E airspace area extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at the Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR, to contain private-use special instrument flight procedures in support of passenger shuttle, medevac, and cargo operations.

Published Document: 2026-22116 (91 FR 68045)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or the Department).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule amends the Child Support regulations that were unnecessary or obsolete in the following sections: State Plan Approval and Grant Procedures, State Plan Requirements, Standards for Program Operations, Federal Financial Participation, Program Performance Measures, Standards, Financial Incentives, and Penalties, Computerized Support Enforcement Systems, Annual State Self-Assessment Review and Report, Tribal Child Support Enforcement (IV-D) Program, and Computerized Tribal IV-D Systems and Office Automation.
DATES:
This rule is effective on November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam N. Jones, Deputy Chief of Staff, Immediate Office of the Assistant Secretary, Administration for Children and Families, Department of Health and Human Services, Washington, DC, 202-417-0115 or
Deregulation@acf.hhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Statutory Authority
This rule is published under the authority granted to the Secretary of Health and Human Services by section 1102 of the Social Security Act (the Act), 42 U.S.C. 1302. Section 1102 of the Act authorizes the Secretary to publish regulations, not inconsistent with the Act, which “may be necessary for efficient administration of the functions for which the Secretary is responsible under the Act.” This rule is also published in accordance with section 455(f) of the Act, 42 U.S.C. 655(f). Section 455(f) authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations governing the grants to Tribes and Tribal organizations operating child support programs.
II. Background
The Child Support Enforcement Program, established under Title IV-D of the Social Security Act, is a Federal-State-Tribal partnership designed to help children receive financial support from their noncustodial parents. The program operates through State and Tribal child support agencies that provide child support enforcement services including locating noncustodial parents, establishing paternity, establishing and enforcing support orders, and collecting and distributing child support payments. Since the program's establishment in 1975, OCSE has worked with States and Tribes to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of child support program operations. Over time, Congress has amended Title IV-D to expand and refine program responsibilities, and ACF has promulgated implementing regulations to support consistent national administration of the program while providing flexibility to States and Tribes.
See, e.g.,40 FR 27156 (June 26, 1975) (initial implementation of the Child Support Enforcement Program regulations); 54 FR 15761 (Apr. 19, 1989) (revising interstate and enforcement procedures to improve program effectiveness); 57 FR 30658 (July 10, 1992) (implementing Family Support Act amendments and strengthening automated processing and distribution requirements); 63 FR 44795 (Aug. 21, 1998) (implementing provisions of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 related to program automation); 69 FR 16638 (Mar. 30, 2004) (implementing direct funding of Tribal Child Support Enforcement programs); and 81 FR 93492 (Dec. 20, 2016) (modernizing child support program operations and emphasizing family-centered enforcement approaches).
ACF has determined many of these regulations were originally adopted during periods of substantial statutory expansion of the Title IV-D program, when ACF sought to provide introductory program descriptions, restate newly enacted statutory requirements, promote national consistency during early implementation efforts, or codify administrative practices that were not yet well established among State agencies.
See, e.g.,40 FR 27156, 27160-61 (describing the need for foundational regulations to establish uniform State plan requirements during initial implementation of Title IV-D); 57 FR 30658, 30659-60 (explaining that several provisions were intended to clarify statutory responsibilities and standardize administration among States); 63 FR 44795, 44795-96 (stating that certain amendments were intended to codify statutory changes enacted by Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) and provide operational guidance to States during implementation); and 81 FR 93492, 93493-95 (describing the purpose of regulatory amendments as improving program flexibility and modernizing existing practices). In several instances, prior preambles explained that the regulations were intended primarily to clarify statutory requirements, provide organizational context, or assist States during transitions following major legislative amendments.
ACF has also determined that many of those rationales no longer support maintaining these provisions in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) because the Title IV-D program has matured substantially and State and Tribal agencies now operate within a well-established statutory and administrative framework supported by decades of program guidance, policy issuances, automated systems requirements, and operational practice. In addition, Congress has amended Title IV-D numerous times to codify core program requirements directly in statute, thereby reducing any independent regulatory effect of certain provisions. As a result, ACF has concluded that retaining regulations that restate statutory text, provide historical or descriptive information without imposing substantive obligations, or address matters more appropriately administered through sub-regulatory guidance and technical
( printed page 68046)
assistance, is no longer necessary to ensure effective administration of the Title IV-D program.
Rescinding such regulations is also consistent with the President's directives in Executive Order 14219,
Ensuring Lawful Governance and Implementing the President's “Department of Government Efficiency” Deregulatory Initiative
(Feb. 19, 2025), which seeks to restore the constitutional separation of powers by ensuring regulations are authorized by federal statutes and ending federal bureaucratic overreach, and Executive Order 14192,
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,
which requires that for every one new regulation issued, at least ten existing regulations must be identified for repeal.
This final rule therefore rescinds multiple regulations in 45 CFR Chapter III that ACF has determined are duplicative, unnecessary, or obsolete. Duplicative regulations are those that include requirements stated elsewhere, such as in statute, and that ACF has determined are unnecessary as they do not impose new or additional requirements on State or Tribal child support programs. Obsolete regulations are those that are outdated, have been superseded

Published Document: 2026-22239 (91 FR 68601)

ACTION:
Notice and request for public comment.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites the public and other Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on proposed information collections, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, Public Law 104-13 (44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)). Currently, the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund (CDFI Fund), the Department of the Treasury, is soliciting comments concerning the Performance Progress Report and Financial Statement Audit Report Form. The Performance Progress Report and Financial Statement Audit Report Form are online forms submitted through the CDFI Fund's Awards Management Information System (AMIS).
DATES:
Written comments must be received on or before December 29, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments via the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov
via Docket No. CDFI-2026-0202. Follow the instructions on the website for the submission of comments. In general, all comments will be available for inspection at
www.regulations.gov.
Comments, including attachments and other supporting materials, are part of the public record. Do not submit any information in your comments or supporting materials that you consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information should be directed to Trefor Henry, Acting Program Manager, CDFI Fund, U.S. Department of the Treasury, 1500 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20220, (202) 653-0423 (not a toll-free number). Other information regarding the CDFI Fund and its programs may be obtained on the CDFI Fund website at
https://www.cdfifund.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Performance Progress Report and Financial Statement Audit Report Form.
OMB Number:
1559-0050.
Abstract:
Recipients of the Community Development Financial Institutions Program (CDFI Program), the Native American CDFI Assistance Program (NACA Program), CDFI Equitable Recovery Program (CDFI ERP) and the Small Dollar Loan Program (SDL Program) submit the Performance Progress Report via the CDFI Fund's AMIS once a year, three (3) months after their Period of Performance end date or fiscal year end, and the Financial Statement Audit Report via the CDFI Fund's AMIS once a year, six (6) months after their Period of Performance end date or fiscal year end. Recipients
( printed page 68602)
respond to the questions below by providing numerical figures, “yes” or “no” answers, or narrative responses, as appropriate. These reports are used to determine Recipient compliance with their Assistance Agreement. There are no significant content changes to the forms.
Current Actions:
Extension without change of currently approved collection.
Type of Review:
Regular.
Affected Public:
Businesses or other for-profit institutions, non-profit entities, and State, local and Tribal entities participating in the CDFI Fund programs.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
1,114.
Frequency of Responses:
Annually.
Estimated Total Number of Annual Responses:
2,228.
Estimated Annual Time per Respondent:
0.75 hours.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
1,671 hours.
Requests for Comments:
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval. All comments will become a matter of public record and may be published on the CDFI Fund website at
http://www.cdfifund.gov.
Comments are invited on: (a) whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of technology; and (e) the accuracy of the estimates of the burden of the information collections.
An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the collection of information displays a valid OMB control number.

Published Document: 2026-22238 (91 FR 68489)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
The Cleveland Cuyahoga County Port Authority, grantee of FTZ 40, submitted
( printed page 68490)
a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) on behalf of Atlantic Veal & Lamb, LLC for the company's facilities in Creston and Sterling, Ohio, within Subzone 40Q. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (15 CFR 400.22) was received on September 30, 2026.
Pursuant to 15 CFR 400.14(b), FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material(s)/component(s) and specific finished product(s) described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via
www.trade.gov/ftz.
The proposed finished products include: bovine products (chilled carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; chilled bone-in primal and subprimals; chilled boneless primal and subprimal cuts; cured, dried, or smoked meat; cured, dried, or smoked offal; tallow; fat; frozen carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; frozen bone-in primal and subprimals; frozen boneless primal and subprimal cuts; edible bones; frozen edible offal; frozen tongues; boneless, chilled veal trim and manufacturing beef; boneless, frozen veal trim and manufacturing beef; raw breaded or battered cutlets, chops, and portioned cuts; raw breaded or battered bone-in chops and racks; raw seasoned or marinated cuts, cutlets, and chops; raw seasoned or formulated ground patties; raw, ready to cook, formulated meatloaf and meatballs; cooked prepared dishes, including braised shanks, with or without sauce; ready to eat cured, smoked, and fully cooked; unformulated concentrated extract; bone broth, stock, and concentrated stock); sheep products (tallow; fat; edible bones; fresh lamb carcasses and half carcasses; fresh bone in lamb; fresh boneless lamb; frozen lamb carcasses and half carcasses; frozen bone in lamb; frozen boneless lamb; seasoned, breaded, or cooked; seasoned, breaded, or cooked lamb; bone broth, stock, and concentrated stock); raw, ready to cook, formulated bovine and pork meat; and, demi-glace, fond, sauce base, and soup base containing meat extract (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 6.
4% and from 0.
43¢/kg to 4.
4¢/kg).

The proposed foreign-status materials/components include: bovine components (chilled carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; chilled bone-in primal and subprimals; chilled boneless primal and subprimal cuts; cured, dried, or smoked meat; cured, dried, or smoked offal; tallow; fat; frozen carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; frozen bone-in primal and subprimals; frozen boneless primal and subprimal cuts; edible bones; frozen edible offal; frozen tongues; boneless, chilled veal trim and manufacturing beef; boneless, frozen veal trim and manufacturing beef); and sheep components (tallow; fat; edible bones; fresh lamb carcasses and half carcasses; fresh lamb bone in; fresh lamb boneless; frozen lamb carcasses and half carcasses; frozen lamb bone in, frozen lamb boneless) (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 2.3% and from 0.43¢/kg to 4.4¢/kg).
The request indicates that certain materials/components are subject to duties under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41).
Public comment is invited from interested parties. Submissions shall be addressed to the Board's Executive Secretary and sent to:
ftz@trade.gov.
The closing period for their receipt is December 9, 2026.
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.

Published Document: 2026-22233 (91 FR 68492)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that Société Nouvelle des Couleurs Zinciques (SNCZ) did not make sales of strontium chromate from France in the United States at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR) November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024.
DATES:
Applicable October 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jonathan Schueler or Rachel Accorsi, AD/CVD Operations, Office VIII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-9175 or (202) 482-3149, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 8, 2026, Commerce published the
Preliminary Results
of this administrative review in the
Federal Register
.[1]
Between June 1 and 5, 2026, Commerce conducted verification of SNCZ in Beauchamp, France.[2]
On August 7, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the final results until October 28, 2026.[3]
On August 21, 2026, Commerce invited interested parties to comment on the
Preliminary Results
and SNCZ's Verification Report.[4]
No interested party submitted a case brief. Commerce conducted this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
The product covered by this
Order
is strontium chromate from France. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the
Preliminary Results
PDM.
Verification
As provided in section 782(i) of the Act, in June 2026, Commerce conducted on-site verification of the sales and cost data reported by SNCZ. We used standard verification procedures, including an examination of relevant accounting and sales records, and original source documentation provided by SNCZ.[6]
Changes Since the Preliminary Results
Commerce is implementing certain changes due to verification findings that have no impact on the dumping margin.[7]
As no parties submitted comments regarding the
Preliminary Results
or Commerce's verification findings, we made no further changes to the
Preliminary Results
and no decision memorandum accompanies this notice.
Final Results of Review
As a result of this review, we determine the following weighted-average dumping margin exists for the POR, November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024:
Exporter or producer
Weighted-average dumping margin
(percent)
Société Nouvelle des Couleurs Zinciques
0.00
Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose to parties in this proceeding the calculations performed for these final results of review within five days of a public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of the notice of final results in the
Federal Register
, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.224(b).
Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), Commerce has determined, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review. As there are no entered values on the record for SNCZ's sales, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), we calculated importer-specific per-unit duty assessment rates based on the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales to the total quantity of those sales. To determine whether an importer-specific per-unit duty assessment rate is
de minimis,
we calculated an estimated entered value. If either SNCZ's weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis
within the meaning of 19 CFR 351.106(c), or an importer-specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
we instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.[8]
Accordingly, because SNCZ's weighted-average dumping margin is zero percent, we will instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
Commerce's “reseller policy” will apply to entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by the company included in these final results of review for which the reviewed company did not know that the merchandise it sold to the intermediary (
e.g.,
a reseller, trading company, or exporter) was destined for the United States. In such instance, we will instruct CBP to liquidate unreviewed entries at the all-others rate if there is no rate for
( printed page 68493)
the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.[9]
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for SNCZ will be equal to the weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review (
i.e.,
0.00 percent); (2) for merchandise exported by a producer or exporter not covered in this review but covered in a prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding in which the producer or exporter participated; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review, a prior review, or the original less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation, but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the rate established for the most recently completed segment of the proceeding for the producer of the merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers and exporters will continue to be 32.16 percent
ad valorem,
the all-others rate established in the LTFV investigation.[10]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers Regarding the Reimbursement of Duties
This notice serves as a final reminder to importers of their responsibility under 19 CFR 351.402(f)(2) to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during the POR. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties.

articles.title: Foreign-Trade Zone (FTZ) 38, Notification of Proposed Production Activity; ElringKlinger South Carolina, LLC; (Automotive Battery Subassemblies); Easley, South Carolina
articles.full_text:
ElringKlinger South Carolina, LLC submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) for its facility in Easley, South Carolina within FTZ 38. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (15 CFR 400.22) was received on September 24, 2026.
                    Pursuant to 15 CFR 400.14(b), FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material(s)/component(s) and specific finished product(s) described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via 
                    www.trade.gov/ftz.
The proposed finished products include: battery cell interconnection assembly; battery distribution and sensing assembly; and flexible printed circuit (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 3.4%).
The proposed foreign-status materials/components include: cleaning paste; plastic resin; insulating plastic film; plastic protective cover; steel bolts; steel screws; copper busbar; aluminum sheet; aluminum connector; plastic support used to secure busbar; plastic fastener for screws; flexible printed circuit; flexible electrical connector; and plastic carrier used to support busbar (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 8.5%).
The request indicates that certain materials/components are subject to duties under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 or section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 232 and section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41).
                    Public comment is invited from interested parties. Submissions shall be addressed to the Board's Executive Secretary and sent to: 
                    ftz@trade.gov.
                     The closing period for their receipt is December 9, 2026.
                
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.
                    For further information, contact John Frye at 
                    John.Frye@trade.gov.
                    Dated: October 27, 2026.
Colin Agostisi,
Executive Secretary.

articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a component of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), announces the issuance of an Amended Order under Sections 361, 365, 368, and 369 of the Public Health Service Act, and associated implementing regulations, prohibiting the boarding of any person who is not otherwise subject to an exemption on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the person presents a signed attestation confirming the person h...
articles.full_text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a component of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), announces the issuance of an Amended Order under Sections 361, 365, 368, and 369 of the Public Health Service Act, and associated implementing regulations, prohibiting the boarding of any person who is not otherwise subject to an exemption on any aircraft destined to the United States from a foreign country unless the person presents a signed attestation confirming the person has not been present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the 21 days prior to boarding a flight to the United States. This Amended Order was issued on October 28, 2026, to become effective at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (EST) on November 3, 2026, and shall remain in effect through 11:59 p.m. EST on December 18, 2026. This Amended Order may be amended or rescinded prior to that time at the discretion of the Secretary or his designee.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is planning to submit an information collection request (ICR), “Motor Vehicle and Engine Compliance Program Fees (Renewal)” (EPA ICR No. 2080.09, OMB Control No. 2060-0545) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act Before doing so, EPA is soliciting public comments on specific aspects of the proposed information collection as described below. This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through July 31, 2027. An Agency may not conduct or sponsor and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 29, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, referencing Docket ID Number EPA-HQ-OAR-2013-0119, to EPA online using
www.regulations.gov
(our preferred method), or by mail to: EPA Docket Center, Environmental Protection Agency, Mail Code 28221T, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. EPA's policy is that all comments received will be included in the public docket without change including any personal information provided, unless the comment includes profanity, threats, information claimed to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Noah Goldberg, Implementation, Analysis, and Compliance Division, Diesel Engine Compliance Branch, Environmental Protection Agency, 2000 Traverwood, Ann Arbor, MI 48105; telephone number: (734) 214-4772; email address:
goldberg.noah@epa.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This is a proposed extension of the ICR, which is currently approved through July 31,
( printed page 68516)
2027. An agency may not conduct or sponsor and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
This notice allows 60 days for public comments. Supporting documents, which explain in detail the information that the EPA will be collecting, are available in the public docket for this ICR. The docket can be viewed online at
www.regulations.gov
or in person at the EPA Docket Center, WJC West, Room 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The telephone number for the Docket Center is 202-566-1744. For additional information about EPA's public docket, visit
http://www.epa.gov/dockets.
Pursuant to section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, EPA is soliciting comments and information to enable it to: (i) evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (ii) evaluate the accuracy of the Agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (iii) enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (iv) minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate forms of information technology. EPA will consider the comments received and amend the ICR as appropriate. The final ICR package will then be submitted to OMB for review and approval. At that time, EPA will issue another
Federal Register
notice to announce the submission of the ICR to OMB and the opportunity to submit additional comments to OMB.
Abstract:
As required by the Clean Air Act, EPA has regulations establishing emission standards and other requirements for various classes of vehicles, engines, and evaporative emission components. These regulations require that compliance be demonstrated prior to EPA granting a “Certificate of Conformity”. EPA charges fees for administering this certification program. In 2004, then in 2008 the fees program was expanded to include nonroad categories of vehicles and engines, such as several categories of marine engines, locomotives, non-road recreational vehicles, many nonroad compression-ignition and spark-ignition engines and evaporative emission components. Manufacturers and importers of covered vehicles, engines and components are required to pay the applicable certification fees prior to their certification applications being reviewed by the Agency. Under section 208 of the Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7542(c)) all information, other than trade secret processes or methods, must be publicly available. Information about fee payments is treated as confidential information prior to certification.
Form Numbers:
3520-29.
Respondents/affected entities:
Manufacturers or importers of passenger cars, motorcycles, light trucks, heavy duty truck engines, nonroad vehicles or engines, and evaporative emissions components are required to receive a certificate of conformity from EPA prior to selling or introducing these products into commerce in the U.S.
Respondent's obligation to respond:
Required to obtain or retain a benefit (40 CFR part 1027).
Estimated number of respondents:
633 (total).
Frequency of response:
An average of approximately eight responses per respondent per year.
Total estimated burden:
1058 hours (per year). Burden is defined at 5 CFR 1320.03(b).
Total estimated cost:
$96,118 (per year), includes $15,179 annualized capital or operation and maintenance costs.
Changes in Estimates:
There is an increase of 36 hours in the total estimated respondent burden compared with the ICR currently approved by OMB. This increase is due to the greater number of responses in the number of certificates and, therefore, the number of fees paid from year to year. The estimate of the costs associated with the fees program have increased from $77,444 to $96,118 due to wage estimate increases, as well as an average higher pay grade for cert reps. The average increased due to employee progression, as well as attrition.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the annual 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 28, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Abby Jahn, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA is 37,936 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA has been or will be reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and 679.20(d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 37,436 mt and is setting aside the remaining 500 mt as incidental catch because it is necessary to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance has been or will be reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA to prevent exceeding the annual apportionment of pollock TAC for this area.
While this closure is effective the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on pollock catch in a timely fashion and would delay the closure of directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on pollock catch in Statistical Area 630 in the GOA only became available as of October 27, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

AGENCY:
Office of Government Ethics.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendments.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is updating its executive branch regulation on financial disclosure to reflect the retroactive statutory increase of the reporting thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements. OGE is also updating the executive branchwide standards of ethical conduct regulation to raise the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling tied to these thresholds. This latter change is not retroactive.
DATES:
Effective date:
This final rule is effective October 28, 2026.
Applicability date:
The amendments to 5 CFR 2634.304 and 2634.907 are applicable as of January 1, 2026.
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is amending pertinent sections of its executive branchwide ethics regulations on financial disclosure and standards of ethical conduct, as codified at 5 CFR parts 2634 and 2635, in order to update the thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements, as well as the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling.
Increased Gifts and Travel Reimbursements Reporting Thresholds
First, OGE is revising its executive branch financial disclosure regulation at 5 CFR part 2634 to reflect the increased reporting thresholds for gifts, reimbursements, and travel expenses for both the public and confidential executive branch financial disclosure systems. The increased thresholds are applicable as of January 1, 2026. These increases conform to the statutorily mandated public disclosure reporting thresholds under the Ethics in Government Act as amended, 5 U.S.C. 13104(a)(2)(A) and (B), and are extended to confidential disclosure reporting by OGE's regulation. Under the Ethics in Government Act, the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds are tied to the dollar amount for the “minimal value” threshold for foreign gifts as the General Services Administration (GSA) periodically redefines it.
GSA raised the “minimal value” amount under the Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act, 5 U.S.C. 7342, to $525 for the three-year period 2026-2028 (from the prior level of $480) in a December 29, 2025, Federal Management Regulation Bulletin. See Gen. Servs. Admin., GSA Bull. FMR B-2025-01, Foreign Gifts and Decorations Minimal Value (2025) (revising, effective January 1, 2026, the foreign gifts minimal value definition as codified at 41 CFR 102-42.10).
Accordingly, applicable as of January 1, 2026, OGE is increasing the thresholds for reporting of gifts and travel reimbursements from any one source in 5 CFR 2634.304 and 2634.907(g). The thresholds have been raised to “more than $525” for the gifts and travel reimbursements aggregation thresholds and “$210 or less” for the de minimis exception for gifts and travel reimbursements that do not have to be aggregated. As noted, these regulatory increases implement the underlying statutory increases effective January 1, 2026. OGE is also updating the examples following those sections, including appropriate adjustments to gift values.
OGE will continue to adjust the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds in its part 2634 regulation in the future as needed in light of GSA's redefinition of “minimal value” every three years for foreign gifts purposes. See OGE's prior three-year adjustment of those regulatory reporting thresholds, as published at 88 FR 37753 (June 9, 2023) (for 2023-2025, the aggregate reporting thresholds were more than $480, with a $192 or less de minimis exception).
Increased Dollar Ceiling for the Exception for Nonsponsor Gifts of Free Attendance at Widely Attended Gatherings
OGE is also increasing the exception ceiling for nonsponsor gifts of free attendance at widely attended gatherings from $480 to $525 in the executive branch standards of ethical conduct regulation, as codified at 5 CFR 2635.204(g)(3) (and as illustrated in the examples following paragraph (g)). This separate regulatory change is effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
, on October 28, 2026. As OGE noted in the preambles to the proposed and final rules on such nonsponsor gifts, that ceiling is tied to the financial disclosure gifts reporting threshold. See 60 FR 31415 (June 15, 1995) and 61 FR 42965 (Aug. 20, 1996). Thus, OGE is again increasing the nonsponsor gift ceiling to match the further increase in the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds described above. The nonsponsor gift ceiling was last raised in June 2023. See 88 FR 37753 (June 9, 2023). The other requirements for acceptance of such nonsponsor gifts, including an agency interest determination and expected attendance by more than 100 persons, remain unchanged.
II. Other Technical Changes
Designation of Notes and Examples
OGE is designating various notes and examples in §§ 2634.304 and 2634.907. The designation of those notes and examples are technical amendments involving no substantive changes to the regulations.
III. Matters of Regulatory Procedure
Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A) and (B), as Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I find that good cause exists for waiving the general notice of proposed rulemaking and public comment procedures as to these technical amendments. The notice and comment procedures are being waived because these amendments concern
( printed page 67766)
matters of agency organization, procedure, and practice. Further, notice and comment is unnecessary because these are technical amendments unlikely to be of significant interest to the public. Finally, it is also in the public interest that the accurate and up-to-date information be contained in the affected sections of OGE's regulations as soon as possible. The increase in the reporting thresholds for gifts and reimbursements is based on a statutory formula and lessens the reporting burden. Therefore, that regulatory revision is retroactively applicable as of January 1, 2026, when the change became effective under the Ethics in Government Act. For the reasons described above, this rule may take immediate effect pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1) and (d)(3).

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
                    ACTION:
Final rule; correction.
                    SUMMARY:
                        This action corrects a final rule published by the FAA in the 
                        Federal Register
                         on September 22, 2026, establishing Class E airspace at OSF St Elizabeth Medical Center Heliport, Ottawa, IL. This action corrects a typographical error in the airspace legal description.
                    
                    DATES:
                        The effective date of the final rule published in the 
                        Federal Register
                         on September 22, 2026 remains 0901 UTC, December 24, 2026. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.
                    
                    ADDRESSES:
                        FAA Order JO 7400.11M, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, and subsequent amendments can be viewed online at 
                        www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/. You may also contact the Airspace Regulation Group, Operational Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
History
                    The FAA published a final rule for Docket No. FAA-2026-8548 in the 
                    Federal Register
                     (91 FR 59987; September 22, 2026), establishing Class E airspace at OSF St Elizabeth Medical Center Heliport, Ottawa, IL. After publication of the final rule, an FAA database review noted that the incorrect heliport (OSF St Francis Medical Center Heliport) was used in the legal description. This action replaces the incorrect heliport with the correct heliport, OSF St Elizabeth Medical Center Heliport. This correction represents a ministerial change. It does not change the airspace dimensions or operating requirements. Accordingly, the FAA finds good cause that recirculating the NPRM for notice and comment is unnecessary.
                
Correction of Final Rule
                    Accordingly, pursuant to the authority delegated to me, the final rule for Docket No. FAA-2026-8548, as published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     on September 22, 2026 (91 FR 59987; FR Doc. 2026-19391), is corrected as follows:
                
On page 59988, in the third column, amend Paragraph 6005 “Class E Airspace Areas Extending Upward From 700 Feet or More Above the Surface of the Earth.” by revising the legal description for “AGL IL E5 Ottawa, IL” to read as follows:
AGL IL E5 Ottawa, IL [Establish]
OSF St Elizabeth Medical Center Heliport, IL
(Lat. 41°21′30″ N, long 88°49′30″ W)
That airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 6.8-mile radius of the OSF St Elizabeth Medical Center Heliport.
* * * * *
                    Issued in Fort Worth, Texas, on October 26, 2026.
Jerry J. Creecy,
Acting Manager, Operations Support Group, ATO Central Service Center.
