AGENCY:
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule focuses on deregulatory actions identified in HHS regulations regarding health information technology standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria and regarding certification programs for health information technology. This final rule reduces burden, offers flexibility to both developers and providers, and supports innovation through the removal and revision of certain certification criteria and regulatory provisions.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 28, 2026, except for amendatory instructions 7, 10, and 12 which are effective January 1, 2027. The incorporation by reference of certain material listed in the rule was approved by the Director of the Federal Register between February 12, 2010, and October 1, 2025.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Michael Lipinski, Office of Programs and Implementation, Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 202-690-7151.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose of Deregulatory Action
B. Summary of Major Provisions
1. Health Information Technology Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria and Certification Programs for Health Information Technology (Part 170)
a. Certification Criteria for Health Information Technology
b. Standards and Implementation Specifications for Health Information Technology
c. Terms and Definitions
d. Conditions and Maintenance of Certification Requirements for Health IT Developers
e. ONC Health IT Certification Program Administrative Requirements
C. Severability
D. Costs and Benefits
II. Background
A. Statutory Basis
1. Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria
2. Health IT Certification Program(s)
B. ONC Health IT Certification Program Regulatory History
C. General Comments on the Proposed Rule
D. Comments Beyond the Scope of Certification Program Proposals
III. Health Information Technology Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria and Certification Programs for Health Information Technology (Part 170)
A. Certification Criteria for Health Information Technology
1. Clinical Certification Criteria
a. Clinical Decision Support
b. Family Health History
c. Implantable Device List
2. Care Coordination Certification Criteria
a. Transitions of Care
b. Clinical Information Reconciliation and Incorporation
Since the inception of the ONC Health IT Certification Program (Certification Program) (42 U.S.C. 300jj-11(c)(5)), ONC has aimed to implement and administer the Certification Program in the least burdensome manner that supports an administration's policy goals. Throughout the years, we have worked to improve the Certification Program with a focus on ways to reduce burden, offer flexibility to both developers and providers, and support innovation. Over the past 15 years, we have established a set of regulatory requirements that have provided a foundation for our voluntary Certification Program. As we look to the future, we reviewed the existing requirements and made updates. Through both formal notice and comment rulemaking and informal engagements, we received suggestions on how to update the Certification Program to meet current market needs. This final rule includes deregulatory actions that: take into consideration suggestions and comments received on the Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity Proposed Rule (90 FR 60970) (“Proposed Rule”); account for the current and future state of technology; reduce burden on health IT developers; and promote innovation for health IT developers, providers, and other interested parties.
These efforts directly align with Administration goals as outlined in E.O. 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity through
( printed page 67917)
Deregulation) [1]
and E.O. 14267 (Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers).[2]
By removing burdensome and unnecessary requirements of the Certification Program, this final rule supports providers in caring for their patients. Developers of certified health IT will have more time to support providers' specific technological needs. Further, by increasing competition in the certified health IT market that will come from reduced barriers to entry for the certification of health IT, providers also will have more choices to meet their health IT needs.
America's interoperability arc in healthcare has bent decisively toward Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®)-based application programming interfaces (APIs). An open, interoperable health data ecosystem invites entrepreneurship, drives innovation, and cements American leadership and competitiveness in the expanding digital health marketplace. As discussed in this deregulatory final rule, we aggressively reduce and remove long-standing functionality-oriented and non-FHIR-based certification criteria from the Certification Program. While this approach will directly and rapidly reduce compliance burdens for health IT developers that participate in the Certification Program, more broadly, it will enable ONC to reset the Certification Program's regulatory scope and establish a new foundation on which to build FHIR-based API requirements in the future. This will allow more creative super intelligence [3]
(SI)-enabled interoperability solutions that combine FHIR with newer standards to emerge, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP), which “standardizes how applications provide context to Large Language Models (LLMs),” [4]
and will further embrace the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) (Cures Act)'s reference to successor technology and standards in the API Condition of Certification.[5]
While FHIR provides the potential for better, faster, and more consistent ways to address emerging market needs and policy imperatives, more work is needed for certain use cases. We intend to continue to fully engage industry and our Federal partners, such as CMS, to rapidly advance FHIR specifications for regulatory readiness. We also intend to sharpen the Certification Program's future focus to prioritize FHIR-based APIs that, consistent with all legal requirements: (1) enhance automation and API performance; (2) move beyond read-only interactions; and (3) expand the scope of data available

AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to modernize the framework governing personnel management and strategic human capital management in Federal agencies. This rule amends the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies to streamline human capital planning and reporting requirements, strengthen the authority of agency Chief Human Capital Officers (CHCOs), update employee survey requirements, and align the regulatory framework with Executive branch priorities for a high-performing Federal workforce. OPM carefully considered all public comments received on the proposed rule and has made targeted revisions in response.
DATES:
Effective November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jeanne Jacobson, Acting Deputy Associate Director, Center for Workforce Strategy, Design, and Insights, Office of Personnel Management, 1900 E Street NW, Washington, DC 20415; email:
workforce@opm.gov;
phone (202) 606-1800.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978 established the foundational framework for merit-based personnel management in the Federal Government. Pursuant to the CSRA and subsequent statutory authority, OPM is responsible for promulgating Governmentwide regulations governing Federal human capital management, including the systems and standards by which agencies plan, implement, and evaluate their human capital strategies.
Part 250 of title 5 of the Code of Federal Regulations establishes the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies. Subpart A sets standards for agency personnel actions and delegation agreements. Subpart B—Strategic Human Capital Management-defines the systems, standards, and metrics agencies must use to manage human capital, currently organized around the Human Capital Framework (HCF) and the Human Capital Operating Plan (HCOP), Human Capital Reviews (HCR), and HRStat quarterly reviews. Subpart C—Employee Surveys—governs the administration and public disclosure of annual Federal employee surveys and establishes a core set of 16 required survey questions.
On July 2, 2026, OPM published a proposed rule (91 FR 40435) to amend 5 CFR part 250 to modernize strategic human capital management across the Federal Government. The proposed rule proposed to: (1) consolidate and streamline human capital planning requirements by replacing the HCOP, HCR, and HRStat framework with Annual Staffing Plans (ASPs) and associated review processes; (2) strengthen CHCO authority and visibility; (3) require each agency to establish a Strategic Hiring Committee to oversee hiring within the agency; (4) revise the employee survey framework under subpart C, including changes to the Governmentwide core question set and survey administration; and (5) remove references to workforce diversity from the regulatory text.
In response to public comments, OPM has made targeted revisions to the proposed rule. Key changes from the proposed rule include: (1) clarifying the terminology distinguishing strategic human capital planning from operational staffing planning and tying Annual Staffing Plan development to the budget formulation cycle under the annual Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget, Part 6 (OMB, Circular No. A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget (Aug. 29, 2025),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/a11.pdf); (2) adding an annual agency-head-certification requirement to ensure CHCO visibility, oversight, and control; and (3) permitting agencies to integrate Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews into existing performance review processes. Each of these changes is discussed in detail in the comment-response section below.
In response to comments, OPM also clarifies several matters that do not change the regulatory text, including the effect of the removal of nonstatutory references to a “diverse” workforce and the scope of the Strategic Hiring Committee's role; those clarifications are addressed in the same section.
Digest of Public Comments
In response to the proposed rule, OPM received nine comments during the 30-day public comment period ending August 3, 2026. These responses came from a range of sources: individual citizens; nonprofit and professional organizations; and a former Federal employee writing in a private capacity. All nine comments are substantive and have been considered in full. All comments were posted and made available to the public in the docket. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
the four-digit number associated with the location in the docket) at
https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OPM-2026-0368-nnnn.
The comments are summarized below, together with OPM's responses, including where OPM has adopted, partially adopted, or declined commenter suggestions, along with OPM's reasoning. The comments are organized by issue category.
General Comments
Comment 0010 expressed general support for the proposed rule, noting it “will strengthen accountability, improve hiring practices, and enhance morale and recruitment across the federal workforce.” Comment 0010 offered additional recommendations to strengthen protections against political-to-career conversions (“burrowing in”), discussed further below.

Published Document: 2026-22089 (91 FR 68028)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection; the Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations by adding the Republic of Malta (Malta) to the list of countries whose pleasure vessels may be issued U.S. cruising licenses. The U.S. Department of State has notified CBP that yachts used and employed exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States are allowed to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in Maltese waters without complying with formal entry and clearance procedures. Therefore, CBP is extending reciprocal cruising privileges to Maltese-flagged pleasure vessels.
DATES:
This amendment is effective October 29, 2026. These reciprocal privileges became applicable for Malta as of June 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
W. Richmond Beevers, Chief, Cargo
( printed page 68029)
Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, Regulations and Rulings, Office of Trade, (202) 325-0084,
ccrbranchcomments@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Under 46 U.S.C. 60504, the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) may allow foreign-flagged yachts used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from U.S. ports and cruise in U.S. waters without paying any duties or fees, provided that the President is satisfied that the foreign country allows yachts owned by U.S. residents and used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from its ports and cruise in its waters without entering, clearing, or paying any duties or fees. The statute also provides the Secretary discretion to require foreign yachts to obtain cruising licenses and to prescribe the form and conditions of those licenses.
See46 U.S.C. 60504; Public Law 109-304, 9(b), 120 Stat. 1485, 1680-81 (2006).
The Secretary has delegated to the Commissioner of CBP the authority to prescribe and approve cruising licenses for foreign countries under section 4.94(b) of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
See
DHS Delegation No. 07010.3, Revision 03.2. Accordingly, CBP has promulgated regulations governing cruising privileges for U.S. and foreign pleasure vessels. Section 4.94(a) of title 19 of the CFR provides that U.S.-documented vessels with a recreational endorsement, used exclusively for pleasure, not engaged in any trade, and not violating the customs or navigation laws of the United States, may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing, and is not subject to entry upon its arrival in the United States, as long as they have not visited hovering vessels, received merchandise while in the customs waters beyond the territorial sea, or received merchandise while on the high seas. When returning from a foreign port or place, such pleasure vessels are required to report their arrival pursuant to 19 CFR 4.2.
Generally, foreign-flagged yachts entering the United States are required to comply with the laws applicable to foreign vessels arriving at, departing from, and proceeding between ports of the United States.
See
section 433 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1433). However, CBP may issue cruising licenses to pleasure vessels from certain countries if it is found that yachts of the United States are exempt from formal entry and clearance procedures (
e.g.,
filing manifests, obtaining permits to proceed, and paying entry and clearance fees) in those countries.
See19 CFR 4.94(b).
To obtain a cruising license, the owner of a foreign-flagged yacht must file an application with a port director. 19 CFR 4.94(c). If CBP issues a foreign-flagged yacht a cruising license, the yacht may arrive at and depart from the United States and cruise in specified waters of the United States without entering and clearing, without filing manifests and obtaining or delivering permits to proceed, and without the payment of certain fees.
Id.
Such fees include entrance and clearance fees, fees for receiving manifests and granting permits to proceed, duty on tonnage, tonnage tax, or light money.
Id.
A port director may issue a cruising license for a period not to exceed one year.
Id.
Upon arrival at each port in the United States, the master of a foreign-flagged yacht with a cruising license must report the fact of arrival to the appropriate CBP office.
Id.
Section 4.94(b) sets forth the list of countries whose yachts are eligible for cruising licenses.
By diplomatic note dated February 4, 2026, the Embassy of the Republic of Malta, in Washington, DC, informed the Department of State that Malta allows yachts from the United States, used exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States, to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in the waters of Malta without entering and clearing Maltese Customs and without the payment of any related charges for entry or clearance, dues, duty per ton, tonnage, taxes, or charges for a cruising license. By letter dated June 10, 2026, the Department of State advised the Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, CBP, that the Maltese treatment of U.S. pleasure vessels in Maltese waters appears to satisfy the conditions for reciprocal privileges and therefore recommended that Malta be added to the list of countries under the provisions of 19 CFR 4.94(b).
The Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, has determined that satisfactory evidence has been furnished to grant the reciprocal privileges allowed under 19 CFR 4.94(b), effective June 10, 2026. Accordingly, under the authority of 46 U.S.C. 60504, Maltese-flagged yachts used only for pleasure may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing and are not subject to entry upon arrival at a U.S. port, including the payment of any duties or fees. This final rule revises the list of countries in 19 CFR 4.94(b) to include Malta for the above reasons.
Administrative Procedure Act

Published Document: 2026-22078 (91 FR 68043)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a safety zone for certain navigable waters of the Sanders Ferry, near Hendersonville, TN. This safety zone is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards during a fireworks show at various times from October 29, 2026, through October 31, 2026. This rulemaking prohibits entry of vessels or persons into this safety zone during enforcement periods unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Ohio Valley or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 7:15 a.m. local time on October 29, 2026, through 5:30 p.m. local time on October 31, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact MST3 Zachary T. Epps, Sector Ohio Valley Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (206) 815-7006, or email
STL-SMB-MSDNASHVILLE@USCG.MIL.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On July 17, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that it will sponsor two fireworks displays launched from a barge on the Cumberland River near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The first fireworks display (including a 15-minute safety buffer before and afterwards) is scheduled to occur on October 29, 2026, from approximately 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., Central Time. The second fireworks display is scheduled to occur on October 31, 2026, from approximately 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., Central Time. On October 16, 2026, the Coast Guard published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) titled Safety Zone; Cumberland River, Hendersonville, TN (91 FR 65698). In that NPRM, we stated why we issued the NPRM and invited comments on our proposed regulatory action related to this fireworks display.
Under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, the COTP has determined that this rule is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the fireworks. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or their designated representative.
Because of the hazards associated with this event, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. We must establish this safety zone by October 29, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
III. Discussion of Comments and the Rule
During the comment period that ended on October 23, 2026, we received two comments. Two commenters identified inconsistencies in the NPRM concerning the dates and times of the planned fireworks displays and associated safety-zone enforcement periods. Specifically, the commenters noted that the NPRM contained conflicting references to October 30 and October 31 for the second enforcement period, as well as inconsistent morning enforcement periods for October 29. One commenter also requested clarification regarding the difference between the overall effective period and the periods when the safety zone would be actively enforced; the basis for pre- and post-display safety buffers; the applicable local time zone; notice to mariners; and procedures for requesting entry into the safety zone.
In response to these comments, the Coast Guard has revised the
( printed page 68044)
enforcement periods to accurately reflect the scheduled fireworks displays. The safety zone will be enforced from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., on October 29, 2026, and from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., on October 31, 2026. It is always standard that in Coast Guard safety zone rulemaking documents refer to the local time at the location of the safety zone, in this case that is Central Daylight Time (CDT). These enforcement periods include a 15-minute safety buffer before and after each fireworks display to allow for final safety preparations, fireworks-launch operations, monitoring for falling debris, post-display safety assessment, and cleanup.
The Coast Guard has also corrected the conflicting references to an October 30 enforcement period and clarified that the safety zone will not be continuously enforced between the two specified enforcement periods. In other words, this safety zone will be enforced for one hour on October 29, 2026, from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., and 45 minutes on October 31, 2026, from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m. The Coast Guard will provide notice of enforcement through a Broadcast Notice to Mariners on VHF-FM channel 16. The Broadcast Notice to Mariners will include information regarding the enforcement periods and may include sponsor contact information for event-related coordination, as appropriate. Only the Captain of the Port (COTP), Ohio Valley or the COTP's designated representative may authorize entry into the safety zone.
This rule establishes a safety zone on all navigable waters of the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to mile marker 222 near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. During the stated enforcement periods, no vessel or person may enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analysis based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA), 5 U.S.C. 601-612, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. ACTION:
Notice of information collection; and request for public comment.
SUMMARY:
The Department of the Treasury, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites the general public and other Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing information collections, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. Currently, the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund (CDFI Fund), Department of the Treasury, is soliciting comments concerning the New Markets Tax Credit Program (NMTC Program) Community Development Entity (CDE) Certification Application, which Applicants will submit through the CDFI Fund's Awards Management Information System (AMIS).
DATES:
Written comments must be received on or before December 29, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments via the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov
Docket No. CDFI-2026-0201. Follow the instructions on the website for the submission of comments. In general, all comments will be available for inspection at
www.regulations.gov.
Comments, including attachments and other supporting materials, are part of the public record. Do not submit any information in your comments or supporting materials that you consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information should be directed to Shannon McKay, Acting Program Manager for the Office of Certification Policy and Evaluation, CDFI Fund, U.S. Department of the Treasury, 1500 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20220 or by phone at (202) 653-0300. Other information regarding the CDFI Fund and its programs may be obtained through the CDFI Fund's website at
http://www.cdfifund.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
( printed page 68601)
Title:
New Markets Tax Credit Program Community Development Entity (CDE) Certification Application.
OMB Control Number:
1559-0014.
Abstract:
Title I, subtitle C, section 121 of the Community Renewal Tax Relief Act of 2000 (the Act), as enacted in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2001 (Pub. L. 106-554, December 21, 2000), amended the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) by adding IRC 45D and created the NMTC Program. The Department of the Treasury, through the CDFI Fund, administers the NMTC Program, which provides an incentive to investors in the form of tax credits over seven years, expected to stimulate the provision of private investment capital that, in turn, will facilitate economic and community development in low-income communities. In order to qualify for an allocation of tax credits through the NMTC Program, an entity must be certified as a qualified CDE and submit an allocation application to the CDFI Fund. Nonprofit entities and for-profit entities may be certified as CDEs by the CDFI Fund. In order to be certified as a CDE, an entity must be a domestic corporation or partnership, that: (1) has a primary mission of serving or providing investment capital for low-income communities or low-income persons; and (2) maintains accountability to residents of low-income communities through their representation on any governing or advisory board of the entity.
The CDE Certification Application is being updated to ensure that Applicants are meeting the statutory and regulatory disclosure requirements as well as protecting government resources in alignment with Administration priorities where appropriate. The specific changes include: (1) removal of references to “Minority-Owned or Controlled” in terms of Applicant's structure; (2) addition of a new subsection on “Affiliate Information” to gather information about ownership, control, and foreign interests for affiliates; (3) addition of a new subsection on “Government Investigations and Enforcement” to gather more information on government investigations, enforcement actions and related matters; and (4) additional detailed language for federal anti-discrimination, alignment with specific Executive Orders, and prevention of fraud, waste, and abuse.
Current Actions:
Revision of currently approved collection.
Type of Review:
Regular.
Form:
CDE Certification Application.
Affected Public:
CDEs and entities seeking CDE certification, including business or other for-profit institutions, nonprofit entities, and State, local and Tribal entities.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
150.
Frequency of Response:
Annually.
Estimated Total Number of Annual Responses:
150.
Estimated Annual Time per Respondent:
4 hours.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
600 hours.
Request for Comments:
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record at
http://www.cdfifund.gov.
The CDFI Fund is seeking input on the content of the revised CDE Certification Application. The application and related guidance may be obtained on the CDFI Fund's website at
https://www.cdfifund.gov/programs-training/certification/cde.
Comments are invited on: (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the CDFI Fund, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the CDFI Fund's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of technology; and (e) the accuracy of the estimates of the burden of the information collections.

AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice and request for comments on a request for renewal with modification of a currently approved information collection.
SUMMARY:
In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), this notice announces that the Information Collection Request (ICR) summarized below will be submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval. The ICR describes the nature of the information collection and its expected burden. This document describes a collection of information for which NHTSA intends to seek OMB approval on the State Data Transfer (SDT) program for Vehicle Crash Information. A
Federal Register
Notice with a 60-day comment period soliciting comments on this information collection was published on June 25, 2026. NHTSA received one public comment.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection, including suggestions for reducing burden, should be submitted to the Office of Management and Budget at
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
To find this particular information collection, select “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comment” or use the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For additional information or access to background documents, contact Liza Lemaster-Sandbank, Office of State Data Reporting System Division (NSA-0120), telephone (202) 744-5942, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, W43-481, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. Please identify the relevant collection of information by referring to its OMB Control Number, 2127-0753.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.), a Federal agency must receive approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) before it collects certain information from the public, and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information by a Federal agency unless the collection displays a valid OMB control number. In compliance with these requirements, this notice announces that the following information collection request will be submitted to OMB.
Title:
State Data Transfer (SDT).
OMB Control Number:
2127-0753.
Form Number(s):
N/A.
Type of Request:
Renewal with modification of a currently approved information collection.
Type of Review Requested:
Regular.
Length of Approval Requested:
Three years from date of approval.
Summary of the Collection of Information:
The State Data Transfer (SDT) program is a voluntary collection of motor vehicle crash data. Participating States electronically transfer Police Crash Report (PCR) data, supplemental crash reports, and crash images to NHTSA using automated electronic data transfer (EDT) protocols. Transfers typically occur nightly in Extensible Markup Language (XML) or JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) formats via web services. This information collection updates the burden estimates and removes the legacy State Data System (SDS) protocol, which is being sunsetted, leaving only the automated EDT protocol in place. The program includes Non-SEDC States that voluntarily transmit data under the terms of a memorandum of understanding, as well as SEDC States participating under the State Electronic Data Collection (SEDC) discretionary grant program, which requires states to modernize their crash data repositories, align with Model Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria (MMUCC) Sixth Edition standards, and transfer data electronically.
Description of the Need for the Information and Proposed Use of the Information:
NHTSA uses SDT data to identify existing and emerging highway safety trends, evaluate the effectiveness of motor vehicle safety standards, and develop countermeasures to reduce deaths and injuries from motor vehicle crashes. The data allows NHTSA to study the effectiveness of emerging technologies, such as advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), and supplies critical volume to support cost-benefit analyses for Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rulemakings regarding vehicle mass and fatality rates. Furthermore, automated SDT data pre-populates several NHTSA systems and special studies, including the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), and Crash Investigation Sampling System (CISS). This electronic transfer significantly reduces the administrative and technical burden on States by eliminating manual, redundant data entry into Federal databases.
60-Day Notice:
NHTSA published a 60-day notice on June 25, 2026, requesting comment on NHTSA's intention to submit this ICR to OMB for approval (91 FR 38472). During the comment period, NHTSA received one comment from Mr. Eric Hein.

RI 20-64B, Information on Electing a Survivor Annuity for Your Former Spouse, is a pamphlet that provides important information to retirees who want to provide a CSRS survivor annuity for a former spouse.

AGENCY:
Office of the Assistant Secretary for Public and Indian Housing (PIH), HUD.
ACTION:
Request for information.
SUMMARY:
HUD is issuing this Request for Information (RFI) to solicit feedback from stakeholders on the Melania Trump Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) initiative. HUD will use the information gathered through this RFI to make recommendations to Congress (1) to improve program operations; (2) to assist youth in navigating the housing search process and preventing returns to homelessness after the subsidized rental assistance sunsets; and (3) on how Federal, State, and local stakeholders can best support participants as they transition from foster care to successful adulthood.
DATES:
Comments are requested on or before December 14, 2026. Late-filed comments will be considered to the extent practicable.
ADDRESSES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments responsive to this RFI. Copies of all comments submitted are available for inspection and downloading at
https://www.regulations.gov.
To receive consideration as public comments, comments must be submitted through one of the two methods specified below. All submissions must refer to the docket number and title above.
1.
Electronic Submission of Comments.
Interested persons may submit comments electronically through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov.
HUD strongly encourages commenters to submit comments electronically. Electronic submission of comments allows the commenter maximum time to prepare and submit a comment, ensures timely receipt by HUD, and enables HUD to make them immediately available to the public. Comments submitted electronically through the
https://www.regulations.gov
website can be viewed by other commenters and interested members of the public. Commenters should follow the instructions provided on that site to submit comments electronically.
2.
Submission of Comments by Mail.
Comments may be submitted by mail to the Regulations Division, Office of General Counsel, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20410.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ryan E. Jones, Director, Housing Voucher Management and Operations Division, Office of Public and Indian Housing, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20410; telephone number (202) 402-2677. (This is not a toll-free number.) HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit
https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/telecommunications-relay-service-trs.
Questions about this document can be sent to
FUPVouchers@hud.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The Melania Trump Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) was established in 2019 in response to the advocacy of foster youth and alumni regarding the need for housing assistance for young people upon their exit from foster care. According to the Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System, on average 15,000 young people age-out of foster care each year, and nearly 25 percent of youth responding to the National Youth in Transition Database report experiencing homelessness after leaving foster care. Yet, there were no Federal housing resources solely dedicated to serving this population.
Prior to the establishment of FYI, the primary Federal housing resource for young people transitioning out of foster care was the Family Unification Program (FUP). Through public housing agencies (PHAs), FUP provides housing choice vouchers (HCVs) that can be issued to either child welfare-involved families or youth transitioning out of foster care.[1]
FUP participants use their HCVs to rent housing in the private market and generally pay 30 percent of their adjusted monthly income towards rent while the voucher pays the remaining portion of the rent. However, FUP vouchers are only available in a small number of communities [2]
and have been primarily used to assist child welfare-involved families, rather than youth transitioning out of foster care. When FYI was established in 2019, 95 percent of FUP vouchers were being used to serve child welfare-involved families, and the remaining 5 percent were being used to serve youth transitioning out of foster care.
FYI provides a dedicated source of vouchers for youth transitioning out of foster care. Since fiscal year (FY) 2020, Congress has appropriated a total of $165 million for new incremental FYI vouchers. Further, in FY 2021, Congress codified an on-demand distribution mechanism for FYI vouchers, meaning that any of the more than 2,000 PHAs administering the HCV program can establish an FYI program and request FYI vouchers on a rolling basis to serve youth as they are identified.[3]
This enables HUD to provide young people with FYI vouchers that are timed with their emancipation from foster care so that they do not experience homelessness when they leave care.
To establish an FYI program, a PHA must enter into a partnership agreement with a public child welfare agency (PCWA). Under the partnership agreement, the PHA provides the youth with FYI voucher assistance for 36 months, which may be extended for up to an additional 24 months if the youth is working toward economic self-sufficiency or meets one of the statutory exceptions to this requirement.[4]
The
( printed page 68535)
PCWA provides or secures the provision of supportive services for the youth for 36 months. The combination of time-limited rental assistance and supportive services is intended to provide youth with a platform to move toward economic self-sufficiency.
Since the rollout of FYI, HUD has allocated more than 9,000 FYI vouchers to assist individual youth. Yet, HUD recognizes that many more youth can benefit from the program. While FYI has experienced steady growth with the program being administered by 373 PHAs in 48 states and the U.S. Virgin Islands as of June 2026 Voucher Management System (VMS) data, there are still many communities where youth cannot access FYI. Abstract:
The fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.16(u) became effective January 17, 2024, and is due for any application filed under 35 U.S.C. 111 for an original patent—except design, plant, or provisional applications—where the specification, claims, and/or abstract do not conform to the USPTO requirements for submission in the DOCX format. Therefore, the fee is due for nonprovisional utility applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 111, including continuing applications, that are not filed in the DOCX format. See
Setting and Adjusting Patent Fees During Fiscal Year 2020, 85 FR 46932 (August 3, 2020).[1]
The USPTO continues to provide several resources to help applicants submit their applications in the DOCX format. The Patent Center and DOCX web pages contain many resources for applicants, such as FAQs and a training mode through which applicants may file test submissions to practice filing in DOCX.[2]
The USPTO also provides a Patent Center User Guide [3]
and a DOCX Intake in Patent Center Quick Start Guide [4]
to assist applicants in navigating the Patent Center system. The USPTO also provides free training sessions and videos demonstrating how to file DOCX documents in Patent Center.[5]
For one-on-one assistance, the USPTO's Patent Center Help Desk provides step-by-step guidance for submitting applications to the USPTO.
The items in this information collection relate solely to the impacts of the § 1.16(u) non-DOCX filing surcharge fee on the filing of nonprovisional utility applications under 35 U.S.C. 111, including continuing applications. In particular, this information collection accounts for the § 1.16(u) non-DOCX filing surcharge fee itself, as well as an additional 30 minutes of time to
( printed page 68496)
accommodate (i) extra review that some respondents might undertake when filing in the DOCX format and (ii) submissions of the back-up applicant-generated PDF that some respondents will opt to submit.

articles.title: How Yair Alon went from building Portrait Mode at Google to founding researcher at Poetiq
articles.summary: After 10 years at Google Research and DeepMind, Yair Alon joined Poetiq to build an AI that improves itself.
articles.full_text:
Yair Alon spent a decade at Google Research and DeepMind.
He built the deep learning models behind Portrait Mode on Pixel phones.
He published papers on efficient deep learning.
He designed models for Search, Ads, and YouTube.
His last project was VideoPoet, a video generation system.
Everything was great, by his own account.
But he felt that small startups had become where the most exciting innovations were happening.
So when former DeepMind collaborators told him they were starting a company, he knew immediately he wanted in.
That company is Poetiq (YC S26, San Francisco).
In one sentence: Poetiq is building an AI system that can optimize any other AI system, including itself.
Leaving Google after a decadeYair had been at Google since his PhD internship at CMU, where he studied machine learning and computer vision.
He knew how to be productive and successful inside that ecosystem.
Leaving felt scary.
"I was there for so many years," he says.
"I knew how to be productive and successful in that environment so leaving felt like a scary new thing.
" He already knew the founders and trusted the technical direction, so the real hurdle was personal.
He had to find the courage to walk away from something comfortable toward something unproven.
What he actually does all dayYair is one of a handful of people who started on the first day of the company.
His official title is Founding Research Scientist.
Unofficially, he calls himself Coffee Evangelist.
In practice, being early means working on everything, sometimes in a single day: "You could be working on a new ML technique in the morning, fixing issues with the DB later in the day and then in the afternoon meeting a realtor to look at a potential new office.
"One project he is particularly proud of is the experimentation infrastructure.
At Google, entire teams handled experiment launchers, dashboards, and visualization.
At Poetiq, none of that existed, and the work is novel enough that off-the-shelf tools were not relevant.
He and the team built a first-tier experimentation system from scratch, with detailed analysis of how their optimizer is performing.
Building an AI that improves itselfPoetiq's core bet is on recursive self-improvement: an optimizer that can improve any AI system — harnesses, agents, skills — and that can also improve itself, so the rate of improvement accelerates.
Yair puts it simply: "The main thing we are building at Poetiq is an AI that can improve other A.
I.
s and itself.
I think nothing can top that.
"Early on, the work was split between two tracks: figuring out the algorithmic foundations of the meta-optimizer and building the experiment-running infrastructure to validate it quickly.
More recently, his focus has shifted to scaling — identifying what is missing so the system can run longer without human intervention, finding what would cause friction if they wanted to ten-times their experiments, and spending significant time on hiring and prototyping Poetiq's interview process.
People, challenge, autonomyYair describes three things that matter most to him in a company: people, challenge, and autonomy.
On people, he says the team is genuinely enjoyable to spend time with.
On challenge, he frames it as the rare combination of creating a new domain of AI research while simultaneously inventing a new product category.
On autonomy, the founding team — all with deep experience in industry and academic research — avoids micromanagement.
Instead, they run frequent deep-dive syncs to stay aligned on priorities and converge quickly when needed.
He is candid about tools, too.
He has used VS Code, Anti Gravity, and now mostly Claude Code, but he thinks people put too much emphasis on the setup.
"The key thing is knowing what you want to build, having a clear design for it in your mind, and knowing what success looks like.
Then whether you use Claude Code, Codex or whatever doesn't matter that much.
"Who would thrive hereYair's advice for anyone considering an early-stage role is grounded: "Realistically most startups do not become Anthropic.
So you need to go into it with the correct mind set.
The goal is to learn a lot, be part of a small team executing together, and be able to contribute across the board.
Anything more is just icing on the cake.
" If you are an engineer or researcher who wants ownership over the full lifecycle of what you build — and you are drawn to a problem no one has solved before — Poetiq is hiring.

articles.title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
articles.summary: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

articles.title: Errors in the research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
articles.summary:
AI issues its judgment: 138 papers audited 2,035 problems found 147 serious enough to change a headline number 69% of papers have at least one 97% of major and moderate errors with a clear direction overstate the paper’s claim And on the method: Two independent audits of each paper. One by Claude Opus 5.5, one […]
The post Errors in the research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
AI issues its judgment:
138 papers audited
2,035 problems found
147 serious enough to change a headline number
69% of papers have at least one
97% of major and moderate errors with a clear direction overstate the paper’s claim
And on the method:
Two independent audits of each paper. One by Claude Opus 5.5, one by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, neither seeing the other’s work. Each obtained the paper, its appendices and its replication data, recomputed the headline numbers from the authors’ own files and, where possible, from the original sources (tax statistics, national accounts, Federal Reserve and survey data), checked that cited sources say what is claimed, and probed every assumption the conclusions rest on.
Then an adjudicator. A third agent re-verified every claimed problem, tried to refute each one, discarded those that did not survive, searched for problems both auditors missed, and graded what remained by how far it undermines the paper’s own headline claim: major changes a core number materially, moderate affects secondary results or a core result modestly, minor is a presentation or arithmetic slip. Confidence is graded separately.
There is much, much more at the link, which goes through the research paper by paper, and with further sustained analyses behind the links.  The survey is both extensive and thorough.  (And I thank an anonymous MR reader for this work.)
I am not even sure what to say at this point.  We need a radical revaluation of this work, and of the associated policy arguments.  More generally, this is only a single step in the story of how AI is going to revise economic science, and indeed past research more generally.  As I stress in many of my recent talks, there will be significant gains and losses in status, with the losses often outweighing the gains.  I see this as one of those cases.

articles.title: How is AI shaping economic research?
articles.summary:
Does generative AI narrow or widen productivity gaps in research? We study the distributional effects of AI on research productivity in economics using evidence from three sources: NBER working-paper and publication records, text-based measures of LLM-assisted writing, and an original survey of 227 academic economists measuring AI use across research tasks. We first show that […]
The post How is AI shaping economic research? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Does generative AI narrow or widen productivity gaps in research? We study the distributional effects of AI on research productivity in economics using evidence from three sources: NBER working-paper and publication records, text-based measures of LLM-assisted writing, and an original survey of 227 academic economists measuring AI use across research tasks.
We first show that productivity gaps among NBER authors narrowed following ChatGPT’s release: authors without research assistants (RAs) published a larger share of papers in top-tier journals, while authors from smaller teams gained in working-paper output and publication speed.
We then use the survey to examine how individual AI use affects research productivity.
We find weak evidence that AI affects working-paper output on average, but there is substantial heterogeneity.
Triple-difference estimates show that greater AI exposure narrows the output gap between researchers with and without RAs but widens the gap between senior and junior researchers.
Selection into AI use follows a different pattern: junior researchers use AI more intensively and are more likely to use agentic tools.
Thus, these differential productivity effects reflect differences in the returns to AI rather than selection into AI use.
A model with diminishing returns to execution, increasing returns to conceptual capacity, and complementarity between the two explains how AI can alleviate disadvantages in research support while amplifying the returns to accumulated expertise.
Over time, however, early convergence may give way to divergence as execution constraints recede and AI’s conceptual capabilities improve.

That is from Tianyu Jiang, who is this year a job market candidate from the University of Michigan.  The paper is co-authored with Yuqing (Claire) Wang.

articles.title: Inequality in Equal Land
articles.summary:
Adam Nash has a good post on wealth inequality: …Every year, we pull the most recent data from the US Census on household wealth, cut by age. …invariably, the students’ initial response is a reaction to the apparent disparity in wealth between households based on age. For many students, it just doesn’t seem fair at […]
The post Inequality in Equal Land appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Adam Nash has a good post on wealth inequality:
…Every year, we pull the most recent data from the US Census on household wealth, cut by age.
…invariably, the students’ initial response is a reaction to the apparent disparity in wealth between households based on age.
For many students, it just doesn’t seem fair at first blush. Households between the ages of 65 to 69 have a median net worth that is 9.83x that of households under 35. You can almost hear their cries, “the Baby Boomers are hoarding all the wealth!”
Almost all of the graph, however, is aging! Nash considers a totally equal society called Equal Land. In Equal Land:

Everyone works from the ages of 25 to 64, retiring at 65
Everyone lives to the age of 85
Everyone makes the same amount, $100,000 per year
Everyone saves 10% of their income, every year while they work
Everyone makes 8% on their savings, every year
Everyone spends 4% of their portfolio, every year in retirement

The result is that in equal land the distribution of wealth is even more unequal by age than in our world! This is not to say all or even most inequality is explained by age. Most inequality in our world is within-age, not between-age. But when you look at an age-wealth graph specifically, almost all of what you are seeing is just age and the power of compounding.
The post Inequality in Equal Land appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

articles.title: AI hacking risks
articles.summary:
That is the topic of my latest Free Press column (now there are gift links!), here is one excerpt, noting this is a worst-case scenario not a prediction: Yet current systems are likely to prove more robust than that suggests. For one thing, they use a variety of different methods of protection, including public key […]
The post AI hacking risks appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
That is the topic of my latest Free Press column (now there are gift links!), here is one excerpt, noting this is a worst-case scenario not a prediction:
Yet current systems are likely to prove more robust than that suggests. For one thing, they use a variety of different methods of protection, including public key cryptography, AES, and cryptographic hash functions, the latter not qualifying as encryption per se. While it is possible that all could fall at the same time, that seems unlikely.
The more likely scenario, assuming this comes to pass at all, is that public key encryption would become vulnerable first, but the American economy would shift toward the more secure forms of communication, most of all those that have secure cryptographic keys already established. We would also work harder to substitute into the “post-quantum” methods of encryption that are being developed and already are being used in browsers.
The transition would be very costly, but the end result would not be total insecurity. Furthermore, today’s major financial institutions already have invested in various backup systems, including offline security methods and alternative payment-processing channels. Smaller businesses would face more serious problems of transition, although they also would be lesser targets in the first place. As for you the individual, you might have to show up in person at your bank to make a major transaction, and that requirement, imposed collectively, would strain our systems to the utmost.
A second layer of protection is that the new math techniques likely would not be available to everyone. They might require technical sophistication and a willingness to break the law in some very serious ways and also risk hacking retaliation. In addition, many math breakthroughs simply shave down the safety margins on systems, rather than breaking them altogether, and in those cases the criminals still might need a lot of computing power at considerable expense.
That situation is hardly the same as a complete and sudden “open season” on all methods of cryptography. Furthermore, some of the wrongdoers in this position, even assuming they felt they could get away with their crimes, might prefer to siphon off money slowly, rather than bring down the entire financial system, which could hurt their own net wealth as well.
A further source of protection is that the math breakthroughs might come in stages, rather than all at once. For an example from another part of math, OpenAI has proven a quasi-Riemann hypothesis, and Terry Tao told me recently that this may open the door to solving the Riemann hypothesis proper. We now have advance notice that the Riemann hypothesis may be proven (or less likely, disproven). In similar fashion, intermediate advances may signal that cryptographic protections are vulnerable. We thus would have some time to adjust…
The most likely scenarios would play out in terms of probabilities, as people deal with risk before any large-scale hacking attack would come. Right now the chance of public key cryptography breaking down is on the radar screens of a relatively small number of people. Imagine that some advances in math occur, and the more sophisticated market participants start seeing something like a 10 percent chance that some forms of encryption might be vulnerable. Perhaps without much fanfare, some people would start selling their bitcoin, or they might wire their money to more secure banks, or perhaps they would hold more gold and short the market. Some hackers would invest more in the activity, including hacks without advanced AI, under the philosophy of “harvest now, decrypt later,” pulling in classified or confidential materials that previously were not worth capturing. Overall, it would be like the early days of Covid, when major bad news was pending but only a few individuals were acting on it. That state of affairs could persist for some period of time.
In any case it would not be good.
And this: “If you have thoughts on my latest column, or questions about AI or anything else, join me for an AMA (Ask Me Anything) this week on The Free Press Forum.
Paid subscribers can submit questions now. Not a subscriber? For a limited time, you can get 20% off at thefp.com/tyler.”

articles.full_text:
This document amends the Table of TV Allotments (table) of the Federal Communications Commission's (Commission) rules by substituting VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 at Elko, Nevada in response to a petition for rulemaking filed by Reno (KENV-TV) Licensee, Inc.
(Licensee), the licensee of full power television station KENV-DT (KENV-DT or Station), Elko, Nevada.
The Media Bureau (Bureau) previously granted a petition for rulemaking submitted by the Licensee to substitute UHF channel 20 for VHF channel 10 at Elko in the table, and subsequently granted a construction permit for its new channel.
The Licensee states that it was unable to complete construction of the channel 20 facility by the deadline specified in the Station's construction permit.
The Licensee filed the instant petition to amend the table to substitute VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 and allow KENV-DT to continue to operate on channel 10 at its licensed parameters and provide uninterrupted service to viewers.
The staff engineering analysis finds that the proposal is in compliance with the Commission's principal community coverage and technical requirements, including the interference protection requirements.
In support of its channel substitution request, the Licensee filed comments reaffirming its interest and stating that it commits to promptly take any and all steps that may be necessary to effectuate the channel substitution proposed in the petition.
An individual commenter, Steven Quinn Singleton, also filed comments, which, for the reasons discussed in the Report and Order referenced below, the Bureau denied.

articles.full_text: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is publishing a final rule to update the incorporation by reference of several voluntary consensus standards in the Agency's formaldehyde standards for composite wood products regulations under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) due to the standards having been updated or superseded by the issuing organizations. These new standards primarily update test methods and product standards concerning composite wood products that use formaldehyde. EPA is also conforming these updated standards in the scope and definitional sections in the final rule and incorporating by reference a new small scale quality control chamber test method, similar to current methods already incorporated by reference. EPA is also removing one standard that was previously incorporated by reference to avoid redundancy, given that another identical, internationally recognized version of the standard is already incorporated by reference in this rule.

articles.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
articles.summary:

I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM […]
The post Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers’ results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.
From the excellent Eva Vivalt.  As I have been predicting, so much of economics (and science) is going to change, and radically.  Here is Eva’s thread on the paper.  Perhaps we should dispense with many of the more mundane inquiries, and as Eva notes: “But can we not shift to working on those projects that have particularly high uncertainty and upside potential?”
She is one of the best young economists in the world, and this stands some chance of being the most important paper of the year.

articles.title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’
articles.summary: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairsChristine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because ...
articles.full_text:
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.
Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.
She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.
Lagarde said: “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”
The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council made up of EU heads of state appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister of France, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.
She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position.”
To reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process has already started to identify my successor.” She said there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”
Macron said on Thursday that the succession at the ECB must be prepared in “an orderly and balanced way” with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action during her tenure.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”
