articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
articles.summary: Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO saysDoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDas...
articles.full_text:
DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

articles.title: US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%
articles.summary: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loomThe US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its ad...
articles.full_text:
The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.
The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment has more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
The change is in stark contrast to households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.
The consumer price index, a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.
Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.
Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”
Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.
But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.
Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment, measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

articles.summary:

The post How Tyler Cowen and Al...
articles.full_text:
From the Archives-written by ChatGPT.
Both became dramatically more confident in AI’s capabilities while remaining optimistic about its economic potential. Their differences concern how benefits arrive, how seriously to weight emerging dangers, and whether AI might possess consciousness. Cowen emphasizes institutions, bottlenecks, and geopolitical competition. Tabarrok emphasizes inexpensive intelligence, scientific discovery, and—especially in his later writing—concrete safety failures.
The dated passages below trace those changes across the public archive. Quotations are the authors’ own words, including excerpts from their columns; outside material they reproduce is identified separately.
Early views on unequal gains and abundance
Cowen’s early framework grew out of chess. On March 11, 2011, he observed that stronger computers required stronger human partners:
“The required education level — for the team’s ‘wage premium’ — is ratcheted up.”
His concern was already distributional: computers could increase productivity while changing which human skills commanded a premium. He also emphasized learning how to work with computers. What I learn from chess and computers.
Tabarrok’s April 12, 2016 argument was more explicitly reassuring:
“AI will be cheap and ownership will be widespread.”
He compared AI to an increase in the world’s supply of educated people: more intelligence produces useful ideas, and competition spreads the benefits to consumers. But his forecast of comprehensive substitution was cautious—AI becoming a perfect substitute for human intelligence could be “100 years or more” away. Will the proliferation of affordable AI decimate the middle class?
Neither position was absolute. Cowen warned in February 2017 that the Industrial Revolution involved decades of painful adjustment; historical progress did not guarantee quick wage gains. Tabarrok, in October 2019, praised the argument that mediocre automation could displace workers without creating enough additional wealth to compensate. See Cowen’s historical warning and Tabarrok’s Beware the Mediocre Robots!
Rising confidence in AI capabilities from 2020 to 2025
Cowen was already optimistic about language models in July 2020. After publishing a skeptical reader’s assessment of GPT-3, he added:
“I remain bullish, but it is always worth considering other opinions.”
That attribution matters: the skeptical arguments in the post were the reader’s, not Cowen’s. The case against the import of GPT-3, July 23, 2020.
Tabarrok’s shift toward near-term transformative AI became unmistakable by March 2, 2023:
“I never expected to witness the birth of aliens.”
Later that month, he endorsed Microsoft researchers’ description of GPT-4 as exhibiting an incomplete form of general intelligence: “They are correct.” This is a substantial acceleration from his 2016 outlook, although perfect substitution for humans and early general intelligence are different thresholds. See AGI is Coming and Baby AGI is Here, March 24, 2023.
Cowen reached an especially explicit formulation on April 16, 2025, discussing o3:
“I think it is AGI, seriously.”
But he immediately separated capability from adoption:
“It still will take us a long time to use it properly.”
His growing enthusiasm about the technology did not imply an equally dramatic forecast for immediate economic growth. o3 and AGI, is April 16th AGI day?
Economic transformation and the pace of adoption
On January 6, 2025, Tabarrok wrote:
“The intelligence revolution is going to be bigger, more impactful and more wrenching than the industrial revolution.”
This is his own concluding sentence, following a quotation from Sam Altman. The Intelligence Revolution.
Cowen’s February 23, 2025 response to rapid-takeoff expectations focused on a different constraint:
“Human bottlenecks become more important, the more productive is AI.”
Energy, regulation, organizational habits, and weak human collaborators can constrain the economic value of better models. He offered an explicitly tentative estimate of an additional half percentage point of annual growth—large when compounded, but far from an immediate economic explosion. Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow.
By September 3, 2026, Tabarrok was developing the distributional implications:
“A smaller share of a much larger economy can still mean more income for labor.”
He argued that even substantial displacement could leave aggregate labor income higher, or make compensation affordable. He explicitly acknowledged painful losses for particular workers. His high-growth calculations are scenarios, not forecasts. How Much Redistribution Will AI Require?
They also converge more than their rhetoric suggests. In May 2026, Cowen rejected mass unemployment while identifying transitional hiring problems. In August 2026, Tabarrok interpreted business-survey evidence as consistent with their shared position that AI had not yet broadly reduced employment. See Cowen, May 13, and Tabarrok, August 31.
Growing attention to safety and institutional limits
Cowen stated his central position on November 19, 2023:
“I view AI as more likely to lower than to raise net existential risks.”
His reasoning was comparative: the world already faces serious dangers, and stronger science could improve our defenses. My summary views on AI existential risk.
Tabarrok’s later writing places more weight on specific vulnerabilities. On April 8, 2026, he described:
“the worrying combination that very powerful AI’s are very vulnerable.”
He was discussing cybersecurity capabilities alongside agents’ susceptibility to manipulation. AI Risks.
On September 17, 2026, he sharpened the institutional objection to assuming that beneficial science will automatically offset dangerous capabilities:
“But faster science does not automatically mean faster defense.”
This can be read as a qualification of Cowen’s earlier optimism: defensive discoveries must pass through institutions that may move slowly. It also applies Cowen’s own bottleneck logic to safety. Pandemic Preparation is AI Safety.
Cowen nevertheless supports safeguards. In August 2026, he proposed government-overseen, industry-led safety audits. In September, he opposed restrictions on recursive improvement as impractical to enforce internationally. His position is therefore selective regulation combined with continued development. See his August 27 proposal and September 22 critique.
The September 2026 exchange about AI leaders
On September 16, 2026, Tabarrok rejected the claim that executives’ safety warnings were merely marketing or regulatory capture:
“Amodei actually believes what he’s saying.”
He did not thereby establish that the warnings or proposed policies were correct. His argument concerned sincerity and incentives. What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like.
Cowen replied the next day:
“I agree with Alex that the standard model of regulatory capture does not apply here”
But he emphasized competition for power: each executive sincerely thinks their own company should win. For Cowen, that complicates treating their warnings as disinterested policy advice. They agree that concern is sincere; they differ over which incentives best explain behavior. The correct model of AI CEO behavior, September 17, 2026.
Consciousness and Tabarrok’s warning about infant pain
On March 17, 2025, Tabarrok’s What Did We Learn From Torturing Babies? drew a moral lesson from medicine’s historical dismissal of infant pain. He described how theories about immature brains allowed physicians to discount babies’ observable distress and perform procedures without adequate anesthesia. His warning explicitly extended to judgments about animals and AI:
“If we must err, let us err on the side of compassion.”
Tabarrok’s position is stronger than mere openness to AI consciousness: he argues for moral caution under uncertainty. The analogy does not establish that AI suffers. It challenges confidence that a theory ruling out suffering is sufficient grounds to disregard possible evidence of it.
On October 14, 2025, he went further in his own commentary following an essay by Jack Clark:
“these systems are becoming self-aware”
He distinguished self-awareness from sentience, while warning against confidently dismissing the latter. His link accompanying that warning points back to the infant-pain essay, making the connection explicit. We Turned the Light On—and the AI Looked Back.
Cowen’s position is much more categorical. On August 31, 2026, he wrote:
“I am very much opposed to the view that the AIs are sentient, or might be sentient.”
He treats AI sentience as a category error, although he accepts that human-like descriptions can sometimes help predict AI behavior. Anthropomorphizing AI?
The disagreement concerns both what AI might experience and how to act when we cannot confidently know. Tabarrok’s historical analogy places greater weight on the moral cost of mistakenly denying consciousness; Cowen expresses much greater confidence that sentience is the wrong category to apply. These are their philosophical assessments, not established findings about AI consciousness.

articles.title: AI dominates human peer reviews
articles.summary:
We show that AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors. We then discuss how this result may inform journal policy choices, with concerning downsides as well as potential paths to […]
The post AI dominates human peer reviews appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
We show that AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors. We then discuss how this result may inform journal policy choices, with concerning downsides as well as potential paths to increase publication speed and quality; reduce adversarial interactions; improve the experience of editors, reviewers, authors, and readers; and advance science.
By Gary King and Steven Worthington, not even using what are now the very best models, rather based on Claude Opus 4.8.  The details of the dominance, as outlined in the paper, are striking.  It is not close.
On my Saez and Zucman post, I find it striking that some people are complaining all of a sudden.  Yet I have been offering, citing, and linking to commentary on published papers for twenty-four years now (and every single day).  Sometimes it might just be a casual offhand remark from me, whether positive or negative.  Typically this is simply taken in stride.  It is when you pull out the bazookas, and offer oodles of high-powered analytics, more astute than human referees, and combined with the ability to pursue follow-up inquiries, that people start getting worried.  Model that.
You can pick at individual criticisms from the AIs all you want, but the most damning observation is that the errors go in the ideological direction of the authors 97% of the time.  That is exactly what (the human) Phil Magness said years ago, based on an extensive canvassing of their work.  Basically we already knew that was true, and the AIs confirmed the human estimate.
On our side, we have taken steps, most of all the new MR archive, to make AI analysis of our work easier.  Soon you will be able to read on MR what the AIs think are our worst posts, respectively (Alex has prepared this).
In the meantime, I encourage the NSF, prize committees, universities, tenure committees, journals, and so on to do as many of their own AI-enabled audits as possible.  So far the world is not jumping at this opportunity.  You can model that too.

articles.title: My design Conversation with Roman Mars
articles.summary:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is part of the episode summary: Roman Mars has built one of podcasting’s great empires out of noticing things everyone else walks past. His show, 99% Invisible, has racked up over 500 million downloads telling stories about the unnoticed design choices that quietly shape how cities and […]
The post My design Conversation with Roman Mars appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is part of the episode summary:
Roman Mars has built one of podcasting’s great empires out of noticing things everyone else walks past. His show, 99% Invisible, has racked up over 500 million downloads telling stories about the unnoticed design choices that quietly shape how cities and objects work…
Tyler and Roman discuss street signs, why classic cars were so much more distinctive than today’s SUVs, Waymos, New Jersey jughandles, yellow streetlights, lane-stripe colors, why Houston keeps growing despite its lack of charm, whether any post-war American suburb is actually beautiful, the Chrysler Building’s rocky reception, brutalism done right and wrong, Central Park as an urban miracle, what Jane Jacobs got wrong, e-bike lanes, Tokyo’s bike-free transit model, the placelessness of global coffee shops, why the iPhone looks boring now, the ugliest country he’s visited, his love for Australia’s polymer notes, his soft spot for the dollar’s “locked in amber” weirdness, underground power lines, how to warn future civilizations about nuclear waste, why highway signs lie to you about speed limits, the principles of a great city flag, the Pocatello redesign saga, his own studio, why 99% Invisible works precisely because it’s audio-only, the most unusual habit behind his long productive career, and more.
Excerpt:
COWEN: Yes. One of my favorite topics, currency design. What’s your favorite currency in terms of how it looks?
MARS: Favorite? It’s like I love almost any of them with the US currency in dead last. I find things to love about them. I’ve done a story on Australian currency, which was one of the early polymer notes. I just like utility in currency. I like different sizes. I like different colors. I like the fact that they put on artists and people of note that are not founding fathers and presidents and stuff like this. I don’t know if I have a particular favorite, but I was entranced by the thoughtfulness and utility of Australian currency when I did a story about it. You could be blind and know what note you’re holding because of the size. They stand up pretty well, and they care about all kinds of things rather than just presidents and stuff.
COWEN: I loved Swiss currency pre-2021. They had Le Corbusier on, Giacometti, Honegger. In the 1980s, they had Euler on, the mathematician. Imagine putting Euler on your country’s currency.
MARS: That is a canvas that’s so available to us to represent more values than we have in the United States than just founding fathers and presidents and stuff. I think it’s just such a wasted opportunity.
COWEN: I like the dollar, though. I’m surprised you’re so negative. I like the weird esotericism: the eye, the pyramid. The design is bizarre. It announces to the world: “We’re crazy.”
MARS: There are things to love about it. I just think that its fussiness and filigree, we’re locked in, I think for important reasons, which is because the dollar is the most important currency in the world, to which all other currencies are pegged, and therefore you don’t change it lightly. You have to be very, very careful. It really locked it into amber in a way that is both beautiful to admire, but also really limits its utility as things move on, we get better things than linen-paper hybrids and especially different sizes and utility for people with different needs. I think that’s important. There’s definitely things to love about the dollar. The dollar has some charm.
COWEN: I like the arrogance of it also. A sense of we don’t need to make the denominations look so different. If you’re a foreigner, we expect you’ll come here a lot, you’ll master dollars. Maybe you use them in your home country as well. They don’t need to be different colors.
MARS: It is definitely a bold statement that you’re going to adapt to our way of being if you’re going to use the dollar, for sure.
Opinions throughout!
The post My design Conversation with Roman Mars appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

AGENCY:
Rural Housing Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Rural Housing Service (RHS or the Agency), a Rural Development (RD) agency of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), is amending the Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Program (SFHGLP) regulation to permit the financing of single family homes with income producing Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and clarify the eligibility of properties with features designed to accommodate home-based operations using non-commercial real estate features.
DATES:
This final rule is effective December 28, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stephanie Freeman, Finance & Loan Analyst, Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Division, Rural Development, U.S. Department of Agriculture, STOP 0784, Room 2250, South Agriculture Building, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20250-0784. Telephone: (314) 457-6413; or email:
stephanie.freeman@usda.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Abbreviations

CFR Code of Federal Regulations

FHLMC Freddie Mac

§ Section

Statutory Authority
The SFHGLP is authorized by Section 502(h) of the Housing Act of 1949 (42 U.S.C. 1472(h)), as amended, and implemented by 7 CFR part 3555.
( printed page 68026)
Background
RHS offers programs to develop and enhance housing and critical community infrastructure in rural areas. The Agency provides loans, grants, and loan guarantees for single and multi-family housing, childcare centers, emergency service facilities, hospitals, libraries, nursing homes, schools, and housing for agricultural workers, among other essential projects. RHS partners with non-profits, tribal governments, and state/federal agencies to provide technical assistance and supplementary financing to local communities.
Title V of the Housing Act of 1949 authorizes RHS to provide SFH loan guarantees, providing low and moderate income individuals in rural areas an opportunity to own decent, safe, and sanitary dwellings and related facilities.
To boost homeownership, the federal government has introduced new initiatives providing prospective buyers with greater flexibility to finance properties with ADUs. Growing demand for affordable housing and limited land availability in many rural communities have made financing properties with ADUs increasingly important. Homeowners can create ADUs within or attached to the primary dwelling through attic or basement conversions, building over existing structures like garages, or constructing standalone residential units.
Homeownership options remain limited for many Americans. The Agency recognizes ADUs offer multiple benefits, including expanding a community's housing supply by introducing new and innovative housing typologies of smaller scale, providing more affordable options for low- and moderate-income residents. ADUs also provide borrowers with a means to generate additional income. Together, these benefits support the broader goal of increasing affordable housing stock and promoting long-term homeownership stability.
Discussion of Public Comments
RHS published a proposed rule on March 31, 2026 [91 FR 15914] to amend the Single Family Housing Guaranteed Program (SFHGLP) regulation at 7 CFR part 3555. RHS received comments from 28 respondents, including individuals, interested parties, and associations. One comment received was not applicable to the contents of the rule.
The following summary presents the relevant comments:
Public Comment:
Nineteen respondents supported the proposed rule, stating it would accommodate more buyers in rural America.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the support and has determined no action is required.
Public Comment:
Four respondents expressed support for the proposed rule but recommended expanding eligibility to include small home-based operations with commercial real estate features, as well as clarifying ADU eligibility and income.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments. While the rule amends 7 CFR 3555.102(c) to permit properties with home-based businesses, 7 CFR 3555.102(b) will continue to prohibit purchasing or improving property principally used for income-producing purposes to ensure financed properties remain primarily residential. Regarding income, 7 CFR 3555.152(a)(3) states lenders may not use income to calculate an applicant's ratios if they cannot verify the source, if the income is not stable, or if it is unlikely to continue. The Agency determined potential income from an ADU falls into this category and will not include it in income calculations.
Public Comment:
One respondent agreed the proposal would expand housing opportunities in rural America but raised concerns about consistent enforcement, broader policy implications, and RHS' statutory authority.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments. The changes fall within the statutory authority granted by the Housing Act of 1949 (42 U.S.C. 1471et seq.), as amended. RHS recognizes ADUs can increase housing supply, offer additional affordable housing options, and support low- and moderate-income households through the receipt of potential supplemental income. These benefits support RHS' rationale for expanding affordable housing opportunities and promoting long-term homeownership stability.
Public Comment:
One respondent expressed support for the proposal and recommended addressing ADU income and room rent income in the final rule.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments and recognizes rental income from an ADU can support homeowner financial stability. However, 7 CFR 3555.152(a)(3) states lenders may not use income to calculate an applicant's ratios if they cannot verify the source, if the income is not stable, or if it is unlikely to continue. The Agency determined potential income from an ADU falls into this category and will not include it in income calculations.
Public Comment:
Two respondents expressed support and offered additional suggestions regarding homebuyer education, home-based operations, renovation funding at purchase, expanding the ADU definition to include non-income producing ADUs, and establishing more precise property standards.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates these comments and agrees supporting home-based operations is important. As clarified through this rule, properties accommodating a home-based operation are eligible. articles.title: How Harsh Vardhan Goenka became founding engineer #1 at Kalpa Labs
articles.summary: From ICPC World Finals to competitive programming clubs to building generalist audio models as the first engineer at a YC startup.
articles.full_text:
Before Harsh Vardhan Goenka joined Kalpa Labs, he was at Rubrik Inc.
, where he helped build Rubrik Cloud Vault from its early days and rewrote the company's testing infrastructure so that test suites that took hours ran in minutes.
He'd always gravitated toward small teams and hard problems — competitive programming took him to the ICPC World Finals, and engineering at scale brought him to Rubrik.
But the pull toward something smaller, scrappier, and more frontier kept growing.
When his former college seniors founded Kalpa Labs (YC F25), a company building generalist audio models, the timing finally clicked.
An 11 PM interview on a spare Windows laptopHarsh knew the Kalpa Labs founders, Prashant and Gautam, from undergrad, where they'd co-founded a competitive programming club and spent hours debating algorithmic and mathematical problems.
When Prashant first offered him a role, Harsh passed.
But conversations continued, and four months later, he was looking for a change.
Prashant asked if he'd like to interview for an open position.
"It was roughly 11 PM and all I had was a spare Windows laptop," Harsh says.
"I ended up giving a 3 hour long interview, where I was given a problem around file system.
I hadn't felt the same rush in the last few months, what I felt during that interview.
" He pauses.
"All I feel it is God's plan.
"What Kalpa Labs is building — and why it mattersKalpa Labs is building generalist audio models.
The vision is that audio hasn't had its GPT-3 moment yet.
Rather than being limited to text-to-speech, the team wants one model that can voice a podcast from a script, sing a song in your voice, or generate audio that follows a detailed text prompt describing mood and tone.
Some of those capabilities are already unlocked.
The coolest thing Harsh says he's built? "A voice model that sounds like human.
Not kidding.
"From infra engineer to ML researcher in five monthsHarsh joined as Founding Engineer and Researcher, initially focused on ML infrastructure and software problems.
But from day one, his founders pushed him toward ML research — a domain where he had no prior expertise.
"It has not always felt the best because there were times where I was clueless," he says.
But that discomfort is part of the Kalpa Labs philosophy: everyone on the team is expected to stretch into unfamiliar territory.
The thinking is that when someone builds expertise in a new domain, they bring a fresh perspective to hard problems that specialists might miss.
For Harsh, being an early engineer means refusing to limit yourself to engineering.
"Have a great amount of ownership for the product — own different verticals, be it design, product workflows, anything that can help your product and user experience better.
In this whole journey we somehow naturally push our limits that we have been limiting ourselves to.
"Late nights, launch videos, and the cosine curve of startup lifeOne of his favorite moments had nothing to do with code.
Three people in a room, brainstorming the script for their first launch video, recording takes, spending the night editing and hiding jokes in the final cut.
"There were lot of cuts that didn't make it in the final video but was fun.
"Working directly with the founders means discussing product direction, roadmap, hiring, and sales — and also game nights and house parties.
Harsh appreciates that Prashant and Gautam are open about their own mistakes, talking through what went wrong and how to avoid it next time.
"This removes an anxiety, fear, impostor syndrome within me that what if I end up making a huge mistake in anything I am working on.
"He describes the emotional arc of startup life as a cosine curve: weeks where everything feels stuck, then a breakthrough that sends a dopamine rush through the team.
"You need to recall all your wins and have the faith in each other that you will iterate and come out better.
"How Harsh evaluates a startup — and who should join oneWhen someone asks how to evaluate a startup before saying yes, Harsh has a clear hierarchy:Who is on the team? — the most important factor.
What are we building?How much runway do we have?Harsh sees himself starting a company of his own someday, and the founders actively mentor him toward that.
But for now, the problem at Kalpa Labs is too exciting to leave.
If you're an engineer who thrives on small teams, isn't afraid to be clueless for a while, and wants to help build generalist audio models at the frontier — Kalpa Labs is hiring.

articles.title: How Dylan Anderson became founding engineer at Adam
articles.summary: Dylan left Minnesota for San Francisco to build AI agents for CAD software as the first engineer at Adam (W25).
articles.full_text:
Dylan Anderson was a software engineer at, in his words, "some random place in Minnesota.
" Then a friend-of-a-friend connection changed everything.
A roommate of Adam's founders was asked if he knew any cracked engineers.
Dylan's name came up.
He did a work trial, moved to San Francisco, and became the first engineer at Adam (W25), a company building AI agents for CAD software.
Why he said yesDylan didn't need a long pitch.
During the work trial, he noticed two things right away: the founders gave him real freedom and real trust from day one, and there was almost no friction in how the team worked together.
"I recognized the talents of the founders that would make this work really well, each person complementing my own weaknesses and I complementing theirs," he says.
He also saw clear, relentless drive from everyone involved.
The move to SF was something he'd wanted anyway — to be at the center of things — and Adam gave him a reason to actually do it.
Building the engine, not fitting into oneAs engineer number one, Dylan touches pretty much everything.
The codebase has been rewritten multiple times.
The systems in place are systems he built, shaped to his preferences and workflow.
"If I want to build something to improve my life I do it, if something bothers me I fix it," he says.
He draws a sharp contrast with big-company engineering: "At a big company you're like a part of an engine, like an interchangeable piece that fits into a preexisting slot, you're an input to a function, whereas at Adam you're the one building the engine, you are the one molding everything to fit you.
"His coolest build so far: adam.
new.
Work as identity — without the burnout framingDylan is careful to say this isn't about bad work-life balance.
It's that the boundary between work and life is blurred in a way that feels right.
"I'm working on my passion, and I'm working with people that share the same passion," he says.
The founders aren't just coworkers — they're some of his closest friends.
That closeness raises the stakes on communication and teamwork, but it also means he cares more deeply about his craft than he ever could at a job he could mentally disconnect from.
"It means my work is part of my identity in a more readily available way.
"As Adam grows, Dylan expects his role to expand into mentorship and leadership.
For now, the biggest shift has been internal: he's become more intentional, more value-driven.
"Each of my actions directly impacts the performance of the company.
Gone are the days of tinkering with something for purely academic purposes.
Now I think about the value each thing I build provides.
"His toolsAI coding: Claude Code and CodexEditor: Zed (sometimes)Advice for anyone considering an early startup roleDylan's guidance is blunt: "Think about value deeply.
Don't join a startup that's a tarpit idea.
If you join and you put a lot of work into something that's a shitty idea, you'll hate everything you do and develop passive nihilism.
"The right person for a role like this is someone who wants to own everything they build, cares about the problem more than the title, and is ready to let the work become a genuine part of who they are.
If that sounds like you, Adam is hiring.

articles.title: How Andrew HunzekerHesed became Employee #1 at 10x Science
articles.summary: A principal engineer left consumer-scale software to build AI-native scientific analysis tools as the founding engineer at 10x Science.
articles.full_text:
Andrew HunzekerHesed spent years building software seen by millions of people — food delivery logistics, CPG stocking at Walmart, video streaming at Major League Baseball, and most recently serving as Principal Engineer at Grindr.
The work was fun and visible, but the general software development lifecycle was starting to look the same everywhere: "Exec to Design to PM to Engineer, with ever-increasing velocity due to AI.
" Then he met the founders of 10x Science (W26) at a talent summit, and something shifted.
A conversation that didn't sound like every other one in tech10x Science creates AI-native software for scientific data analysis, currently focused on proteomics and drug discovery with plans to expand across the life sciences.
But what drew Andrew in wasn't a pitch deck.
It was how the founders talked.
"I talked to David about the beauty of math and working from first principles, and Vishnu talked about music, the science of sound, and how inefficient generative AI can be," he says.
"It had been years since I had talked to people in the technology space who were not completely AI-pilled and were instead talking about how the principles behind AI can be used to create solutions instead of merely wrapping the commercial foundation models.
"The interview process was rigorous — a multi-day work trial where Andrew had full access to the founders and they had access to him.
When it ended, he still wanted to keep working on the problem they had given him "because it was so intriguing and their passion for the work so infectious.
"All hands on deck, even hands that just showed upAndrew's first week at 10x Science tested whether the startup energy was real.
An opportunity came up to pitch a top-ten pharma company on a solution to a problem the team didn't even know existed.
They had three days to bring Andrew up to speed on the problem space, design a solution, build it, and package it for a Friday demo.
"The thing we built has become a cornerstone in our tooling and has had applications outside of the initial pitch session," he says.
"Other places I have worked would have pushed my start date back in order to just handle it on their own, but at a startup it is all hands on deck, even if those hands just showed up.
"Finding The Thing, not just scaling the thingFor Andrew, being Employee #1 means something specific.
It's not about scaling challenges — he's quick to point out that "there are thousands of ex-FAANG engineers who can help your company scale.
" What excites him is the earlier, harder phase: "Figuring out not the technical problems associated with the thing, but the actual thing itself.
Do you have a hand in making the thing, or just in the scaling of the thing? The Thing, that is what being early means to me.
"That discovery work has taken him places a big-company engineering role never would.
At 10x Science, his name has appeared on posters presented at scientific symposiums, and he has submitted work to the American Chemical Society.
The company is now transitioning from exploratory research to locking down features for paying customers, which Andrew calls "really exciting.
" His tools are deliberately simple — the command line, VS Code, and whichever AI model "is the most SOTA that week.
" He bounces between providers and avoids getting sucked into prompt-tweaking rituals.
Who should joinAndrew's advice for anyone considering an early-stage role is direct:"Let your ego go, roll up your sleeves, and help out.
""Will you get rich? Probably not.
Will you gain more experience in six months than you can in years at a big company? Yes.
""Life is too short to worry too much about these things, and life is too long to live with regret.
"If you want to work with smart people on hard scientific problems, ship to real customers in the life sciences, and have the agency to build what needs to be built in the best way you know how — 10x Science is hiring.

articles.title: How Max Friedlander became founding operations at Petrarch
articles.summary: A math major who turned down safe internships to lead high-stakes deals at a YC S26 startup supplying data for frontier AI labs.
articles.full_text:
Max Friedlander was building voice agents for service businesses when a LinkedIn message changed his trajectory.
Ian, one of the founders of Petrarch, reached out to pick his brain about voice AI data.
Max told them the idea wouldn't work.
They kept talking anyway.
When the team mentioned they had a YC interview coming up, Max asked them to keep him posted.
A few weeks later, they got in — and a couple days after that, they asked if he wanted to be an intern.
"Just based on the vibes from the call we had before," Max says.
He was employee number five.
He's 20 years old, an applied mathematics major at Middlebury College, and he does sales at Petrarch, a YC S26 company that supplies data for frontier AI labs.
Why he said yesMax had tried starting his own ventures before and been stood up at the last minute for other opportunities.
He had traditional internship offers on the table — SDR and BD roles at bigger companies — but they felt wrong.
"What felt safe began to feel suffocating and limiting," he says.
"I wanted to be pushed and flexible, seeing what I could learn.
"The deciding factor was the founders themselves.
They were driven and ambitious, but also people he'd want to hang out with outside of work.
"When it comes to evaluating whether the company is the right choice, it's more of a gut feeling than anything else, especially when it comes to people.
"Leading deals with complete autonomyWithin his first months, Max was leading his own deals and negotiating high-stakes contracts — the kind of responsibility that wouldn't come for years at a large company.
He handles legal review, sales, and communication with all parties on his own.
The reality is less glamorous than it sounds.
One night, the team believed they had a multiple five-figure deal secured.
Everything fell apart at the last minute.
Max had to restructure the entire deal within 36 hours and secure three signatures.
"It was challenging, but it was also incredibly rewarding to have such autonomy and the freedom to make my own decisions," he says.
He's also built tools to support his work — a scraper and harness to find obscure leads and automate outreach so prospects book directly into his calendar.
His stack includes Claude Code in the terminal, Apollo, and VS Code.
The highs and lows are realMax is candid about what startup life actually feels like.
"It's really hard to be level," he says.
"The highs and lows are emotionally jarring, a lot more than any other type of job I have worked in, for better or worse.
"What surprised him most was how much his strategic ideas mattered.
The founders listen.
There are no strange dynamics around seniority — everyone on the team is the same age, and Max describes the culture as one where people can be serious when they need to be but still crack jokes and be themselves.
"In a startup you spend a ton of time with the team, even more than with a partner or significant other," he says.
"That's key to success.
"The experience has changed him in a specific way: confidence.
"The more you do, the less afraid you are to act like a founder.
"Who would thrive hereMax plans to start his own company one day.
For now, he has a clear message for anyone weighing whether to join a startup early:"It's hard, rewarding, fast, and you will act like a founder more than an employee.
You need to be a fast learner and super curious.
It will ultimately condition you to be a thinker, not just a worker.
"If you want autonomy over real deals, a team that treats you like a co-founder, and a front-row seat to the AI data business, Petrarch is hiring.

articles.title: How David Mount became employee #2 (for the second time) at 10x Science
articles.summary: A veteran engineer finds his next act helping scientists discover cures, one amino acid at a time, at YC W26 startup 10x Science.
articles.full_text:
David Mount has started four companies, served as CTO, watched funding dry up, and built a passion project about nuclear energy called Atomic Ambitions.
When his previous startup, Chinchill.
AI, ran out of money, he signed up on YC's Work at a Startup.
Two weeks later, a founder from 10x Science reached out — someone who had actually taken the time to experience Atomic Ambitions.
That detail mattered.
10x Science (W26) uses AI to process scientific data and unlock bio-chemical discovery, with work already proven in cellular-scale advances across medicine, biotech, and pharmacology.
A work trial that felt like a final examThe interviews clicked, and Mount was invited for a two-day, on-site work trial.
The problem he was given to solve was, in his words, "more than a stretch.
" After a day of research and design, he spent the night cramming proteomics, deep AI theory, and new frameworks in a proprietary application.
On the second day, he explained to Codex what to build and cranked away until time was up.
"I felt like I was back at college going for as much partial credit as I could get, while having to face the fact that I hadn't quite measured up," he says.
"Or had I? Perhaps the best measure comes from a challenge that pushes someone to the limit.
"Full stack, zero delegationMount is employee number two — a position he has held before at another company, which earns him the self-appointed title of "Elder Statesman.
" At a big company, he says, he would be a VP or CTO: lots of responsibility, all delegation, no hands-on action.
At 10x Science, he works directly on anything and everything:Full-stack development, mostly Rust and Vue.
jsZero-to-one features and rapid improvementsAgent orchestrationBenchmark runners and a showcase for newcomers who want to run scientific analysis routines in isolation and learn the associated science and mathThe build process itselfHe is still on a steep learning curve and says one of his coolest accomplishments so far is learning to identify the twenty amino acids found in humans.
"Neat," he adds, without irony.
Why this company, why nowMount evaluated 10x Science the way he evaluates any opportunity — with a short checklist:Is this company helping humanity?Are the people smart, upbeat, driven, friendly?Is the product idea real enough? Is the timing favorable? Is the field green and open?Do they like me?"The founders made it easy.
Everything they said checked the boxes for me.
Their rigorous yet compassionate evaluation of me sealed the deal.
"He describes the founders' backgrounds as uncommonly varied — one from the Bahamas, one a product of Silicon Valley, one from North Carolina, all converging in a research lab at Stanford.
Their first hire was a circus performer before jumping into software.
"10x Science is assembling quite the crew for this grand adventure.
Real diversity.
"Working with the foundersMount calls the experience of working directly with the founders "amazing.
" They are open, visionary, and productive.
"Assignments feel more like opportunities.
We get all of the rope we need along with a safety harness, the sense that nothing can go too far off of the rails.
We're building a warp drive, so to speak.
"His setup reflects the company's willingness to invest in its engineers: a top-of-the-line MacBook Pro, a Keychron Q1 Max keyboard ("for that extra clicky-clacky typing"), an ultrawide monitor, and unrestricted access to Claude, Codex, and whatever models help maximize leverage.
Who would thrive hereMount has been through a dozen startups.
He has no illusions.
His advice for anyone considering an early role: "Learn to be okay with ambiguity.
Forget about work-life balance.
Work in bursts.
Take breaks as needed.
Stay fluid.
Try ideas quickly.
Shed whatever is not working.
Polish nothing.
Despair leads to inspiration.
Enjoy the ride.
"If you want to help scientists searching for cures, are comfortable building across the entire stack, and can stomach a two-day work trial that might keep you up studying proteomics — 10x Science is hiring.

articles.title: How Varsha Parthasarathy became engineer #1 at Flex — solving a problem she'd experienced
articles.summary: From Lyft's self-driving division to fixing HSA/FSA payments, Varsha joined Flex as its first engineer and built from scratch.
articles.full_text:
When Varsha Parthasarathy was pregnant, she needed a letter from her doctor's office just to use her own HSA money on pregnancy-related expenses.
Everything was already in her chart.
She still had to send her husband or her sibling to the admin office to chase down the paperwork.
Four months after her first kid was born, running on very little sleep and definitely not planning a career move, she sat down with her former Lyft colleague Miguel — one of the cofounders of Flex (S23) — to work together for a week in San Francisco.
By the end of that week, she was in.
Flex helps businesses accept HSA and FSA payments, so people can use their pre-tax health dollars on products and services they're already buying.
It plugs into a merchant's existing checkout and shows up as another way to pay, like Klarna or Google Pay.
From self-driving cars to healthcare paymentsBefore Flex, Varsha worked at Lyft's self-driving division on the autonomy side — data annotation pipelines, supervised metrics, sensor data stores, offline ground-truth perception.
She also spent a couple of years as an engineering manager there, which taught her that the people matter the most.
She already knew Miguel as a coworker.
Then Sam, Flex's other cofounder, reached out as a reference call that turned into something much longer.
"I came away really liking Sam," she says.
But she also knew that working with someone at a big company is different from building something from scratch with a handful of people.
So she tested it: a week side by side, watching how Miguel thought through problems and made decisions.
"By the end of that week, I just knew these were people I wanted to build with.
"What being engineer #1 actually looks likeVarsha was Flex's first engineer.
She doesn't have a formal title.
If pressed, she describes herself as "the engineer who also does support, analyzes queue failures and metrics, and every now and then jumps on a sales call or helps onboard a merchant.
"She still remembers the company's first Thanksgiving.
She was on call for both engineering and support — answering questions from customers and merchants having trouble checking out while simultaneously chasing down a decimal computation bug.
"In that one weekend, I touched more parts of the product than I would have in months at a big company, and I loved every bit of it.
"Sales calls, merchant onboarding, content pipelines, marketing compliance — none of it was in her job description.
None of it existed before she did it.
A Slack bot that became Flex's first line of triageOn-call comes around often on a small engineering team, and Varsha wanted to spend less time on support and more time building.
So she started writing small bots.
One was a Slack bot that helped her figure out what was going on when a payment failed.
Over time, it grew into the Flex Investigator.
Give it an order number or a customer email, and it traces what happened across Flex's systems in about fifteen seconds — something that used to take around twenty minutes.
Today it's the team's first line of on-call triage.
Nobody had to sign off on it first.
"Sam and Miguel trust us to go build what the team needs, and we deliver.
"She also built a personal agentic bot that lives behind a Slack emoji: an agent that listens for events, finds answers to questions people ask her, and keeps working around the clock, even pushing PRs.
On the tools side, she reaches for Claude Code for implementation, Codex for brainstorming and planning, and a personal finance bot she built and named Paisa Bot — paisa means money in her language — to track markets and think through investing strategies.
Founders who are "very human"Varsha says anyone on the team can go to Sam and Miguel with uncomfortable or awkward questions, directly, and they actually want that.
"It goes both ways.
They've given the team a lot of trust, and we trust them right back.
Whenever those questions come up, there's always some action that comes out of it.
It never just ends with a conversation.
"What surprised her most about startup life: she never felt like she had to choose between work and her kid.
"And the founders — I didn't expect them to be this fun and chill.
They're very human, and that makes them so easy to work with.
"Who would thrive hereVarsha's advice is specific:If you enjoy solving problems across different domains and don't have much ego about which problems you work on, a startup is a great space for you.
Pick a company where you truly believe in the mission.
"There aren't many companies working where payments and healthcare meet, and building something that keeps getting better for both customers and merchants is far from easy.
There are still so many hard problems left to solve, and that's exactly the kind of environment I enjoy.
"

articles.title: How Sherif Amer went from electronics engineer to employee #1 at Indemni
articles.summary: A layoff, two years of travel, and a self-taught pivot to software led Sherif Amer to become the founding engineer at Indemni.
articles.full_text:
Before he ever wrote a line of code for a startup, Sherif Amer was designing embedded systems and verifying mixed-signal chips at Infineon.
Then an unexpected layoff changed his trajectory.
Rather than jumping back into semiconductors, he spent two and a half years traveling the world, teaching himself software engineering, and building his own product — a project called Roamies.
That winding path eventually brought him to Indemni (W24), a San Francisco startup that combines driver verification, carrier intelligence, and real-time shipment monitoring to help freight brokers detect fraud and move loads with confidence.
Sherif was employee #1.
From hardware to founding engineerSherif's official title is Founding Engineer, but he describes himself as "a product-minded engineer who happens to write a lot of code.
" His background in electronics gave him a deep instinct for understanding how things work from the ground up — an instinct he now applies to software architecture, product design, and everything in between.
When he evaluated Indemni before saying yes, he wasn't chasing a title.
"I cared less about titles and more about the people I'd work with, the problems we'd solve, and how much ownership I'd have," he says.
He wanted founders who welcomed technical disagreements and trusted engineers to contribute beyond writing code.
He found that.
Building the infrastructure from scratchSherif designed and built much of Indemni's asynchronous processing and notification infrastructure — Redis Streams consumers, message recovery, concurrency controls, rate limiting, and delivery.
He's also built out the verification infrastructure, connecting external identity providers, orchestrating multi-step workflows, and designing how the company processes and analyzes verification results.
"Rather than automatically reaching for a managed cloud service for every problem, I got to evaluate the trade-offs and build solutions that made sense for our scale and needs," he says.
The range is wide: one day it's distributed systems and reliability, the next it's database models, analytics dashboards, or a customer-facing feature.
"And when something breaks, there's no mysterious infrastructure team to hand it off to.
That's usually my problem too.
"One project he's especially proud of: building a job scheduler by extending Indemni's existing Redis Streams infrastructure.
He used an AI coding agent as a collaborator, providing architectural context and constraints while delegating implementation.
What made it satisfying wasn't that AI wrote the code — it was that he could approach the problem as an architect, choosing the technologies, defining the trade-offs, and reviewing the result.
Autonomy, accountability, and a lot of rope"A lot of rope!" is how Sherif describes the working relationship with Indemni's founders.
He's not expected to just agree with an idea and go implement it.
"We challenge each other, debate approaches, and sometimes disagree quite strongly, but there's always room for an honest conversation.
" Those conversations aren't limited to engineering — he can question product decisions, suggest new directions, or flag opportunities the team hasn't considered.
As Indemni has grown and more engineers have joined, Sherif's role has shifted.
He now spends more time on architecture, establishing engineering guidelines and code quality standards, and mentoring newer team members.
"One of the most rewarding changes has been seeing those engineers become increasingly independent," he says.
"They now make solid technical decisions and ship quality work without needing my input at every step.
"What surprised him mostComing from a large semiconductor company with layers of review and clearly defined responsibilities, Sherif was struck by how much startup life revolves around making decisions with incomplete information.
"You have to be comfortable making reasonable decisions, moving quickly, and adjusting as you learn more," he says.
"I've come to appreciate that a lot.
"He was also surprised by how much trust the founders placed in him — not just over engineering, but over product direction and company decisions.
"I expected to have ownership as a founding engineer, but I didn't necessarily expect to have such a strong voice in decisions beyond engineering.
"Who would thrive hereSherif's advice for anyone considering an early-stage role is direct: be honest with yourself about what you want.
The work is rewarding, but only if you're comfortable with uncertainty and figuring things out without a guide.
You won't always have perfect requirements or established processes.
You might design a system in the morning, implement it in the afternoon, and troubleshoot it in production the next day.
You'll get exposure to parts of engineering and business that might take years to experience at a larger company.
If that sounds like the job you've been looking for, Indemni is hiring.

articles.title: Better Incentives, More Kidneys, More Lives
articles.summary:
The organ procurement system has long been a miasma of inefficient monopoly providers. In 2024 I quoted some shocking facts from a great Statecraft interview with Jennifer Erickson and Greg Segal: “Organs are literally lost and damaged in transit every single week. The OPTN contractor is 15 times more likely to lose or damage an organ in […]
The post Better Incentives, More Kidneys, More Lives appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
The organ procurement system has long been a miasma of inefficient monopoly providers. In 2024 I quoted some shocking facts from a great Statecraft interview with Jennifer Erickson and Greg Segal:
“Organs are literally lost and damaged in transit every single week. The OPTN contractor is 15 times more likely to lose or damage an organ in transit than an airline is a suitcase.”
Organs are not GPS-tracked!
“In an era when consumers can precisely monitor a FedEx package or a DoorDash dinner delivery, there are no requirements to track shipments of organs in real time — or to assess how many may be damaged or lost in transit.
“If Amazon can figure out when your paper towels and your dog food is going to arrive within 20 to 30 minutes, it certainly should be reasonable that we ought to track lifesaving organs, which are in chronic shortage,” Axelrod said.
Here’s one more astounding statistics:
“Seventeen percent of kidneys are offered to at least one deceased person before they are transplanted….”
Did you get that? The tracking system for patients is so dysfunctional that 17% of kidneys are offered to patients who are already dead–thus creating delays and missed opportunities.
Fortunately, even then there were changes in the works. In 2019 President Trump issued Executive Order 13879 to improve the performance of OPOs with better incentives and to allow living donors to recover more of their costs. The government being what it is, it has taken years to implement some of the new rules and enforcement of the  OPO performance measures was deferred to 2026-2027. Nevertheless, there have been improvements. For example, many OPOs now GPS-track kidney transfers. And a new report estimates there have been significant gains from the changes.

The Advancing American Kidney Health initiative was launched by President Donald Trump via Executive Order 13879 on July 10, 2019. In this Data Point, we estimate the range of increased growth in transplants that might be attributed to the policies launched through the Executive order and the economic value of that increased growth.
The estimated impacts of the Executive Order (EO) range from a conservative 1,055 additional transplants annually to an upper estimate of 2,110 additional transplants. The range reflects variation in the counterfactuals used to compare with post-2019 transplant growth.
Under the conservative-case scenario, the policy is estimated to be associated with approximately 23,214 additional kidney transplants between 2019 and 2040, generating about 147,410 life-years gained and 21,821 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained. Under the optimistic-case scenario, the policy is estimated to be associated with approximately 46,428 additional kidney transplants between 2019 and 2040, generating about 294,819 life-years gained and 43,643 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained.

The biggest and most consequential change would be to allow payment to living organ donors. The End Kidney Deaths Act, H.R. 2687, proposes a $50,000 refundable tax credit over five years for qualifying nondirected living kidney donors. The act has bipartisan support. Because dialysis is so expensive—and the federal government pays for much of it through Medicare’s special kidney-failure entitlement—the Act could save taxpayers money as well as saving lives.
Hat tip: The indefatigable Elaine Perlman.
The post Better Incentives, More Kidneys, More Lives appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

articles.title: Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll finds
articles.summary: Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday AmericansGovernment corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own ...
articles.full_text:
Government corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.
Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem, according to the survey.
Three-quarters (76%) of voters said that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. Voters were more likely to say that government corruption (65%) is more concerning than corporate power (29%). Just under 10% said that neither concerns them.
The rising cost of living is still expected to drive the election, with 36% of voters saying it is the single most important issue to how they plan to vote in the midterms. But in a slate of other issues including immigration, housing costs, abortion, crime and safety and AI, corruption was the next top issue.
The results come after nearly two years of Donald Trump’s second term, where the president has both figuratively and literally reshaped Washington.
The president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make way for a $400m ballroom – $335m of which he said is coming from private donors, including companies such as Apple and Nvidia. The federal government is down more than 420,000 workers after Elon Musk was given the power to introduce huge jobs cuts after donating nearly $300m to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Meanwhile, Trump’s sons are running the family’s lucrative cryptocurrency business that has made Trump $1bn since returning to the White House. And Trump himself accepted a $400m private jet as a gift from the Qatari royal family.
These actions have not gone unnoticed. Voters in the Harris poll were twice as likely to say that Republicans have a bigger corruption problem than Democrats. Forty per cent of voters, including 29% of Republicans, said the GOP has a bigger corruption problem. A third (32%) of voters said that both parties have the problem equally, while 21% said that Democrats have the bigger problem.
Independents, whose votes will be key in swing races across the country, were much more likely to say that Republicans have more of a corruption problem, with 34% saying that Republicans have the bigger issue and 13% pointing to Democrats. Most Independents (42%) said that both parties share the problem equally.
The economy as experienced by everyday Americans has been vastly different from the portrait painted by Wall Street. The stock market has been soaring on the back of never-ending AI spending. In early October, both the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq stock indices hit record highs.
The gains have been a boon for a relatively small group of Americans. Americans in the top 1% of wealth own half of the stock market while the bottom 50% own just over 1% of the market.
Armed with more funds than ever, America’s wealthiest people have been driving even more donations into elections. After the supreme court’s 2010 Citizens United case removed limits on campaign contributions, each election year has brought in new records of cash. The midterms have already cost $11.2bn in ads, according to NBC News, the most ever for a midterm cycle.
A chunk of these donations are coming from the ultra-rich. Just 40 donors have already contributed $2.5bn to races this year, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Last week, billionaire Michael Bloomberg announced he was contributing $80m in last-minute funding for Democratic candidates, while Donald Trump said his political action committee was contributing a total of $400m to Republicans.
For everyday Americans, this flood of cash has changed the motivations of elected officials, who many believe will ultimately prioritize themselves and their donors over their constituents. A majority of voters (78%) in the Harris poll agreed that “elected officials care more about enriching themselves than helping people like me”.
“Government corruption has shot up to become the second most important issue in the midterms after cost of living. Americans are triggered by leaders they now see as both responsible for and profiting off their growing economic hardship,” said John Gerzema, CEO of Harris Poll.
Regardless of who ends up controlling Congress after the midterms, voters across the political spectrum are expecting solutions to address the ongoing affordability crisis that is affecting their lives.
Out of a slate of policies to address the cost of living, a third (32%) of voters said that there should be limits on the influence of companies and lobbyists on government decisions. The second most popular policy was removing tariffs (29%), followed by limiting how much companies raise prices on goods (24%).
On Tuesday, voters in California will decide on a ballot measure that could place a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires in the state. Tech billionaires have been spending an estimated $1m a day, altogether more than $340m, to fight the measure. Half (50%) of voters in the new poll, including 56% of independents, said that billionaires do not pay their fair share of taxes. Just 28% of Republicans said the same.
Some in corporate America are catching on to the discontent. Last week, the United Airlines CEO, Scott Kirby, said in an interview that he supports a national wealth tax, a comment that got him backlash from some Republicans.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 22 October to 24 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 2,065 US adults, among whom 1,481 are likely to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.

articles.title: Are there too many misdemeanor convictions?
articles.summary:
Maybe so: Misdemeanors account for three-quarters of criminal cases filed annually in the United States, yet causal evidence on the impacts of misdemeanor conviction is scarce. We combine administrative and survey data to provide novel evidence of how misdemeanor conviction affects the socioeconomic outcomes of defendants and their families. Using data on nearly seven million […]
The post Are there too many misdemeanor convictions? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Maybe so:
Misdemeanors account for three-quarters of criminal cases filed annually in the United States, yet causal evidence on the impacts of misdemeanor conviction is scarce. We combine administrative and survey data to provide novel evidence of how misdemeanor conviction affects the socioeconomic outcomes of defendants and their families. Using data on nearly seven million defendants from 11 states, we characterize the types of people involved with the misdemeanor system. We estimate causal impacts of a conviction relative to a charge using seven county reforms that sharply reduced conviction rates. Regression discontinuity design estimates yield precise null average effects of the reforms on criminal and labor market outcomes. Defendants dismissed by the reform are unlikely to re-offend if dismissed, but also unlikely to be harmed by conviction—marginal defendants are older and more likely to have been charged with minor crimes than the average defendant. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that conviction harms young and first-time defendants, implying that interventions targeting dismissal toward these groups would be beneficial. Finally, our causal estimates imply a negative Marginal Value of Public Funds of misdemeanor conviction, even under plausible estimates of general deterrence effects.
That is from recent research by Nikhil Rao and James Reeves, note that Rao is this year on the job market from University of Michigan.

The post Chronicle of Higher Education interviews me on AI and education appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Scott Carlson did the work (gated, but free with registration), here is one excerpt:
Cowen: …Another proposal I’ve made is that schools should let people do one class, only one class, AI-only — no professor, except a professor grades at the end. The professor grades not answers to an exam but the workflow of how the student used AI to learn the Glorious Revolution, or the Civil War, or whatever the student learned. Eventually, another AI will grade your AI log. But let’s start today with a professor, and try this for one class. I’m not sure how it will go. But especially for small schools that don’t offer that many classes, a student now can create a class in literally everything.
If it’s successful, let them try two classes. I think the students doing this on their own are more likely to figure out how to blend AI and education than we would from a distance with some kind of centralized vision. Let them experiment.
Carlson: Students should be leading the change at colleges and universities?
Cowen: Absolutely. Students know more about AI than their professors do. Some of this comes from cheating, which is unfortunate. But the notion that the professors teach the students AI — I wish. It’s not always possible. You could imagine setting up a class where the students teach the professors AI, and we give the students credit for teaching. I’m half joking, but it’s not, in fact, a crazy idea. We need to experiment along a number of fronts. I’m quite convinced no one knows how to do this. It hasn’t been done before. So again, just one class. In general, schools hate this idea. They see it as opening the door to rendering some professors obsolete.
And this:
Carlson: There are a number of students who are deeply opposed to AI. What place do they have in this university that you’re thinking about?
Cowen: I would love to have different schools with different policies. If some universities try to ban AI altogether, that’s great. Let the competitive process operate. Personally, I would bet against those schools. For a long time, I’ve been worried that within a given tier of school — big state school, community college, Ivy League — there’s not enough diversity. AI policies will force a kind of diversity on us. So I’m all for no-AI schools, even though I would not go to one.
Recommended.
The post Chronicle of Higher Education interviews me on AI and education appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
